articles.title: [OPINION] Twilight time for the CPP-NPA’s forever war
articles.summary: The communist party could take the cue from the its counterparts in Nepal, who signed a peace agreement with the Nepalese government in 2006 and became the ruling party through democratic elections…

blocks.text: After the split in the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) in 1993, many doubted that the communist insurgency waged by the CPP and its New People’s Army (NPA) would ever recover. But it did, even surpassing the peak armed strength achieved in the 1980s, first in 2005 then again in 2017.
Since then, however, the CPP-NPA, reeling from the government’s intense counter-insurgency operations, has fallen into a slump, in fact, into the most serious crisis in its entire 58-year history.
Is it twilight time for the CPP-NPA insurgency?

From very modest beginnings, the CPP-NPA grew into a powerful nationwide rebel force during the era of President Ferdinand Marcos, Sr. When the NPA launched its Maoist-style “protracted people’s war” in 1969, it started out as a ragtag band of about 60 fighters, nine automatic rifles and 26 single-shot rifles and pistols in Central Luzon. During the period of martial law, the NPA established guerrilla fronts in all of the country’s strategic mountainous areas outside of the Moro areas. NPA guerrillas engaged the Philippine military in tactical offensives, and built up its armed strength.

In the early 1980s, some CPP cadres advocated adjustments to the party’s revolutionary strategy, arguing that its Maoist strategy, which involved “encircling the cities from the countryside” was much too weighted in favor of military over political struggle and rural over urban struggles. They put forward such alternative strategies as the Vietnamese version of “protracted people’s war” which regarded both military and political struggles as fundamental and decisive, and the “insurrectional strategy” of the Sandinistas in Nicaragua, which had asserted the primacy of the “insurrectional mass movement” over the military struggle.

Because of the CPP’s boycott of the 1986 presidential election, the CPP and the open “national democratic” (ND) movement were left out of the “people power” uprising. But apart from being a tactical mistake, the boycott fiasco also showed up the flaw in the CPP-NPA’s revolutionary strategy. While its forces were still struggling to develop its military struggle along the stipulated stages of Mao’s “protracted people’s war,” the Filipino masses had toppled the Marcos dictatorship through an unarmed insurrection.

Peace negotiations between the government of the late president Corazon Aquino and the CPP’s politico-diplomatic arm, the National Democratic Front (NDF) in 1986-87 quickly collapsed. The government had demanded that the CPP-NPA-NDF lay down its arms, while the NDF had insisted that the talks address the roots of the country’s problems. (The NDF conducted peace talks with each of the post-authoritarian administrations, but did not reach a comprehensive political settlement with any of them.)

For a while after the boycott fiasco, the NPA continued to grow, reaching its highest level in 1987. The NPA was widely reported to have swelled to 25,000 fighters, although CPP founding chair Jose Ma. Sison later belied that the NPA ever reached that number in the 1980s. The CPP-NPA measures its armed strength mainly in terms of high-powered rifles (such as M16, M14, AK-47 and M1 Garand). According to Sison, the NPA’s armed strength “increased to 6,100 automatic rifles in 1986 and still further increased by some hundreds in 1987,” its highest level up to that time.

Then the decline started. The political fallout from the boycott fiasco started impacting on the CPP-NPA. This was compounded by the revelations about the killings of hundreds of suspected government spies in the CPP-NPA’s anti-infiltration purges in 1982-89. The fall of the socialist states in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union raised questions about the very rectitude of the revolutionary left’s socialist project.

Disagreements within the CPP leadership related to revolutionary strategy, analysis of the contemporary situation, alternative social order, intra-party democracy and other major questions reached a boiling point in the early 1990s. Sison wrote up “Reaffirm Our Basic Principles and Rectify the Errors,” in which he lashed out at those critical of the party’s Maoist tenets, accusing them of propagating a line of “military adventurism” and “insurrectionism.” The CPP split into “reaffirmists” and “rejectionists,” with the “reaffirmists” emerging as the legatee CPP. Through most of the 1990s, the CPP-NPA suffered an ebb.

At the turn of the millennium, however, the CPP-NPA started to recover. NPA guerrilla attacks picked up in many regions. The CPP-NPA intensified its collection of “revolutionary tax” from mining, agribusiness, telecommunications and construction firms, as well as of “permit-to-campaign” fees from politicians campaigning in or near NPA zones during election periods. In 2005, the NPA armed strength, it was claimed, surpassed the earlier 1987 peak by a few hundred high-powered rifles.

Various counterinsurgency measures undertaken during the administration of President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, however, soon took their toll on the CPP-NPA, which then suffered a decline. In 2002, following the 9-11 terrorist attacks in the U.S., the CPP and the NPA had been included in the list of “foreign terrorist organizations” (FTOs) of the US, the European Union and Australia. The next year, as government-NDF peace talks seemed to be going nowhere, President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo added the CPP-NPA to her government’s counter-terrorist Oplan Bantay Laya, which originally targeted the Abu Sayyaf only. The Oplan strategy combined combat, intelligence and civil-military operations, and emphasized the “neutralization” of communists. Scores of open ND leaders and activists were arrested, tortured, disappeared or summarily executed. In 2006, Arroyo declared an “all-out war” against the CPP-NPA and the extrajudicial killings of leftists worsened. NPA armed strength was said to have dropped by 21.6% over 2006-2009.

Starting in 2010, however, the CPP-NPA recovered again. NPA guerrilla operations intensified all over the country. In Mindanao, where the NPA was strongest, tactical offensives reportedly increased from 250 in 2010, 350 in 2011, 400 in 2012, more than 400 each in 2013 and 2014, and more than 500 in 2015. The NPA’s arena of operations, it was further claimed, expanded to 110 guerrilla fronts in 73 of the country’s 81 provinces. According to Sison, NPA armed strength “surpassed the previous 2005 peak by 3 per cent” – that is, to over 7,000 high-powered rifles.

But storm clouds were brewing. In late 2018, President Rodrigo Duterte adopted a “whole-of-nation” approach in combating the CPP-NDF insurgency, a year after it had terminated peace talks with the NDF. The approach, which sought to mobilize and synchronize civilian government agencies, local government units, and military forces in counterinsurgency efforts, combined barangay development projects (roads, water systems, other infrastructure, schools, health stations and livelihood assistance) with localized peace engagements (including local integration of former rebels) in conflict-affected areas. To implement such a strategy, Duterte created a multi-agency National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC), headed by the president himself. President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. continued Duterte’s “whole-of-nation” approach.

From the government’s viewpoint, the “whole-of-nation” strategy has been a tremendous success. In 2024, Marcos claimed that no NPA guerrilla fronts remained active across the country. The NTF-ELCAC added that the NPA had been reduced to only 785 “remnants.” In the light of many reports of clashes between the military and the NPA over the last two years, the government’s exultant claims are not credible.

But the CPP-NPA has indeed suffered grave setbacks. Since the launching of the “whole-of-nation” approach, NPA numbers have dropped considerably, and guerrilla attacks have declined. The International Crisis Group (ICG) estimates that the NPA has shrunk to between 1,200 and 2,000 fighters. The CPP-NPA no longer provides figures of NPA tactical offensives, but the number of clashes between government forces and Red fighters are indicative of the CPP-NPA’s decline. According to the international NGO Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), only 106 clashes occurred between government forces and the NPA in 2025 versus 273 in 2020 – a 61% decline in five years. Mindanao, as a whole, is no longer the main NPA flash point. The main areas of armed encounters have shifted from Western Visayas and Northern Mindanao to Eastern Visayas and Caraga.

blocks.caption: [OPINION] How the Philippine Left lost its way

blocks.text: Over the past eight years, many top CPP-NPA leaders have been killed by the military – in combat or through summary execution. Among them are CPP chairman Benito Tiamzon and secretary-general Wilma Tiamzon, as well as Julius Giron, Antonio Cabanatan, Jorge Madlos, Menandro Villanueva, Maria Concepcion Araneta, Eugenia Magpantay, Randall Echanis and Mariano Adlao. Some other top leaders, such as Victor Ladlad and Rey Casambre. have been arrested and incarcerated.

The Philippines’ “all-of-nation” approach has been widely criticized for thousands of human rights violations – illegal arrests, detentions, torture, extrajudicial killings and disappearances. Many open, legal progressive activists have become easy targets of government harassment and repression. Obsessed with its counterinsurgency drive, the government has largely ignored the criticisms and denunciations of human rights groups.
According to the ICG, the CPP-NPA is at its lowest ebb in decades. Will it be able to recover as it has in the past?

One factor that will make recovery difficult is that the CPP-NPA has lost many of its most experienced leaders over the past eight years or so. Apart from top leaders killed or arrested and imprisoned by the military, some senior, long-serving leaders have passed away peacefully, among them Sison himself, Jose Luneta, Fidel Agcaoili and Luis Jalandoni. A few other veterans have been incapacitated by health problems. The loss of the likes of Sison, Jalandoni and Madlos has also left a big gap in the CPP-NPA’s public-facing spokespersons.

The CPP-NPA may partially recover for a while, but one thing is definite: it will never be able to achieve the total military victory that it has long aspired for. Its fundamental Maoist principles stipulate that before the revolutionary forces can triumph, the “protracted people’s war” has to progress from guerrilla warfare to regular mobile warfare and eventually to positional warfare; and from strategic defensive to strategic stalemate and eventually to strategic offensive. All through nearly six decades of fighting, the NPA has been stuck in guerrilla warfare and the strategic defensive.

Endeavoring to extricate the CPP-NPA from its guerrilla warfare rut, NPA chieftain Romulo Kintanar had pushed for the establishment of bigger NPA formations and for “regularization” in the 1980s. Sison accused him of “military adventurism” and had him expelled from the CPP-NPA, then assassinated. Kintanar had established extensive international linkages for the NPA, knowing that only external sources could provide a sizeable and steady supply of arms and ammunition needed for moving up to regular warfare. This international network withered away after the takeover of the NPA by the “reaffirmist” CPP leadership. (It must be noted here that the Moro National Liberation Front and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, during their wars for secession, did manage to secure arms from external sources, but still did not achieve military victory against the government.)

The CPP-NPA’s “protracted people’s war” has gone on much longer than any of America’s “forever wars.” As defined by Cambridge Dictionary, a forever war is “a war that never ends because it cannot be won.” It is a prolonged, open-ended armed conflict without a clear, achievable endpoint or decisive victory. The war without end between the government and the CPP-NPA has already claimed between 40,000 to 60,000 lives. Yet, each year, on the NPA’s anniversary on March 29, it celebrates the protraction of its “people’s war.”

It’s twilight time for the CPP-NPA’s forever war. Mao’s rural and peasant-based “protracted people’s war,” employed in “semicolonial, semifeudal” China a century ago, simply has been a bad fit for an urbanizing Philippine society with a middle income economy that has shifted away from agriculture and is increasingly dominated by wage labor and the service sector.

Communist insurgencies are on the wane worldwide. The CPP-NPA insurgency is one of a handful of major communist insurgencies still surviving in the contemporary world. Two of them, both Maoist, have not fared any better than the CPP-NPA. India’s Naxalites (Communist Party of India – Maoist), who have waged a 59-year-old “people’s war,” are dwindling, reduced to isolated pockets and struggling with recruitment and funding, with a leadership severely degraded. Peru’s Shining Path (Communist Party of Peru), whose founder, Abimael Guzman, was captured in 1992 and died in prison in 2021, has been all but dismantled, with a few splinter groups financing themselves mainly through cocaine trafficking.

If the CPP still hopes to come to power, it should work out a comprehensive political settlement with the government and strive to turn its still appreciable mass base into an electoral base. All of the government-NDF peace negotiations have come to naught. The CPP-NPA-NDF has only been interested in eking out tactical gains – propaganda, release of political prisoners, immunity for “NDF negotiators,” so-called “belligerency status” – while still obdurately aiming for total military victory. Protracted negotiations was merely a tactic in its “protracted people’s war.”

The CPP could take the cue from the its counterparts in Nepal, the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist, now Maoist Centre), which signed a peace agreement with the Nepalese government in 2006 and became the ruling party through democratic elections in 2008–2009 and has been in the ruling coalition several times since then.

Back in 1991, writing under the pseudonym Omar Tupaz, I commented on the CPP-NPA’s Maoist “protracted people’s war” strategy: “It will be difficult, if not impossible, to win a revolution in the 1990s by continuing to adhere to a basic strategic framework of a bygone era.” Unfortunately for the CPP-NPA, this seems to be coming to pass. – Rappler.com

Nathan Gilbert Quimpo authored Contested Democracy and the Left after Marcos and co-authored Subversive Lives: A Family Memoir of the Marcos Years. In the 1980s and 1990s, he penned critiques of the communist party’s revolutionary strategy under the pseudonym Marty Villalobos and Omar Tupaz.

articles.title: DR Congo reports over 10,000 Ebola cases as the outbreak spreads abroad, with no approved vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo virus
articles.summary: DR Congo has reported more than 10,000 Ebola cases and nearly 4,900 deaths. The outbreak involves a virus for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment, complicating efforts to contain…

image.caption: DR Congo has reported more than 10,000 Ebola cases in what Africa CDC calls the fastest-growing outbreak in history (FILE 22/10/2026)Image: Tony Karumba/AFP

blocks.text: Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo reported that Ebola cases had risen to 10,060, with 4,887 deaths since the outbreak was identified in mid-May.

The outbreak involves the Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention has described it as the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
Where else have cases been reported?
Kenya has confirmed nine infections, including two deaths, after a patient traveled from DR Congo through Uganda to the capital, Nairobi.

Nigeria also confirmed an infection in a Swiss woman, the wife of a Swiss diplomat, who fell ill after visiting Uganda. Authorities are investigating where she contracted the virus. She was evacuated to Switzerland.
Nigeria on alert after traveler tests positive for Ebola
Why is the outbreak difficult to contain?
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person. It can cause fever, diarrhea and, in some cases, bleeding.
Early symptoms can resemble malaria, potentially delaying isolation and treatment.
The lack of an approved vaccine or specific treatment against the Bundibugyo virus further complicates efforts to control the outbreak.
Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak

articles.title: ‘I’m still innocent,’ says Comey as Trump calls him a ‘dirty cop’ – US politics live
articles.summary: The US justice department is attempting to prosecute the former FBI director for the third time

blocks.text: ‘I’m still innocent,’ says Comey as Trump calls him a ‘dirty cop’
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Donald Trump has called the former FBI director, James Comey, a “dirty cop”, Reuters reports. The US justice department is attempting to prosecute Comey for a third time, on the grounds of sharing sensitive national security information in ⁠2016, according to court documents ⁠made public on Monday.

The case was revealed in a court document known as a “criminal information” that the justice department said ⁠it filed to stop the 10-year statute of limitations on the offense from expiring earlier this month.

The document, filed in Washington federal ⁠court, charges Comey with transmitting and conspiring to transmit national defense information. It alleges he shared classified information with a reporter from ‌the New York Times ‌in October 2016.
“I think he’s a dirty cop,” president Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, when asked about Comey. “I don’t know much about ‌it,” he said.

Comey said in a video on Instagram that “they’re back again” and ‌referenced the Justice Department, but did not provide further details. “I’m still innocent,” he added. Comey’s lawyers have already asked a judge to dismiss the case, arguing it is legally improper.
In other developments:

items: Donald Trump campaigned in Corinth, Mississippi in support of Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith and told the crowd his rallies have “totally changed the dialogue”. “Nobody’s ever campaigned like I have for midterms,” he said.
A vocal protester then attempted to engage the president in some dialogue, on the subject of his ballroom, and where it might be most appropriately located.

Trump lashed out in racist terms at his predecessor, Barack Obama, for joking over the weekend that his renovation of the White House, with “gold everywhere”, has “the White House looking like Saddam Hussein open a Cheesecake Factory.”

Trump told reporters that Obama “doesn’t notice dirt and filth” of the White House before he rehabilitated it. Trump said then that he was “a very clean person” but, “you have to explain that to Obama” because the former president doesn’t understand and is “not smart at all.”
Trump said that the comeback victory of Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, over his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, “looked like another rigged election, frankly.”

blocks.caption: George Chidi

blocks.text: George Chidi

Social media feeds are awash with an unprecedented flood of AI-driven disinformation ahead of November’s US midterm elections, according to experts, who warn many posts are likely “slipping through the cracks”.
As tens of millions of Americans prepare to cast their vote, social media companies have scaled back their efforts to protect voters from lies meant to manipulate elections.

While the backlash against Facebook after the Cambridge Analytica scandal prompted social media giants to bolster their trust and safety operations, a counter-backlash from the right over fears of speech restrictions – which intensified after Elon Musk’s takeover of X, formerly Twitter, and the election of Donald Trump in 2024 – has led to significant layoffs from relevant teams.
Artificial intelligence has made it easier than ever to launch a disinformation campaign. And platforms are increasingly relying on AI, rather than human intervention, to respond.

“You can run an information operation now with quality that was impossible in 2016 for super, super cheap,” said Frances Haugen, a former Facebook data engineer turned whistleblower and advocate for transparency and accountability in Big Tech. Operatives playing dirty tricks can get around content moderation rules “because you can just keep tweaking the post a little bit each time you create them, and some of them are going to get through”, she said.

President Donald Trump and secretary of state Marco Rubio on Tuesday plan to show off a newly arrived oil tanker filled with Venezuelan crude to be processed in Texas refineries, according to a congressional aide and two US officials.
The visit to Port Arthur, Texas, comes on the same day that Trump is campaigning in the state for Republican candidates in the midterms, AP reported.

The president has rallies scheduled in Corpus Christi and Lubbock. Trump is trying to shore up support for US Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who is locked in a tight race with Democratic candidate James Talarico.

It’s not clear whether Rubio, who also serves as Trump’s national security adviser, would take part in any campaign events. But it’s the first time that he’s hitting the road with Trump as the president barnstorms the country.
The two US officials and the congressional aide spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss Rubio’s plans before they were publicly announced.

It’s highly unusual for the nation’s top diplomat to participate in political travel. Rubio’s trip would be the latest example of how Trump’s second presidency has blurred the lines between governing and campaigning. Attorney-general Todd Blanche has already been appearing at rallies alongside Republican candidates.

Rubio previously ran for president in 2016 and is considered a top prospect in 2028. He has not said whether he will run, and his political activities have been limited since becoming secretary of state.

articles.title: Flurry of new mayors elected in eastern Ontario, preliminary results show

image.caption: Conny Glenn is the new mayor of Kingston, having defeated incumbent Bryan Paterson in a close race during Monday's municipal election, according to the unofficial results released by the city. (Submitted by Conny Glenn)

blocks.text: Ottawa
Voters have elected new mayors in a number of eastern Ontario communities, including Kingston, where a close race ended in victory for Conny Glenn, according to Monday's unofficial results.
Coun. Conny Glenn beats incumbent Bryan Paterson in Kingston after close race
Glenn, a councillor for the city, defeated incumbent Bryan Paterson with 16,451 votes compared to his 15,658, once all the polls had reported.
Paterson has served as mayor for three terms while Glenn has represented District 10 (Syndenham).
The city's certified results are expected to be posted Tuesday.
Voters have also elected new mayors in Belleville, Brockville, Perth and the Township of Rideau Lakes.
Like Kingston, Belleville also saw an incumbent mayor defeated by another candidate. Current mayor Neil Ellis was bested by newcomer Paul Fleming.
In Perth, incumbent Judy Brown decided not to run again as mayor, choosing instead to compete for one of five seats on councillor but failing in her bid.
The community has elected Deputy Mayor Ed McPherson as its new mayor.
Mayors' exits pave way for new leaders
In Brockville, Mayor Matt Wren also decided not to serve another term. Coun. Cameron Wales will replace him after Monday's election.
"I just want to say how grateful I am for the confidence of residents in the city, and even more so for the time that residents took with me at the doors," he told CBC News.
The Township of Rideau Lakes was notable for ushering in an almost entirely new council on Monday.
The council's current term has been riven with infighting, with three members suing all but one of their council colleagues over alleged abuses of their public positions.

items: Inside the messy rural council conflict the mayor says reflects dysfunction 'beyond repair'

blocks.text: The only one not involved in that lawsuit, Dustin Bulloch, was the lone councillor to be re-elected Monday.
John Fenik, a former mayor of Perth, was elected mayor of the Township of Rideau Lakes on Monday night, according to unofficial results. (Ashley Burke/CBC)
John Fenik, a former mayor of Perth, was elected mayor of Rideau Lakes. He said he's looking forward to forging a positive new path in the community.

Fenik added that he does not plan to use the controversial strong mayor powers now available to municipal leaders. The use of that tool by outgoing mayor Arie Hoogenboom, who decided not to run again, proved divisive among councillors.

"It undermines democracy," Fenik said of strong mayor powers on Monday, moments after being elected. "The council is made up of people, and the democratic process is that the majority vote carries the day. So I will never, ever use strong mayor powers."
New mayors also came to power in Cornwall and Pembroke.
Good defeats Towndale in Cornwall
In Cornwall, Sarah Good held a strong lead over incumbent Justin Towndale before the city released its unofficial results declaring Good mayor.
Pembroke saw Stephanie LeMay elected over incumbent Ron Gervais.
And in Quinte West, where outgoing mayor Jim Harrison did not seek an additional term, Zack Card drew an ace over the two other candidates vying for the top seat.
Sarah Good is the new mayor of Cornwall, defeating incumbent Justin Towndale according to the city's preliminary election results. (Sarah Good/Facebook)

guy.quenneville@cbc.ca

articles.title: Trump’s cuts have exposed US to ‘cascade’ of El Niño dangers, experts warn
articles.summary:
President has taken an axe to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, stalling climate research on and response to extreme weather events

Sweeping cuts to the premier US climate…

blocks.text: Sweeping cuts to the premier US climate agency under Donald Trump have severely hampered the country’s capacity to forecast, research and respond to extreme weather events, former government officials and scientists have warned, as the US faces a cascade of hazards fueled by a potentially historic El Niño this winter.

From the start of his second term, the president has taken aim at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa), slashing staff levels, canceling contracts and grants, and shutting down databases and research laboratories. The agency that has long been considered a global crown jewel in climate science and forecasting, has lost roughly 20% of its staff since January 2025.

The National Weather Service, which is housed within Noaa, has also taken a hit. Weather stations have had to delay data collection and cut operating hours, with hundreds of meteorological and other technical positions still vacant across its 122 forecast offices.

The effects have already been felt at Noaa, where a chaotic and volatile environment has plummeted morale, increased burnout and hampered vital work. While capacity has quietly unravelled, a large-scale disaster will quickly expose the most dangerous gaps.
“The system has not really been tested since all the cuts happened,” said Tom Di Liberto, a former Noaa climate scientist who now works as the media director of Climate Central.
That test could soon be coming.

This year’s super El Niño, a climate phenomenon characterized by warmer than average equatorial sea surface temperatures, has the ability to fuel extreme weather events around the world. It’s already climbing off the charts and is expected to strengthen through the northern hemisphere’s autumn and winter.

Along with dangerous spikes in temperature, El Niño will supercharge storms in parts of the American west, raise sea levels in California by up to a foot, and set the stage for debris flows, land slides and flash floods.
“Whether we as a country can handle the kind of coast-to-coast extremes that could potentially happen this winter is a big question,” Di Liberto said.

Noaa plays a pivotal role in public safety and provides key insights and forecasts relied upon by a vast array of communities and industries, from weather shifts that could affect crop schedules, to emergency response preparations when hurricanes are brewing or fire conditions are aligning. The agency operates early warning systems for tsunamis, monitors seafood supply chains and provides ocean data needed for safe shipping and port operators.

blocks.caption: Waves crash into damaged homes as a powerful ocean surge and very high tides generated by Tropical Storm Rachel batter the southern California coastline on 11 October 2026.  Photograph: David McNew/Getty Images

blocks.text: While the losses are expected to have a profound effect on the American public, they will be felt globally, too. Scientists and forecasters around the world depend on Noaa satellites, studies, and intelligence, including data-sharing arrangements that track severe weather across Europe, coordination for disaster response in the Caribbean and monitoring deforestation and the effects of the climate crisis in the Amazon rainforest.

“I worry about loss of life and about our inability to be protected at a time when we need our government the most,” said Monica Medina, who served as the principal deputy administrator of Noaa during the Obama administration.
The risks are but a taste of what’s to come as the world warms. “If this is a real test”, of a hotter, more precarious future, she added, “we’re going to flunk”.
Budget and research cuts

Gaps in staffing, operations, and engagement with the public are the top three concerns for Rick Spinrad, who spent three decades at the agency and served as Noaa administrator for the Biden administration.

The agency was already shorthanded in those areas when Trump took office, according to Spinrad. But since January 2025, Noaa has lost more than 3,000 staffers, according to workforce data from the US office of personnel management which was last updated in August this year.

It’s the biggest staffing drop in the last decade, and includes hundreds of people who lost their jobs during massive layoffs or who took incentives to retire or resign as the administration worked to systemically shrink the size of the federal government last year, along with those who left voluntarily.
Some departments have been hit harder than others.

The public affairs team that helps disseminate important information, was roughly halved. Information technology management workers, who provide vital support for forecasting and data infrastructure among other things, were reduced by roughly 27%. The data showed a loss of more than 500 staffers across a range of science positions with only 46 new hires.

There were also about 10% fewer meteorologists and meteorology technicians as the US went into autumn this year, even after the National Weather Service rushed to staff up in the aftermath of the Trump administration’s massive 2025 layoffs.

blocks.caption: Workers at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Center for Weather and Climate Prediction headquarters in College Park, Maryland. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: The NWS analyzes and collects roughly 6.3bn observations each day. They release 1.5m forecasts and up to 50,000 warnings each year. Cracks have begun to show, however, as the agency has tried to takes on its enormous and essential workload with fewer people.

Staffers had to work double shifts to keep some forecasting offices open, the Washington Post reported last September. Staffers who spoke to the Post at the time described an agency pushed to its limits.
Only 40 Meteorologists were added to the ranks across Noaa between January and August this year, with hundreds of vacancies across the country still open as a tumultuous winter approaches.
Overall, the agency was able to bring on just 525 new hires since January 2025, leaving a gaping 2,500-person deficit.

Already, staffing limitations have shown up in delayed or limited weather balloon launches that left parts of the Great Plains unprepared for tornadoes and limited warnings to rural communities in Alaska, where more than 1,500 people were displaced by floods earlier this year. The NWS also failed to adequately provide multilingual weather alerts due to staffing and funding cuts, the government accountability office (GAO) found, leaving 26 million people in the US at higher risk.

“There has been this hollowing out – there’s no time to do anything other than the very basics,” said Dr Anna Zivian, a climate researcher and policy expert. “I suspect we haven’t seen the worst outcomes from the loss of capacity yet,” she added. “You can’t pick up that kind of slack.”

blocks.caption: Waves batter the shoreline in Laguna Beach, California, during a period of high tides associated with El Niño. Photograph: Mike Blake/Reuters

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the Trump administration terminated dozens of grants representing a loss in more than $28m in funding for states, cities, non-profits and universities, according to calculations from Grant Witness, an organization that tracks science-related grant making by the federal government. Climate research has been the most affected, according to their analysis, which found that the number of grant awards in fiscal year 2026 was 37% lower than the 2021-2024 average.
Despite these concerns, the administration has outlined more plans to slash budgets and research capacity.

Trump has proposed cutting $1.6bn in Noaa funding – a 26% drop – for next year’s budget. While many of the cuts won’t make it through the budget process, they showcase how the president views the essential services the agency provides the American public and puts more pressure on the staff still working at Noaa.

“People at Noaa are nervous,” Di Liberto said, adding that employees across the organization are afraid they will get in trouble if they say something that conflicts with the administration’s anti-climate narrative.

“You want people doing their best work when we face these extremes,” he said. Denials of human-caused climate crisis coming from the top have only made their jobs harder, as scientists and forecasters work to put urgent information into context for the American public and others around the world.
“It’s incredibly difficult,” Di Liberto said. “Imagine being told the number six doesn’t exist and then being asked to do math.”
Requests for comment sent to Noaa and its parent agency, the Department of Commerce, were not returned before publication.
A missed learning opportunity

An El Niño year can be high risk, but it’s also an incredible chance to learn and prepare, offering a glimpse of what the world might expect as temperatures rise. In that regard, experts worry a shrunken Noaa is missing a vital research opportunity.

“This El Niño is so useful in a sense of getting an understanding about where we stand for dealing with extreme weather around the world,” Di Liberto said. “Unfortunately we’re going to learn a lot this winter about our ability to deal with multiple extremes happening at the same time.”

He and other experts have also expressed concerns that not enough has been done to ready communities for the coming hazards or capture important data that will inform the future. “When it comes to preparing for El Niño events – or any weather extreme – the preparation happens during the off season,” he said.

During the last strong El Niño a decade ago, the agency deployed planes, weather balloons, unmanned aircraft and a research ship to collect data. This year, only “a handful of unmanned watercraft”, will be deployed into the Pacific, NPR reported in September.

blocks.caption: Protesters gather outside the headquarters of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) in Silver Spring, Maryland, to protest job cuts at the agency. Photograph: Jay Mallin/ZUMA Press Wire/REX/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The Trump administration has also begun removing ocean monitoring systems that provide important data during El Niño and shaved roughly $6bn off of an investment secured for weather satellites that would have propelled major advancements in future weather predictions. The sharp reduction could create a gap in satellite coverage, according to an analysis from the government accountability office, severely disrupting data.
Funding for a decade-long project to monitor the oceans using autonomous robotic devices called Biogeochemical-Argo floats – part of a global effort – will also expire at the end of October.

“We are more capable than we have been in the past because of the developments in the technology, the satellites that were flying, the observing systems that we’ve put in place,” Spinrad said. “But everything that this administration is doing suggests that we cannot and will not sustain those capabilities. So the real question is – are we at a turning point now?”

articles.title: The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionaires
articles.summary:
It is essential not just to fund the public goods the nation needs, it is indispensable to restore a sense of fairness

Money doesn’t buy happiness, we’re told. Even some economists agree.…

blocks.text: Money doesn’t buy happiness, we’re told. Even some economists agree. The Nobel Prize-winning economists, Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton, once proposed that rising income increased people’s emotional wellbeing only up to a ceiling of about $115,000 in today’s money.

They probably hadn’t met many billionaires. The ultra-rich may not pursue happiness in the joyful sense of the word. But they will try every trick in the book to hang on to their stash and woe befall the tax authority that tries to lay a finger on their treasure.
And this poses one of the most intractable challenges not only to the solvency of the American state, but to the survival of American democracy.

From the technological Olympus of Silicon Valley to the urban canyons of Wall Street, a narrow club of vastly wealthy plutocrats sits on a ballooning share of the nation’s resources. One percent of Americans at the apex of the economy are hoarding over 31% of the nation’s total wealth, a cool $55tn in net worth.

Getting them to share with the rest of society, to fund redistribution or pay for public goods, is proving pretty much impossible. Their ability to move resources around, hide profit across jurisdictions, and minimize income to hoard wealth until they die appears to put them beyond the reach of taxation.

One recent research paper found that the country’s richest 384 oligarchs paid only 24% of their economic income in 2025, compared with 30% for the average taxpayer. And not all of them are getting top notch tax advice. Reporting by ProPublica revealed that some of the richest Americans – like Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Warren Buffett and Michael Bloomberg – live largely tax free.

California is experimenting with a budgetary Hail Mary pass: In November, Californians will be called to vote on Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires residing in the state on 1 January of this year. If the plutocracy’s income is off limits, the thinking goes, best to target its gargantuan assets.

California’s gambit is “the first-ever tax on billionaire wealth enacted anywhere in the world”– according to an open letter endorsing the move by six Nobel Prize-winning economists on the left side of the political spectrum. “It will kickstart a movement to tax ultra-high-net-worth individuals in other states – and eventually at the federal level and in other countries,” they raved. The vote “may well come to be seen as a turning point in the battle between democracy and oligarchy”.

Moreover, Prop 40 could raise real money. As of early October, 260 billionaires lived in the state, according to the Forbes billionaires’ list, amassing nearly $2.5tn in wealth. Based on these numbers, the 5% tax would raise some $110bn, much of which would go to replace Medicaid funding nixed in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year.

Still, the move is proving controversial even among left-leaning economists and politicians. Governor Gavin Newsom, who is virtually certain to run for the Democratic nomination ahead of the 2028 presidential election, is opposed. So is Xavier Becerra, the Democrat running to succeed him as governor. They fear that such a move will spark a flight of the oligarchs to lower-tax jurisdictions.

blocks.caption: People attend a rally against Proposition 40 at the Iron Workers Apprenticeship Training Center on 5 October 2026 in La Palma, California. Photograph: Eric Thayer/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Nobelists note that the California’s proposed billionaire tax was sneaked in to prevent billionaires from fleeing to avoid it: “Some affected taxpayers may have tried to leave between the time they learned about the proposed ballot initiative – in late November 2025 – and January 1st of 2026,” they wrote. “But the window was so short that it is unlikely any significant number of billionaires successfully cut ties with the Golden State in such a short period of time.”

In fact, between January and October the number of billionaires living in California grew by 20. Elon Musk may believe that welfare recipients are the “parasite class” and empathy is “the fundamental weakness of western civilization”. But perhaps California’s billionaires feel enough empathy for less fortunate humans to part with a paltry $110bn, especially since their wealth has grown by a cool $400bn so far this year.

Not all billionaires move to avoid taxes. Trump’s 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which capped the state and local tax deduction, was expected to prompt the rich to flee high-tax blue states in droves, as they could no longer deduct their state and local tax payments on their federal tax returns. But a study by a Cornell sociologist and an economist at the treasury department found almost no impact on the migration rates of the affluent, at least in the first year following the change.

Indeed, the rich in New York City are hit by a top city income tax rate of 3.9% on top of a 10.9% state tax, compared with zero in Miami. Still, there are 154 billionaires in New York state, according to a report by Oxfam. Nine of the 10 richest live in the city. The only state with more billionaires than New York is, wait, high-tax California.

Still, Newsom and Becerra have a point. California’s richest billionaires have gone feral over Prop 40. Google’s Sergey Brin has helped coordinate some $200m to oppose it and promote two countervailing propositions, 41 and 42 that, if passed, would emasculate the tax. One would bar retroactive taxes – putting wealth accumulated in the past off limits – and forbid new taxes on financial assets or other personal property.

The opposition is gaining traction. A poll in September found that Prop 40 falls just short of majority approval. Just in case, the fast money has tried to flee the state, to make it out before deadline. In the run-up to Christmas of 2025 Brin and Google co-founder Larry Page moved many of their business interests out of California. They also bought homes out of state. Travis Kalanick, former CEO of Uber, left following Musk to Texas. Paypal and Palantir mogul Peter Thiel moved his residence to Miami last year.

While some of the more optimistic analyses assume that avoidance tactics by California billionaires will reduce the taxable pot of wealth by only about 10%, others are less sanguine. Even if it passes, the tax will be taken to court, including on grounds that retroactive taxation violates due process, and may not survive litigation. Some assets – real estate, notably – will not be taxed. Foreign billionaires may wiggle out under double taxation treaties. And more billionaires will leave, assuming that though it was billed as a one-time affair, the new tax will become permanent. This will hit future income tax revenues.

Altogether, economists from Stanford University concluded that the new tax would raise only around $30bn, while the flow of lost income tax revenue would cost state coffers nearly $39bn, in net present value. The estimate fits with results from studies of attempts to avoid wealth taxes in Swiss cantons. It also checks with behavioral responses of the rich to other forms of taxation. For instance, Enrico Moretti, an economist at the University of California Berkeley, and Daniel Wilson of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, found the location of the very rich is highly sensitive to estate taxes.

These should be the most American taxes of them all, a good fit for a democratic nation that conceives itself as a meritocracy; a tool to prevent the emergence of a hereditary aristocracy passing economic and political power down the generations. Still, the rich don’t much care for them.

In 2001, George W Bush did what Republican presidents do: he cut taxes. But his Economic Growth Tax Relief and Reconciliation Act included an annoying twist: it eliminated the credit offered by the federal government to offset the estate tax burden imposed by states on the ultra-wealthy. All of a sudden, billionaires’ estate tax liability became dependent on which state they lived in. Dying as a resident of New York, Pennsylvania and Connecticut, which had estate taxes, abruptly become way more costly than dying in a state with none, like Texas, Florida … or California.

By 2010, over a fifth of billionaires in the Forbes 400 list who originally lived in a state that levied an estate tax state had moved to a non-estate tax state, while only about 1% had made a move in the opposite direction. Moretti and Wilson estimated that by 2017 states with estate taxes had lost 23 of 72 Forbes 400 billionaires who lived there in 2001. Altogether, Forbes 400 wealth subject to state estate taxes fell from some $203bn in 2001 to about $122bn 16 years later.

States with estate taxes didn’t just lose the income tax revenue of their departing billionaires. Extra losses not considered in Moretti and Wilson’s analysis include the effect of plutocrats relocating their businesses. Moreover, estate taxes could well deter other billionaires from moving into the state, or encourage those who remained to try more aggressive tax avoidance strategies than usual.

In light of the difficulties in taxing billionaires and even the lesser rich, there is an argument out there that a less progressive, flatter tax structure could do better at raising money. European countries fund a large share of their generous welfare programs with value added taxes on consumption, which are more difficult to avoid but place a heavier burden on lower-income people who consume a larger share of their paychecks.

And yet the idea of letting plutocracy off the hook seems unacceptable. Brin has said Prop 40 reminds him of the Soviet Union, which he fled with his parents in 1979. Apparently he prefers a social arrangement more like the one that prevailed in the Czarist Russia in which a narrow few amass vast riches unencumbered by a responsibility to contribute to societal wellbeing. That’s the America we all live in now.

If American democracy is to survive this moment, it must figure out a way for billionaires to contribute more. It is essential not just to fund the public goods the nation needs to function. It’s indispensable to restore a sense of fairness to the American experiment. Democracy cannot endure without it.

Let’s see what happens next month in California. But the hard truth for blue states eager to raise more revenue to fund the social safety net and pay for public goods is that they are not up to the task, given competition with Republican-run states where taxes are anathema. As Moretti points out, the tax gap between red states and blue states has become enormous. California’s top marginal rate is 13.5%. Florida’s is zero. The temptation for the next Czarist plutocrat to move from the first to the second is not insignificant.

Indeed, Moretti and Wilson have another research paper that looks at what top scientists and engineers do when states raise income taxes. “People do leave,” Moretti told me. “These are not billionaires, but only highly paid workers.”

The good news is that while there are many ways in which California’s attempt at taking a nibble out of billionaires’ wealth may fail, it is not technically impossible to tax the oligarchy. There are various options available. Federal estate tax rules could be cleansed of the myriad loopholes that allow dynastic wealth to accumulate, such as those allowing unrealized capital gains to accrue forever tax free and bequeathed to heirs with the gains reset to zero. Taxes on capital income could be raised to restore fairness between taxation on capital and labor.

Economists Erick Zwick of the University of Chicago and Owen Zidar of Princeton propose that restoring the tax schedule to where it was in the Clinton administration 30 years ago would raise $5tn over a decade and do wonders for America’s public finance. The main challenge to that is political: it requires an overhaul of a political equilibrium that over the last 50 years has largely revolved around cutting taxes.

But restoring fairness and efficacy to the American state is in the end not a task for the states. Altogether, the government collects almost 3% of GDP less in taxes than it did at the turn of the century. Over 2% of that decline was about federal revenues. The average central government in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development today raises twice as much in taxes, as a share of GDP, as the US federal government.

Fixing this is, of course, a political problem, one that will remain intractable as long as half of the political spectrum believes its only job on this earth is to cut taxes. But it would be helpful for the fleet-footed billionaires to give some thought to the social contract in which they want to live; whether they are interested in broad-based prosperity or, rather, they are happy to slink into their castle, raise the drawbridge, and hope societal upheaval does not interrupt dinner.

articles.title: The US urgently needs more bilingual healthcare workers. This clinic might have the solution
articles.summary:
In New Mexico, where a shortage is acute, Casa de Salud trains college and high-school health apprentices who understand the communities they serve

“I’ll be getting a little bit closer to…

blocks.text: “I’ll be getting a little bit closer to you to put the cuff on,” Gisselle Martinez said, demonstrating how to take a manual blood pressure in a trauma-informed manner. “It might be a little tight. Let me know if you feel any discomfort and I can take it off.”

She’s not a doctor or a nurse – at least, not yet – but a 21-year-old college student. Between classes, Martinez works as a bilingual health apprentice at Casa de Salud, a primary care clinic in Albuquerque, New Mexico. On top of taking vitals, Martinez is certified in harm reduction – she can run a needle exchange and give out fentanyl test strips. And she understands how a patient’s trauma and past neglect can show up in an exam room.

“My entire life I had to pretty much translate for my parents whenever they would go to the doctor,” said Martinez, whose parents speak Spanish. That responsibility sometimes felt overwhelming, like when she didn’t know how to translate certain medical terms, or when she herself had to go under anesthesia and explain the risks to her parents.
Now through Casa’s de Salud’s apprentice program, she is working toward becoming the certified nurse anesthetist she wishes she and her parents had access to.
“As a bilingual first-generation student, I aspire to help my community,” she said.

While states across the country face a healthcare workforce shortage, the need is particularly high in rural areas and within Spanish-speaking communities; in New Mexico, 32 of its 33 counties face a shortage. Although they make up 20% of the population, Latinos account for only about 6% of the US physician workforce.

blocks.caption: Trainer and former apprentice Edelin De las Casas shows apprentice Miriam Rios how to run an EKG at Casa de Salud. Photograph: Casa de Salud

blocks.text: To provide that care, not just for the community, but from the community, Casa de Salud’s year-long apprentice program has trained more than 300 bilingual high school and college students since its founding in 2005. The aim is not only to help students from marginalized backgrounds get into medical programs, but to keep them in the community. At least a third of the students Casa de Salud has tracked have gone into the healthcare field, with more than half of those attending medical school.

“You’re more likely to work in a community if you grew up in the community,” said health apprentice program developer Colette Village Center, who is from the Standing Rock Sioux Nation. “We want to see more representation of lower-wealth individuals, under-represented individuals in healthcare, because that saves lives.”
Offering ‘bilingual, bicultural’ care

Casa de Salud opened in 2004 when a local physician approached a group of promotoras – trusted liaisons between the community and healthcare workers – in Albuquerque’s predominantly Hispanic and Latino South Valley neighborhood.

“There were a few of us women who called themselves the promotoras tradicionales, who would do limpias,” said Lorraine Cordova, one of Casa de Salud’s founders, describing a spiritual cleansing common in the Mexican folk healing tradition of curanderismo that often uses herbs, prayer and intention-setting to process emotional stressors.

The group met every few weeks at a gym in the South Valley, where they offered limpias, massage, reiki, accu-detox and other treatments. Seeing the need for connecting culturally grounded caregivers to the healthcare system, Casa de Salud soon after launched its health apprentice program.
Alejandra Casarrubias was among the program’s first students. Today she’s a registered nurse, a sexual assault nurse examiner and clinical manager at Casa de Salud.

“You don’t only have to be bilingual, but bicultural,” she said, describing the importance of training healthcare providers who understand the communities they serve. According to the Association of American Medical Colleges, “patients from minoritized races tend to fare better with doctors of the same race”, across metrics like infant mortality and compliance with healthcare plans.

Casa de Salud provides care to a patient base that is predominantly Spanish-speaking and 80% uninsured. Because of the health apprenticeship’s bilingual requirement, Village Center says 100% of the apprentices are themselves Latino, and many like Martinez are also first-generation college students. She’s thoughtful about recruiting students not only from local colleges, but through the college assistance migrant program, and the nearby high school, where students have historically undergone the same training.

“I already knew about Casa de Salud because my family, back in the day, used to use it,” said Sebastian Hernandez, a 19-year-old health apprentice, who’s currently studying biochemistry and film production and hopes to become an internal medicine physician.

blocks.caption: Apprentice Gisselle Martinez performs an ear lavage on Leslie Fonseca as directed by Edelin De las Casas, a former apprentice and now trainer. Photograph: Casa de Salud

blocks.text: Many of the clinic’s patients continue to use alternative medicines like those its founding promotoras offered. “A lot of the times when those people go to the doctor, they get disrespected for having those kinds of traditions,” said Village Center, who added that the clinic still tries to teach health apprentices about those practices.

When new apprentices arrive at Casa de Salud, they work their way through different stations at the clinic, starting at the front desk, then moving to taking vitals, and ending in the clinic’s lab, where they process tests and learn how to draw blood and run EKGs. While at Casa, apprentices also help with the clinic’s syringe exchange program and learn about its gender-affirming care program.

Alongside their formal training, apprentices also participate in workshops about healthcare history and receive mentorship from their peers and alums. Between patient rooms, the clinic also keeps a bookshelf well-stocked with study materials for university entrance exams and a cabinet full of free scrubs. There are also bulletin boards filled with scholarship opportunities, financial aid advice and information about the local university’s pre-med society.

“Any type of grad school that I had seen, whether it be CRNA [certified registered nurse anesthetist], PA [physician assistant], MD, medical school, all of them are so competitive to get into, so it’s intimidating,” said Fabian Corral, an alum of the program who’s currently enrolled in school to become a physician assistant. “But when you’re surrounded by other people who also want to do that stuff, it’s encouraging.”

Corral and two other students in his Casa apprenticeship class are now enrolled in the same physician assistant program at the University of New Mexico, where they meet for study groups together. They’re among 16 Casa alums who’ve gone to school to become physician assistants, advanced practice providers who are increasingly filling healthcare gaps in rural communities.
“I don’t know what my future holds, but if it has to do with serving the community, then I would feel like I made the right choice,” said Corral.

articles.title: Who is Retrina Fuentes, the judge behind arrest orders vs Duterte critics?
articles.summary: Fuentes once served as executive judge of the Davao City Regional Trial Court

items: Veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was arrested on October 24 over a cyber libel case filed by lawyer Mans Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Lustre was detained for nearly a day before posting bail and is known for his book on extrajudicial killings in the Philippines, while he plans to release a new book amid the Vice President's impeachment trial.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was arrested on Saturday, October 24, over a cyber libel case filed by an unidentified complainant at the time. It was Davao City Presiding Judge Retrina Espe Fuentes who issued the warrant of arrest.
On Monday, October 26, Lustre’s lawyer, Dino de Leon, told Rappler that it was lawyer Mans Carpio — husband of Vice President Sara Duterte — who was the complainant in Lustre’s case.

Based on the Supreme Court’s (SC) tracker, Fuentes is currently the presiding judge of Davao City Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 10. The court is located in Benigno Aquino Hall of Justice, in Matina, Davao City.
Fuentes was Davao City’s 1st vice executive judge in 2016, according to the Philippine Judicial Academy Bulletin. At the time, Presiding Judge Emmanuel Carpio was sitting as executive judge.
Presiding Judge Carpio is the uncle of Mans Carpio. In her 2024 Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth, Vice President Duterte listed Emmanuel Carpio as her uncle-in-law.
At the time of Fuentes’ appointment as 1st vice executive judge, Rodrigo Duterte was president, while his daughter Sara was Davao City mayor during that period.
Based on SC Office of the Court Administrator’s Administrative Order No. 231-2022, Fuentes became Davao City’s executive judge on November 1, 2022 under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

The Fraternal Order of Saint Thomas More in Davao City posted a congratulatory message after Fuentes’ appointment. She held the position from 2022 to 2024, according to SC spokesperson Camille Sue Mae Ting.
“Davao Regional Trial Court Executive Judge is now Judge Rowena M. Apao Adlawan,” said Ting.

According to the SC’s AM No. 03-8-02-SC, the Court may appoint executive judges and vice executive judges in stations where there are more than two RTC branches. Their appointment will be based on their administrative qualifications, experience, and seniority, among others.

“The Executive Judge shall take charge of the administrative work of the Supreme Court in all first and second level courts. The Executive Judge derives his/her powers and prerogatives through delegation by the Supreme Court,” said the order.
Lustre, the 72-year-old veteran journalist was attending the Saturday News Forum event in Quezon City when Quezon City police from the Quezon City Police District arrested him.
After nearly a day in detention, he was able to post a P48,000-bail at past midnight on Sunday, October 25.

Lustre is the author of the book, “Kill, Kill, Kill: Extrajudicial Killings in the Philippines.” It’s about former president Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs that killed nearly 30,000 people, according to several human rights groups. Duterte is now detained in The Hague, Netherlands over his crimes against humanity case that stemmed from the said campaign.

After his release from temporary detention, Lustre said he is scheduled to release a new book titled, “MISFIT SARA Life and Times of Vice President Sara Duterte-Carpio; The Impeachment Trial of a Filipino Vice President.” The Vice President is currently in the middle of her impeachment trial that could remove her from the position and bar her from running for president in 2028.

The information sheet against Lustre reads: “The above-named accused, with deliberate intent, willfully, unlawfully, and feloniously, through his Facebook account under the name ‘Philip Jr. Lustre,’ published and posted written statements, thereby making an imputation of a crime against Atty. Manases R. Carpio, a private individual and on the said date, was actually residing in Davao City, through the internet using the social networking platform called ‘Facebook.com,’ by saying: ‘Sumuka si Mans Carpio ng P300-M sa operasyon ng Marines: P150M kay Mike; P50M kay Levi; at P5M sa bawat isa sa 18 Marines?‘ which published statement, taken in its plain, natural, and ordinary meaning, directly imputes upon Atty. Manases R. Carpio, the commission of a crime, specifically bribery or corrupt.”

blocks.caption: Philip Lustre Jr.’s arrest a ‘warning’ for journalists – lawyer

blocks.text: Fuentes was also the judge who signed the warrant of arrest against another Duterte critic and former vice presidential candidate, Walden Bello.

In 2022, at the height of the campaign season, former Davao City public information officer Jefry Tupas filed a cyber libel complaint against Bello. Tupas was seeking P10 million in damages after being allegedly accused by Bello on social media of being a drug addict and dealer.

Duterte’s aide was embroiled in a controversy in 2021 after attending a beach party in Mabini, Davao de Oro that was later raided by anti-narcotics agents. The operation supposedly happened an hour after Tupas and companions had left the party.
On August 8, 2022, QCPD personnel arrested Bello over a warrant issued by Fuentes for two counts of cyber libel. He was later freed after posting a P48,000-bail for each of the counts.
Bello, at the time, labeled Tupas’ case as “clearly a politically-motivated move.”
The following year, Bello filed a petition with the SC seeking to decriminalize libel in the Philippines.
In February this year, the former vice presidential bet issued an apology to Tupas, saying his statements were “unfounded.”

In 2019, Fuentes was the judge who ordered the arrest of Italian Lorenzo Marchesi, who was 57 years old at the time. He was ordered arrested over alleged possession of child sexual abuse and exploitation materials.
Marchesi was arrested after a search of his electronic devices allegedly revealed a collection of illegal materials.
Last September, Fuentes was the same judge who issued a warrant of arrest against a man wanted for rape. She issued the warrant on September 2, 2026.

“The accused, identified only by the alias ‘Abdul,’ was properly informed of the cause of his arrest and apprised of his constitutional rights, including his rights under Republic Act No. 9745, or the Anti-Torture Act of 2009, in a language or dialect known to and understood by him,” said the PNP.
“The arrested person was identified as a top 3 most wanted person, municipal level, under the PNP e-warrant system,” it added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Neil Young files second lawsuit against Trump for unauthorised use of Rockin’ in the Free World at rallies
articles.summary:
The musician and outspoken critic of the president is suing for $10m in reputational damages – six years after a settlement in which Trump agreed not to use the song again

Neil Young is…

blocks.text: Neil Young is suing Donald Trump’s political action committee Trump 47 Committee Inc for $10m (£7.47m) over alleged copyright infringement of his song Rockin’ in the Free World after the US president used it as walk-up music in recent midterm election rallies.

It is the second time that Young has filed against one of Trump’s organisations over his unlicenced use of the song. He first did so in 2020, against the corporation Donald J Trump for President Inc. Trump settled, promising, according to Young’s suit, that his organisation “would never again use Rockin’ in the Free World without a license and permission from Young”.

Filed on Monday in the US district court for the eastern district of Virginia, the suit states that Trump’s ongoing use of the song meant that Young, a very vocal critic of the president, “has suffered damage to his reputation and brand as a result of the implication that he supports Donald J Trump in any way”.
Trump’s administration has not yet responded to the suit.

Young’s case outlines how diametrically opposed his 1989 song is to Trump’s values, calling it “a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten.

“The lyrics pain vivid street-level portraits – a mother discarding her baby, addicts lost in despair, garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity – while the repeated chorus delivers a savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn’t shared by all. In short, the song is the opposite of everything that Donald J Trump stands for.”
after newsletter promotion

Lawyers for Young cite the playing of the song at the president’s rally in Ohio on 12 October but state that it has been played “numerous times at other rallies designed to encourage Republican votes in the upcoming mid-term elections”. Young also seeks an injunction against further public performances.

Young’s anti-Trump stance is clear: he has repeatedly damned the president in writings on his website and in 2025 released a protest song about his administration, Big Crime. “Don’t need no fascist rules / Don’t want no fascist schools / Don’t want soldiers walking on the streets,” Young sings. “Got to get the fascists out / Got to clean the White House out … no more money to the fascists, the billionaire fascists.”

In the past 12 months, the Trump presidency has amped up its strategy of trolling leftwing musicians – including Olivia Rodrigo, Sabrina Carpenter and SZA – by using their songs to soundtrack ICE propaganda or clips about Trump’s strategy in Iran. In August, Taylor Swift had her song August removed from a video celebrating the Trump presidency.

articles.title: SP Gatchalian to focus on impeachment trial amid call to reject VP post
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said he would remain focused on the impeachment trial amid the call of Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano to reject offers to succeed Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said he would remain focused on the impeachment trial amid the call of Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano to reject offers to succeed Vice President Sara Duterte should she be convicted.
Gatchalian said a lot is still expected to unfold in the impeachment trial as Duterte’s defense team has yet to present its evidence.
“To be fair sa respondent, hindi pa nape-present ng defense ‘yung kanilang ebidensya at testimony. So pakinggan muna natin lahat bago tayo mag-isip ng next steps,” the Senate President said.
(To be fair to the respondent, the defense has yet to present their evidence and testimony. So let’s hear everything first before we consider the next steps.)
Asked if Gatchalian has received any initial offers for the vice presidency, he said, “Ako, impeachment muna ang tinututukan ko eh.”
(My focus is only on impeachment as of the moment)

“Pinag-aaralan namin mabuti, pinag-aaralan ko mabuti. And of course, ‘yung impeachment proceedings, pinag-aaralan din namin mabuti ‘yung dates, ‘yung times. In the next few days, budget season, papasok na sa plenary. So, ito lahat inaayos namin. So, naka-concentrate muna kami sa process,” he added.

(We are studying this carefully, I am studying it carefully. We are also carefully reviewing the impeachment proceedings’ dates and the schedule. In the next few days, the budget will reach the plenary. We are currently organizing all of this now. So we’re only focusing on the process.)
Cayetano earlier called on his fellow senators to declare that they will decline offers for the vice presidency should Duterte get convicted in her impeachment trial.

The Senate Minority Leader made the appeal in response to the statement of Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero---presiding officer of the impeachment court---that he will refuse the vice presidency, if Duterte gets convicted, due to conflict of interest.
Timeline

Gatchalian also said the impeachment trial may extend up to December given that the Senate has to balance it with the ongoing budget deliberations and the upcoming bicameral conference committee meetings to consolidate disagreeing provisions of the budget bill.
“Parang hindi na kaya ng November from the looks of it. So, I'm sure, tingin ko, tatawid ito ng December,” he said.
(It looks like the impeachment trial can’t conclude by November. So I’m sure it will extend to December.)

The impeachment trial is currently suspended to pave the way for the committee deliberations on the proposed 2027 national budget. The Senate impeachment court shall reconvene on November 9 at 10 a.m. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Make LGU funds ‘results-based’ amid pork barrel concerns — World Bank
articles.summary: “We believe that LGSF can support genuine regional development so long as obviously it’s effectively utilized,” World Bank lead urban specialist Makiko Watanabe says

blocks.text: “We believe that LGSF can support genuine regional development so long as obviously it’s effectively utilized,” World Bank lead urban specialist Makiko Watanabe says

MANILA, Philippines – The World Bank said the proposed P58-billion Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) in the 2027 national budget could help power regional development, but recommended tying allocations to actual project results and encouraging local governments to invest together, amid concerns the fund could become a source of political patronage.

Makiko Watanabe, the World Bank’s lead urban specialist for East Asia and the Pacific, said the Philippine government could adopt performance-based or results-based financing to improve accountability and reward local government units (LGUs) that deliver.

“The short answer is, yes, we believe that LGSF can support genuine regional development so long as obviously it’s effectively utilized,” Watanabe said when asked by Rappler during the launch of the World Bank’s From Cities to Corridors report on Tuesday, October 27.
She suggested that allocations be made “performance-based or results-based” rather than set in advance, and that funding encourage “inter-LGU type of investments” rather than isolated projects.
These could include shared transportation and digital infrastructure, as well as disaster resilience projects that have spillover benefits beyond a single municipality or city.

World Bank Philippines division director Zafer Mustafaoğlu likewise emphasized the need for accountability, efficient spending, and timely project completion, while suggesting too that authorities should consider the economic potential of neighboring LGUs when allocating resources.

The proposed LGSF has drawn scrutiny over concerns that it could be used for discretionary spending and political patronage. Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito has questioned the criteria for distributing the more-than-P58-billion fund and called for safeguards to ensure that allocations address local development needs rather than reward political allies. Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian also said that the LGSF needed to be transparent to promote good governance.

blocks.caption: [In This Economy] The 2027 budget: Hocus-pocus prevails once more

blocks.text: The World Bank’s latest report also identifies weaknesses in how local projects secure funding.

Only about 30% of investment proposals endorsed through regional development councils receive funding in a given budget cycle, which may create “uncertainties among LGUs about which of their endorsed priorities will receive the national government support,” the World Bank report said.
It also notes that projects outside local annual investment plans (AIP) can receive funding when they have political backing, while planned projects may go unfunded.

“While AIP is a standard vehicle for investment planning, [focus group discussion] shows that projects are also budgeted outside the AIP when there is political support, whereas AIP-listed items go unfunded when local priorities do not align,” the World Bank said in its report.

blocks.caption: SITTING ON CASH? A World Bank analysis of 2023 year-end cash balance as a share of annual operating revenues by urban LGU size shows that LGUs are not utilizing large amounts of cash on hand. Chart from the World Bank’s report

blocks.text: Beyond the allocation process, many LGUs struggle to spend the funds they already have. Capital investments account for only about 15% of annual LGU expenditure, while poor project preparation and procurement add to delays.

This has left local governments sitting on cash reserves, with large urban LGUs holding an average of P9,263 per person in year-end cash on hand balances in 2023, funds that the World Bank said could have been better used to address infrastructure and service needs.

The report’s main recommendation is to shift away from individual LGU support to what it calls interconnected “corridor-based” development, with aligned national and local plans and better project implementation capacity. – Rappler.com
