articles.title: Canadian 'tremendously sorry' after spending stolen crypto on Lamborghini, BMWs, jewelry
articles.summary: A 20-year-old Canadian who conned cryptocurrency holders out of millions of dollars — and lived large as a teenager in Florida with "extravagant" partying, access to a private jet and luxury cars —…

image.caption: Canadian Trenton Johnston was 19 at the time of his arrest in March 2026 in North Miami. He was sentenced Monday to time served after pleading guilty to a money laundering conspiracy and handing over $3.8 million US worth of stolen cryptocurrency. (Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office)

blocks.text: World·New

A 20-year-old Canadian who conned cryptocurrency holders out of millions of dollars — and lived large as a teenager in Florida with "extravagant" partying, access to a private jet and luxury cars — could soon be headed home to Canada after he pleaded guilty to a money laundering conspiracy and was sentenced to time served Monday.
Trenton Johnston sentenced to time served after pleading guilty to U.S. money laundering conspiracy

A 20-year-old who conned cryptocurrency holders out of millions of dollars — and lived large as a teenager in Florida with "extravagant" partying and access to a private jet and luxury cars — could soon be headed home to Canada.

A U.S. federal judge in Miami on Monday sentenced Trenton Richard David (Trent) Johnston to time served after he pleaded guilty to a money laundering conspiracy and handed over $3.8 million US worth of stolen crypto.

Johnston, then 19, was seated in the back of a Rolls-Royce Cullinan SUV that smelled of "freshly burned marijuana" when he was arrested in March, according to court documents. He's been in custody ever since.

U.S. Homeland Security Investigations found Johnston, a Canadian citizen, impersonated Google tech support staff and representatives of crypto firms to convince unwitting victims to share the codes to their cryptocurrency wallets.
The scheme made him a fortune.
Johnston was arrested after he was found with suspected amphetamine tablets in a Hermes bag while seated in the back of this Rolls-Royce Cullinan. (EpicVIN)
Prosecutors detailed 'extravagant' lifestyle

In one instance in March, Johnston and an unnamed co-conspirator swindled a victim in California out of his life savings — 185 bitcoin, or the equivalent of about $13 million US at the time, court documents say.

"We actually smacked a 185btc target today," Johnston wrote in a series of text messages to his accomplice, according to a criminal complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Miami. "Club feels mad good after today."
"And we ain't done," he added.
Prosecutors said Johston splurged on "an extravagant nightlife and entertainment lifestyle" while living in the Miami area, where he relocated in 2024.
Some of his big-ticket purchases are laid out in court documents: a high-powered Lamborghini Aventador SVJ, two BMWs, jewelry and a private jet rental.
He didn't hide the ruse. According to a witness interviewed by investigators, Johnston showed others how he carried out the thefts by sharing his screen over the social platform Discord.

items: 'Crypto King' trial hears recording of Aiden Pleterski admitting $300M fund 'never existed'

blocks.text: Johnston's defence lawyer Brooke C. Watson said in a recent court filing that after his arrest, the Canadian "turned over all of the stolen cryptocurrency in his possession," approximately $3.8 million US in bitcoin and ether, another typo of cryptocurrency.
"Mr. Johnston quickly admitted his conduct and is tremendously sorry for what he has done," Watson wrote.

Johnston had overstayed his 12-month U.S. tourist visa after crossing from Fort Erie, Ont., to Buffalo, N.Y., in October 2024 at age 18. But the lawyer revealed in a court filing last week that Johnston's scheme started months earlier — when he was just 17 — in January 2024.

In a court filing before sentencing, a defence lawyer for Johnston included pictures titled 'Trenton Johnston, growing up in Canada.' The name of his hometown is redacted in the court documents. (U.S. District Court, Southern District of Florida)
Hometown redacted in court documents

Watson did not respond to CBC News when asked where in Canada Johnston is from. His hometown and the names of his parents — a mechanic and a hair stylist — are redacted in court documents filed last week ahead of sentencing.

In a plea deal, federal prosecutors agreed to withdraw a wire fraud conspiracy charge in exchange for Johnston's guilty plea to one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida had previously announced that Johnston faced 20 years in prison if convicted on both counts.
Prosecutors later said Johnston provided "substantial assistance in the investigation and prosecution" of other unnamed individuals.

items: Canadian cybersecurity exec arrested by FBI accused of working with criminals to defraud his own clients

blocks.text: He still faces a drug possession charge from Florida state prosecutors stemming from amphetamine pills found in a Hermes bag at the time of his March arrest in the back of that Rolls-Royce Cullinan in North Miami.
It's unclear when Johnston will be released from custody.
He already agreed to a removal order issued in April by a U.S. immigration judge.
Eventually, Johnston is expected to be handed over to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to be deported to Canada.
If you have a news tip related to this story, contact CBC News senior reporter Thomas Daigle by email: thomas.daigle@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Long-term medication or modern crash diet? Inside the new world of GLP-1s
articles.summary: GLP-1s were designed and tested for long-term use, to combat chronic health conditions like diabetes and obesity. But what happens when you take these blockbuster weight loss drugs for a short stint?…

image.caption: GLP-1s were designed and tested for long-term use to combat chronic health conditions like diabetes and obesity. But what happens when you take these blockbuster weight loss drugs for a short stint? Scientists are trying to find out. (Matthew Hoddy/CBC)

blocks.text: At a bridal shop in downtown Halifax, Beverley Smith is trying on wedding dresses, but there’s a catch: She's rapidly losing weight since starting a GLP-1.

The 32-year-old has already gone on and off several types of these popular medications to manage weight gain and other side-effects linked to polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), but decided to get serious about her health before getting married next summer.
She’s lost more than 30 pounds since starting the drug tirzepatide back in March, and says related symptoms — like joint pain — have improved as well.
Now she’s asking the same question as millions of GLP-1 users around the world: Is it possible to one day stop taking the drug that’s changed life for the better?
"When you are going off it…. do you taper off of it or do you stop abruptly?" Smith wondered. "What is this really going to look like in the long term?"
As these blockbuster drugs explode in popularity, with more people using them off-label for short-term weight loss, scientists are also striving to find an answer.
"This is a real-world situation that needs to be studied," said Dr. Thomas Leung, a clinician-scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, who’s among the researchers doing exactly that.
Microdosing, drug cycling and more
GLP-1 drugs work by suppressing blood sugar, controlling appetite and slowing stomach emptying, all by mimicking their namesake hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, which is released after you eat.

items: 3 million Canadians use GLP-1 drugs. Survey says that's changing their appetites — and habits
Should everyone be on GLP-1s? What the science really tells us about cancer prevention and other benefits

blocks.text: While these medications only became part of the zeitgeist in the last few years — driven by celebrity endorsements, before hitting the mainstream — they’ve been around for more than two decades.

The earliest forms were studied and approved to treat Type 2 diabetes. Later, options arrived for chronic weight management. What’s relatively new is the myriad ways people are using these medications, often with minimal medical supervision.

At a private appointment inside Kind Bridal in Halifax, Beverley Smith tries on a wedding dress and discusses alterations to accommodate her ongoing weight loss while using a GLP-1. (Hugo Levesque/CBC)
Many patients — or as some drugmakers now call them, "customers" — are treating GLP-1s like a yo-yo diet rather than taking them long term to manage chronic health conditions.

They’re ever easier to get through online pharmacies. And pill forms, versus injections, are becoming more accessible. (Though not yet available in Canada, there is a pill-based form of semaglutide — the drug best known by the brand name Ozempic — already approved in the U.S. from drugmaker Novo Nordisk, alongside a pill version of orforglipron from Eli Lilly.)

items: 1st generic semaglutide injection for weight loss approved: Health Canada

blocks.text: Scroll through social media and it’s easy to find a range of short-term uses, from bodybuilders cycling through different types of GLP-1s (and steroids, too) alongside their gym routines to women "microdosing" the drugs off and on to manage menopausal weight gain to brides and grooms doing quick stints to lose weight before their wedding day.
One recent study from a Danish research team looked at the use of semaglutide for obesity and found roughly half of adults stopped treatment within just 12 months.
Ozempic, other GLP-1 drugs may help with dozens of other conditions
Stop-and-start approach could hinder weight loss

It’s a trend Dr. Leung, the researcher from the University of Pennsylvania, noticed in his own social circle in recent years, as more of his friends and colleagues wanted to try GLP-1s just to drop a few pounds.

Some talked about wanting to shed weight before a vacation or to look good on Instagram or just to feel healthier. The common thread? A desire to go on the meds, then get off them as fast as possible.

"No one had really studied what happens when you model what human behaviour is, which is starting and stopping these drugs," Leung said. "So we’re like, OK, well, obviously you can’t test this in humans. But we can try to do this in mice."

items: Generic Ozempic is now about $100 a month across the country. Canadians are taking note
Health Canada approves 1st generic version of Novo Nordisk's Ozempic

blocks.text: Leung and his research team did exactly that, and found cycling overweight mice through GLP-1 use seemed to make the drugs less effective over time. Mice who started and stopped the drugs every two weeks struggled to lose weight compared to mice who stayed on GLP-1s for the entire months-long study.
Even after two months of consistent use at the end of the study period, the drug-cycling group remained 20 per cent heavier.
If that was happening to mice, Leung started to wonder: What’s actually happening inside the bodies of human patients stopping and starting these body-changing drugs?
Ozempic: the future of addiction treatment?
'Buyer beware' when using GLP-1s off-label
Dr. Sean Wharton sees that regularly in his own patients at the Wharton Medical Clinic for weight and diabetes management in Burlington, Ont.
"People are using it off-label often. Maybe they heard about something on the internet or on Facebook. And if they're using it in this manner off-label, then it’s … buyer beware," he said.
"Because I don't know what type of negative aspects could potentially happen. There could be mainly positive and no negative aspects, but we don't exactly know yet."

items: People regained weight, worsened heart health after stopping weight loss drugs: review
Health Canada warns about fake or unauthorized versions of GLP-1 drugs

blocks.text: Wharton stressed this growing class of drugs has clear benefits as a long-term treatment for obesity, which has a dangerous domino effect on other health issues, like inflammation and cardiovascular disease, when left untreated.
Research also suggests GLP-1s may help curb substance use disorders, cut the severity of sleep apnea or even reduce cancer risk.
Dr. Sean Wharton is an internal medicine specialist and clinical researcher in obesity medicine in Toronto. (Craig Chivers/CBC)

Yet increasingly, these drugs are moving from tested treatment into what Wharton calls the "aesthetic medicine space" for short-term use. And he says the benefits likely vanish when patients rush back off these drugs.

"If losing the weight was the reason why your metabolic condition — like your heart failure, your high blood pressure — got better, then regaining the weight usually means that that blood pressure is going to go back up."

items: Ozempic use, protein-maxxing driving up whey protein prices
We know junk food isn't healthy, but scientists are trying to determine if it's also bad for our brains

blocks.text: Last year, one major research review concluded that the "magnitude and consistency" of these kinds of health effects "underscore the physiological consequences of [GLP-1] discontinuation."
A key need, according to that research team, was treatment guidelines to also address how to stop using the drugs.
What's the best way to go off these drugs?

GLP-1 pioneer Dr. Daniel Drucker agrees with that approach. In Toronto, he’s helping lead a randomized controlled trial — the gold standard of health-care research — to find out the best way for people to safely stop taking the drugs that he helped bring to the masses.

The research team, which includes Wharton and Drucker’s colleague and fellow endocrinologist Dr. Caroline Kramer, is recruiting patients for a 16-week-long study period where they’ll go through regular bloodwork and other metrics to gauge the impact of slowly tapering off a GLP-1 compared to abruptly stopping.

items: How do semaglutides or GLP1's work?

blocks.text: "We’re trying to answer a very simple question: If someone wants to know, can they come off the GLP-1 medicines, what is the best way to do it?" Drucker told CBC News inside a lab at Mount Sinai Hospital.
"Pharmaceutical companies are not good at studying how to stop their medicine," Drucker said, "but we need to answer that question."

GLP-1 researchers Dr. Caroline Kramer, left, and Dr. Daniel Drucker are studying the best way to stop using these blockbuster drugs through a trial based out of Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto. (Lauren Pelley/CBC)

Drucker is among those who sees huge potential for GLP-1s as a way to reduce the dire impacts of obesity — a public health crisis so widespread that just this year, the World Health Organization released its first-ever guidelines to manage obesity starting from childhood.

But tackling long-term medical issues usually requires long-term treatment, he stressed. When you discontinue minoxidil for hair regrowth, for example, hair loss restarts. If you suddenly stop taking statins, cholesterol spikes fast. Why would GLP-1s be any different?

"There is a lot of stigma around staying on a medicine to control your body weight for long periods of time, but we would never have anyone question if they had MS or Crohn's or hypertension or high cholesterol," Drucker said.

"I could list at least 125 diseases where you take the medication for the rest of your life to control the disease, but for some reason with the GLP-1 medicine, people think, well, you should be able to do this yourself."
Short-term use may 'cause more harm than good'
Kramer said there really hasn’t been research to help show if the cardiovascular benefits of being on a GLP-1 can be maintained by gradually tapering off rather than quickly stopping.
The team will also be watching for symptoms and adverse events, given there can be a range of side-effects from common stomach upset to acute pancreatitis to rare reports of vision loss.

items: What does thin mean in the age of GLP1s?
Why cheaper weight loss drugs could be a 'gamechanger' for Canadians

blocks.text: Kramer's advice for Canadians who want to do a short-term stint on a weight-loss drug before her team’s results come in?
"Patients who want to shed, like, three pounds because, ‘I have a wedding in two weeks’ … that is not what the medications were meant for," she said.
"If you are thinking of taking a medication without the proper assessment over a short term … it may cause more harm than good."

articles.title: BARMM, Zamboanga lead in illicit cigarette trade -- study
articles.summary: Illicit cigarettes accounted for more than 80% of cigarette consumption in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) and Zamboanga Peninsula, according to a study commissioned by…

blocks.text: Published October 27, 2026 3:27pm

Illicit cigarettes accounted for more than 80% of cigarette consumption in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) and Zamboanga Peninsula, according to a study commissioned by the Philippine Tobacco Institute (PTI).
The Kantar Open Pack Study recorded an illicit cigarette incidence rate of 85.6% in BARMM and 81% in Region IX between November 2025 and February 2026.

Lanao del Sur posted the highest provincial rate at 93.5%, followed by Zamboanga Sibugay at 87.5% and Zamboanga del Sur at 81.4%. Maguindanao recorded an incidence rate of 77%, while Region X posted 54.8%.
Nationwide, the incidence of illicit cigarettes fell to 16.3% from 17.6% in the previous survey, marking the first decline in five years, the PTI said in a news release on Tuesday.
The figures point to a sharp regional disparity in the illicit cigarette trade, with the problem remaining particularly pronounced in parts of Mindanao despite the recent national decline.
Separately, a study by the EU-ASEAN Business Council estimated that illicit cigarettes accounted for 25.3% of total cigarette consumption in the Philippines in 2025.

PTI president Bayen Elero-Tinga attributed the persistence of illicit trade partly to the widening price gap between legal cigarettes and untaxed contraband, which she said criminal networks exploit as legitimate products become more expensive following annual tax increases.

“Progress may be possible, but the problem remains far too large. We must continue strengthening enforcement, particularly in high-incidence areas... The fight against illicit tobacco is far from over,” Elero-Tinga said.— MCG, GMA News

blocks.text: India news: Arunachal sees more violence as anti-dam protests spread

More violence erupted in India's northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh over proposed hydroelectric projects that locals are protesting. Also, India's top court will hear pleas against the poll body chief. More on DW.

blocks.caption: Anti-dam protests have been erupting across Arunachal Pradesh as locals fear mass displacementImage: ANI News/IMAGO

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: Protests and violence spread in Arunachal Pradesh over proposed Menga Dam
Supreme Court to hear petitions against election body chief Gyanesh Kumar voter roll revision

blocks.text: Here are the top headlines from India on Tuesday, October 27:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
October 27, 2026
Anti-damn protests spread in Arunachal Pradesh
Violent protests broke out against a proposed hydroelectric project in Arunachal Pradesh on Monday in Daporijo town.
Normal life in Daporijo was interrupted as student organizations implemented a 12-hour general strike over the 1,605-megawatt Upper Subansiri hydroelectric plant, also known as the Menga Dam project.
The protesters are demanding authorities permanently withdraw the power project.
Anti-damn protests have been building up in the northeastern mountain state, with locals fearing mass displacement, loss of ancestral land, ecological losses and seismic risks.
India: Indigenous women resist mega dam project

News outlets reported that tensions escalated during the strike leading to fresh violence. At least one police vehicle was damaged and a police constable injured, the Arunachal Times reported. The report said that supporters of the strike also allegedly vandalized an office rented by India's flagship hydroelectric power generation company, setting office equipment on fire.
The Times of India also reported that local police conducted a flag march and appealed for peace.

In the village of Taliha, residents voice strong opposition to the Menga Damn project and the related land assessment exercise in motion. Protesters blocked a bridge to restrict movement, Arunachal Times reported, adding that their demonstrations were largely peaceful.
Not the only controversial dam

Protests and related violence shook Pasighat on October 23 after police fired tear gas at youths protesting the proposed 11,000-megawatt Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP). That's a different, larger but an equally as controversial project as the Menga Dam.
Protesters had allegedly set fire to buildings and vehicles then as well, prompting police forces to arrest dozens of demonstrators.

articles.title: 'A dream come true' - Harry Kane on his Ballon d'Or win

articles.title: Major Chinese brands drop Mbappé as backlash grows over Mao joke
articles.summary: He allegedly said his "favourite meme" is "the one where they put my face on a Chinese dictator".

blocks.text: Even China's foreign ministry has weighed in, with spokesperso Lin Jian: "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."
Neither Mbappé nor the The Bridge have commented on this yet.

It's unclear when the interview was broadcast but Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments on Monday night in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people".

A backlash quickly ensued online, with some users criticising Mbappé – who is hugely popular in China and has big endorsements - of "profiting from the Chinese market yet making remarks that offend the Chinese public".
"International public figures, in particular, should show greater respect and sensitivity, as national sentiment must never be taken lightly," read another comment on Weibo.

Mao founded Communist China in 1949 and ruled through tumultuous decades in the 1960s and 1970s. His attempt at rapid industrialisation, which he called the Great Leap Forward, led to a famine that killed tens of millions. Then came the Cultural Revolution: a violent purge of anyone seen as a threat to Communism, which included Chinese intellectuals, landowners, artists and often rivals within the Party.

His death in 1976 brought a new era for China, which began to open its doors to the global economy. Even as the country moved away from Mao's rule, he continued to be hailed by the Chinese Communist Party as a national icon whose legacy was beyond reproach.
Given how Mao is regarded to this day in China, the may seem unsurprising to many.

The backlash is still growing. Chinese state broadcaster, CCTV, is suspending La Liga matches, according to The Paper. And some reports claim t 's state broadcaster CCTV's news apps no longer have content related to the French striker.
The Chinese brands have not explicitly said why they were terminating the contract but referred to hurt sentiments.
The country's largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people".
Drinks giant Dongpeng, said: "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments."
Given brands have not mentioned the controversial clip, some users on social media are also asking what exactly Mbappé had said or done that was offensive.

Mbappé, who made his debut for Real Madrid in August 2024, has been nicknamed "the dictator" in the football world because of his influence and control over club and international football operations.
In 2024, he sued a French influencer and kebab shop owner for using his name in the description of one of the shop's sandwiches. Some say the incident reinforced his "dictator" portrayal.
The nickname has also made Mbappé the subject of many memes online.

France team-mate Ousmane Dembele jumped on the trend during the 2026 World Cup by calling Mbappé Mobut – a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, for three decades.

In an interview with France Football in September, Mbappé acknowledged the light-heartedness behind many of these memes, but said they "sometimes reveals a lack of political and human awareness among people".
"There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history.
"Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life," he had said.

articles.title: Melting glaciers in Dolomites reveal cache of first world war munitions
articles.summary:
Italian army removes and defuses 250 explosives encased in ice for more than 100 years after hikers’ sightings

A significant cache of unexploded bombs from the first world war emerged this…

blocks.text: A significant cache of unexploded bombs from the first world war emerged this summer from rapidly retreating glaciers in the Dolomites, the Italian army has said.
The devices, which included Italian artillery shells and French mortar bombs, were removed and defused by the army’s Julia Alpine brigade, according to a statement.
The weapons originated from the white war, a battle between the Austro-Hungarian army and Italian troops across treacherous and bitterly cold terrain between 1915 and 1918.

blocks.caption: Soldiers from Italian army’s Julia Alpine brigade at work. Photograph: Julia Alpine brigade

blocks.text: More than a century later, hikers reported several sightings of bombs during the summer, mostly in the area of Canal San Bovo in the Primiero Valley in eastern Trentino. The soldiers then conducted an extensive sweep there and across other high-altitude and glacier locations in the Trentino Alto Adige region of the Dolomites.

They recovered and neutralised 250 explosives, including “18 Italian 75mm artillery shells and 37 Thevetot mortar shells – a French-made device that was also supplied to the Italian royal army during the first world war”, the Julia Alpine brigade.
It is not the first time that relics of the white war have emerged from melting glaciers, whose retreat has accelerated over more than decade.

blocks.caption: A soldier with some of the munitions recovered.  Photograph: Julia Alpine brigade

blocks.text: “It is very much a consequence of global heating,” said Stefano Morosini, a professor at the University of Bergamo and the coordinator of heritage projects at Stelvio national park, where some of the explosives were also found.

“In recent years, at the end of each summer, these dangerous artefacts emerge and each year there is a higher number. They have been conserved by the ice for more than 100 years. Some had already exploded but many hadn’t, so now when they re-emerge, they are very, very dangerous.”
The advice to hikers and mountaineers is to “never touch any type of explosive device you might find, regardless of where it is located” and to promptly report any discovery to police.

Fought mainly in the Dolomites of Trentino Alto-Adige and the Alps of the Lombardy region, the white war was a period of history frozen in time until the 1990s, when global heating started to reveal an assortment of perfectly preserved relics, including weapons, sledges, letters and diaries.
after newsletter promotion

A wooden barracks that had been dug into a cave on the top of Mount Scorluzzo, a 3,095-metre (10,154ft) peak overlooking the Stelvio pass, reappeared in 2015 after the ice which had sealed it off for almost a century completely melted.

The shelter had been hastily locked up when the first world war ended in November 1918, and the soldiers abandoned most of their belongings. Beds made of straw as well as clothes, lanterns, newspapers, postcards, coins, and tinned food were found well preserved inside.
A white war museum to host the relics is scheduled to open in Bormio in June 2027.
The white war is thought to have claimed more than a million lives, although the majority of soldiers were believed to have been killed by avalanches, falling down mountains or hypothermia.
Dozens of corpses, some still in their uniforms, have emerged from the melting ice over the past 15 years.
The relatives of an Italian soldier were able to bury him in 2017 after documents revealing his identity were found with his body on Presena glacier.
Morosini said the intense summer heat was making access to the glaciers in the Dolomites less safe. Eleven people died when a huge mass of the Marmolada glacier broke off in 2022.
“It is becoming more and more impossible to access the glaciers during the summer because of the very long heatwave at high altitude,” he said.
“If you come to the area, you can see how fast the glaciers are retreating and how strong the impact of climate change is.”

articles.title: UK government met 137 businesses over AI datacentres – but no environmental groups
articles.summary:
Investigation finds dozens of ministers and civil servants moved into AI roles as government developed datacentre expansion plans

The UK’s policy on datacentres and AI was developed without…

blocks.text: The UK’s policy on datacentres and AI was developed without any meetings with environmental groups, an investigation has found.

The nonprofit organisation Spotlight on Corruption said a “considerable revolving door” shaped the government’s development of “AI growth zones”, a central plank of the former prime minister Keir Starmer’s AI and economic policy, with 38 ministers, senior civil servants and special advisers hired to positions in AI companies between July 2024 and September 2026.
Meanwhile, even as top officials left government for jobs at OpenAI and Anthropic, government departments largely failed to engage meaningfully with stakeholders outside the technology industry.

Kamila Kingstone, a campaign lead at the NGO, said: “The government totally failed at the most senior level to speak to environmental NGOs or community groups when developing its flagship policy on AI datacentres. This is despite the serious environmental implications of its plans.”

Over 12 months, Spotlight on Corruption filed 40 freedom of information requests to 18 government agencies, seeking details of meetings and investment figures relating to the government’s policymaking on the growth zones, covering the period between July 2024 and June 2026.

The investigation found that ministers, permanent secretaries and directors general involved in developing the policy met 137 businesses – some several times – to discuss Britain’s datacentre policy. By contrast, senior officials met only two community groups and no environmental organisations.

blocks.caption: Approval has been given for a £500m redevelopment of the Truman Brewery site in Brick Lane, east London, to include a datacentre.  Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: Of the 38 senior officials who left government, nine were from the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, which has played a central role in shaping Britain’s AI strategy. These included a former minister for AI and intellectual property, a former AI adviser to the prime minister, a former director of AI opportunities, a deputy director of AI international policy and a head of AI engineering.

AI growth zones were a groundbreaking policy under which the government promised to “turbocharge the economy” and create jobs by building massive datacentres across five regions – in Starmer’s words, “mainlining AI into the veins” of the country.

The policy aimed to pave the way for Britain to build big datacentres, some of them larger than any datacentre that has been built in the country so far. These developments, often partnered with US tech companies, would supposedly bring in thousands of jobs.

Investigations by the Guardian have called the policy into question, suggesting that it rests on assumptions that do not hold up, financial figures that were not audited and exaggerated projections for job creation.

In particular, the Guardian has shown there is little realism behind announced plans to power these developments, and claims that they will use purpose-built renewables. In fact, different government departments appear to diverge on how much electricity the UK’s datacentre plans will actually require – and what their environmental cost will therefore be.

Meanwhile, there has been growing opposition to datacentres in Britain, with campaign groups protesting against planned developments in places ranging from Auchtertool, a rural village north of Edinburgh, to Brick Lane in east London.

blocks.caption: Fourteen local campaigns rallied in September at Holyrood against datacentres planned in Scotland.  Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian

blocks.text: Chi Onwurah, the MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the growing backlash – and the far larger opposition in the US – was a warning that the government needed to seek greater community input.
after newsletter promotion

“It is critically important that AI benefits communities and is also shaped by them,” she said. “I’ve been concerned about what we’ve seen in the US, where there’s a strong feeling that datacentres are being imposed without adequate consultation. We can see the backlash influencing the midterms. It’s really important that communities are involved in datacentres and AI growth zones and see the benefits.”

Spotlight on Corruption’s investigation suggests that previous policy was largely shaped by conversations with business, and that the government “failed to take the environmental and social impacts [of datacentres] seriously”.
While the government met a handful of civil society groups, these meetings were “held a few days before the launch of the policy, meaning they had no meaningful input”, according to the report.

Finally, many further meetings between businesses and Starmer’s administration would not have been disclosed, said Spotlight on Corruption. This is largely because Starmer’s policy was led by a special adviser, Jade Leung, whose role was subject to far less stringent transparency requirements.

Spotlight on Corruption also looked at how other countries – including Canada, Germany and Australia – developed policy. It found these countries consulted far more widely on introducing datacentres and had more stringent environmental criteria. It said the UK had “fallen behind equivalent jurisdictions” in developing an equitable strategy.

A government spokesperson said: “We are clear that datacentres should create British jobs, strengthen supply chains and deliver benefits for the communities that host them, while prioritising clean power and using water responsibly – and meet with these companies to make sure that happens. We want to work closely with industry, local authorities, environmental groups and communities, and welcome opportunities to hear their views.

“For most proposed datacentre developments, community benefits are considered through the relevant local planning processes. We have already announced measures which will enable local authorities hosting datacentres in AI growth zones in England to keep all the additional business rates they generate.”

articles.title: Asthma deaths reach decade-high levels and number of Australians dying of dementia grows
articles.summary:
Dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease, accounted for more than 10% of all deaths for the first time, new data reveals

  • Get our

blocks.text: Dementia has accounted for more than 10% of all deaths for the first time, while the number of people dying from asthma is at decade-high levels, new data published by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) reveals.

There were 188,421 deaths registered in 2025. Of these, 19,019 deaths were caused by dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease, the ABS deaths data released on Tuesday shows. It has been the leading cause of death in Australia since 2024.
The other leading causes of death in 2025 were ischaemic heart diseases, cerebrovascular diseases (such as stroke), lung cancer and chronic respiratory diseases.
Dementia Australia’s chief executive, Prof Tanya Buchanan, said there was an urgent need to act on dementia, given it was a leading public health issue.
“The data underlines the critical need for more recognition and funding to support people living with dementia, their families and carers,” Buchanan said.
There are an estimated 446,500 Australians currently living with dementia, and a further 1.7 million people involved in their care, she said.
“Despite the growing impact of dementia, investment in specific services, supports and prevention have not kept the same pace, and the stigma that surrounds dementia continues,” she said.
“This needs to change.”
The data also revealed the highest number of asthma deaths recorded in a decade.
There were 484 Australians who died from asthma in 2025, up from 478 deaths in 2024.
Women account for almost two-thirds of asthma deaths, and almost two-thirds of all dementia deaths.
Asthma Australia’s CEO, Kate Miranda, said poorly controlled asthma increases the risk and is a preventable reason behind many asthma-related deaths.
“We have effective treatments and clear clinical guidelines, yet too many Australians are not getting the care they need to stay well,” she said.

Research has found the proportion of adults with well-controlled asthma has been falling, with many using little or no preventer treatment. Adherence among those using inhaled corticosteroids was also worsening, Miranda said.
after newsletter promotion
Too many people only used asthma-reliever medications, and rely on it for their symptoms.
“But it doesn’t treat the underlying inflammation,” Miranda said.

“People, especially those with mild cases, think ‘it’s just asthma’, so they don’t get regular checkups and talk to their GP about their medication. People might take preventer medication on high pollen days or when they have a cold, but then they don’t take it otherwise.”
She said people should be aware that asthma guidelines have shifted to recommend anti-inflammatory reliever (Air) therapy, an anti-inflammatory that also treats symptoms.
“People, especially older Australians, are still using medications they had as a child without being aware guidelines have changed and better options exist,” Miranda said.
Drug-induced deaths also remained a public health issue in 2025, rising to 2,063 deaths from 2,007 deaths in 2024.

The ABS’s head of mortality statistics, Lauren Moran, said while opioids and benzodiazepines continue to be the most common drug classes involved in these deaths, there has been substantial growth in people dying after using stimulants, including methamphetamine.
Suicide remained the leading cause of premature death for both males and females in 2025, with men accounting for almost three-quarters of these deaths.

articles.title: Albanese concedes $6m golf club grant in his electorate was not to contain ‘raw sewage’
articles.summary:
Grant part of $560m invitation-only scheme transparency advocates say largely funded projects in Labor-held seats

  • Follow our
articles.byline: Sarah Basford Canales and Kat Wong

blocks.text: Anthony Albanese has admitted he got it wrong after telling parliament a $6m grant to a golf club in his electorate was to stop “raw sewage” going into the nearby river.

The grant given to Marrickville golf club in Sydney’s inner-west is under scrutiny as part of a larger $560m invitation-only grants scheme, which transparency advocates say largely funded projects promised at the 2025 election in Labor-held seats.

Infrastructure department officials told a Senate estimates hearing on Monday afternoon the $6m grant given to the club in Albanese’s electorate did not fund works to prevent raw sewage from flowing into the nearby river, contrary to the prime minister’s claims.
“I can confirm that sewerage is not a component of this grant,” the department’s assistant secretary, Jacinta McDonald, said.
The assistant education minister, Anthony Chisholm, defended the prime minister’s response, saying the scope had changed since the local council’s original proposal.

“I think that was part of the original plan. But as often happens, as the scope of these sorts of announcements happen, the scope can change, and the New South Wales government, is my understanding, stepped in in support of the sewerage work,” Chisholm said.

First reported by the ABC, Albanese, who holds honorary social membership at the club, has swatted away any criticism that he influenced, or benefitted from, the decision, which was signed off by another minister.
In question time in early September, the prime minister told the house the money would go toward “an environmental project stopping raw sewage going into the Cooks River during flooding”.

“[The golf club] has existed for a long time, almost a 100 years, and they have a septic tank because it is on the floodplain, when it floods in Marrickville raw sewage flows into the Cooks River – that is what the funding is for,” Albanese said in another response to questions about his involvement in the decision-making process.

The prime minister was grilled repeatedly by the opposition about the grant in question time on Tuesday afternoon and the shadow energy minister, Dan Tehan, accused the prime minister of misleading the parliament, and urged him to correct the record.

In response, Albanese conceded “it was not correct” to say the funding was for sewerage works but said it was a matter for the infrastructure department, and noted the council was finalising the design of the project – including improvements to the clubhouse, stormwater harvesting, a new toilet and landscaping.
The NSW government committed in September 2025 to address sewerage infrastructure at the club, he said.

“I’m advised that the club, of course, has a long history. And indeed, in the media release announcing the project, it spoke about the venue’s last major remodel being in 1947. So this is a local club, owned by the council,” Albanese said.
“The [federal] funding was going to be for sewerage. The New South Wales government have stepped in, which is appropriate given that New South Wales run water and sewerage.”

articles.title: ‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph
articles.summary:
Binbag-wielding volunteers clear encampment used by thugs to intimidate opponents of deposed government

Student List cleaned up at Serbia’s parliamentary elections. So it was only fitting…

blocks.text: Student List cleaned up at Serbia’s parliamentary elections. So it was only fitting that the morning after a night of raucous celebrations, the movement’s supporters were gathering, bin bags in hand, at Pioneers Park, opposite the national assembly building in Belgrade.

For the previous 18 months, this small patch of greenery – with its established trees and playground – had been a no-go zone. A pro-government camp known as Ćaciland had taken over the space with convicted criminals living there in white tents, happy to attack journalists, or anyone else who came too close. Police stood by but did nothing to prevent the violence.

On election night, it seemed that thuggery might be on the cards again. Half an hour before the polls closed, large numbers of masked, black-clad men started gathering in and around Pioneers Park. Their intimidating presence gave credence to pre-poll predictions that the governing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) would not hand over power without a struggle.

What happened next took almost everyone by surprise. Shortly after the polls closed – and before any projections of the results had been published – Aleksandar Vučić told supporters at SNS headquarters that they had suffered a comprehensive defeat to the Student List. As cheers rang around the heart of Belgrade, he added that he did “not want unrest” or “anything like that on the streets”.

blocks.caption: Hundreds of volunteers joined municipal workers to remove the remains of the Ćaciland camp, opposite Serbia’s national assembly building. Photograph: Guy de Launey

blocks.text: The riot police stood aside and the barriers blocking access to the area around Pioneers Park were removed. The goon squad made a rapid exit – and Student List supporters joyfully ransacked Ćaciland, setting fire to some of the tents.

But this is not a movement that likes to leave a mess. Over the two years of anti-corruption protests that led to the Student List’s victory, participants have always cleaned up after themselves. So the call went out for volunteers to restore Pioneers Park to something approaching its previous state.

Hundreds of people answered the appeal and joined municipal workers to remove the remains of Ćaciland. Some dismantled the mangled white tents, while others painstakingly cleaned and disinfected the climbing frames, swings and slides in the children’s playground.

Radomir Dalic painstakingly combed over the grass to remove cigarette butts and other rubbish. Apparently relishing his labours, he said he was overjoyed that the park was finally rid of “criminals with violent intentions towards us”.
“Yesterday was a big victory, so today is the smell of freedom,” he added. “We are in garbage, but it’s the smell of freedom.”

blocks.caption: Radomir Dalic, who took part in the clean-up, said dealing with the garbage was worth it because Serbia was now free. Photograph: Guy de Launey

blocks.text: Tamara Tomic wore yellow rubber gloves for the occasion – and radiated similar pride in taking part. “Gathering here and cleaning this place just shows that we want to live nicely,” she said. “We want to enjoy the city, enjoy a normal life without violence and without anyone torturing us.”

For now, nobody is asking too many questions about how the Student List will govern. In fact, Serbian voters have taken something of a leap into the unknown – because this is a movement that operates unlike a traditional political party. It has no hierarchy and no leader. Its candidates were chosen by a series of student assemblies, with nominations ranging from academics to athletes, economists to engineers.

The Student List did publish an 11-point plan. Most of these points deal with anti-corruption measures – ironically, the pitch that secured victory in 2012 for Vučić and the SNS. Other commitments include judicial reform, media freedom, affordable housing and improved access to healthcare, with the promise of “a doctor in every village”.

But beyond the domestic priorities – in essence, a clean-up for public institutions – little is clear. The Student List went into the elections without naming a candidate for prime minister, let alone a possible cabinet.

Kurt Bassuener, co-founder of the Democratization Policy Council, said he was concerned about what that might mean when the euphoria of victory died down, and the serious business of forming a government began.

The thinktank chief added: “I’m hoping that there is a dream scenario plan here – they have portfolios and people who have credibility in particular issue areas and they can hit the ground running. Because the danger of a broad coalition like this is that the fissures will show soon after victory.”
after newsletter promotion

Ilija Srdanović, the candidate ranked first on the Student List, has played down the potential for strife. A cardiologist at the university in Novi Sad, the city where a deadly roof collapse sparked the student protests, he has protested alongside the students since the early days. However, he was keen to emphasise that his ranking on the list did not mean he would become prime minister.
“The student movement is fully democratic,” he said, adding that the aim was to buck Serbia’s history of “creating the cult of personality or leadership”.

blocks.caption: Ilija Srdanović, who was ranked first on Student List’s roster of candidates, said the party was fully democratic and would resist ‘the cult of personality’. Photograph: Guy de Launey

blocks.text: The 250 candidates on the Student List were “equal subjects in this struggle”, Srdanović insisted, with “numerous candidates who can be chosen for the prime minister position or any other position”.

But his confidence does little to reassure those who have noticed that the broad spread of views held by Student List candidates could lead to trouble. Despite Vučić’s warnings that a Student List government would impose sanctions on Russia and recognise Kosovo’s unilateral declaration of independence, the movement’s foreign and regional policy remains opaque.
“We have not seen seas of EU flags at demonstrations by students or the marches across Serbia,” said Michael Davenport, a former EU and UK ambassador to the country.

“There are massive policy areas where there is no consensus among the Student List or those have been elected. The approach towards accession to the European Union is not clear, nor is the position with regard to regional issues like Bosnia and Herzegovina and, very particularly, Kosovo.”

Many people are happy to leave these concerns for another day. Vučić and the SNS have fallen – and the cacophony of car horns continued throughout Monday as drivers passed the clean-up crew in Pioneers Park.
One visible symbol of the old regime has been swept away. The Student List voters are hoping more will follow.

articles.title: Israel heads to polls for pivotal election defined by security and democracy
articles.summary: Many fear neither of the leading political blocs will win enough seats for a majority - meaning weeks or months of political wrangling may lie ahead.

blocks.text: Israelis are heading to the polls for what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history.
Polling published on Friday suggests incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu is in a near neck-and-neck race with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot to become prime minister.
But neither of their political blocs are projected to win the 61 seats needed to form a majority government - meaning weeks or months of political wrangling may lie ahead.

The campaign has been shaped by the issue of security - with the opposition bloc hammering Netanyahu for the unprecedented security failure that led to the 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel, in which nearly 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken back to Gaza as hostages.
They have pushed for an independent commission of inquiry into the attacks - something Netanyahu has long resisted, insisting it would be biased against him.

Despite the opposition's attack lines, Netanyahu has once again framed himself as "Mr Security" - pointing to what he says are strategic victories in Israel's wars across the Middle East and his close relationship with US President Donald Trump.

Israel's proportional representation system means governments have always been coalitions - and the race to power can, and has, produced unexpected alliances. But this election looks especially tight - and lines in the sand have already been drawn.
Eisenkot, who leads the newly formed Yashar Party, is the main figure in the so-called "change bloc", a collection of parties who have ideological differences but share the goal of ousting Netanyahu.

Other leaders in the bloc include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security - and Yair Golan, a left-leaning former general.

For Netanyahu, a titan of Israeli politics who first served as prime minister in 1996, a return to power will hinge on another alliance with the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties that make up his current governing coalition - the most right-wing in Israel's history.

There are two Arab party blocs in the running too, as about one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. In theory, they could prove kingmakers. But all but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out working with them.
Eisenkot takes a broadly similar position to Netanyahu on Gaza, and has pledged to end Hamas rule in the territory within 18 months, through a US-led peace plan or, if necessary, military means.

Israel has continued to strike Gaza almost every day since a ceasefire was agreed last year, saying it is targeting Hamas operatives. The Israeli military has killed more than 74,000 people since the start of the war, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel has faced growing international condemnation over its conduct in the war, and relations with its allies around the world have deteriorated.

Eisenkot largely supports Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank - which are illegal under international law - but wants to crack down on extremist Jewish settlers whose attacks are at an all-time high, according to UN figures. He has also spoken about creating the conditions for "autonomy or a state-minus" for Palestinians - under ultimate Israeli security control.
The two-state solution - the creation of an independent Palestinian state in peaceful coexistence alongside Israel - has all but disappeared from mainstream Israeli politics.

Though some have speculated the Arab parties may end up informally propping up an Eisenkot-led minority government - Lieberman, a key prospective member, has ruled out being part of such an arrangement.
Red lines like these mean the electoral arithmetic is complex - but it remains to be seen what kind of concessions, deals and U-turns can be reached once the results come in.
An unprecedented 70,000 people have reportedly flown home from abroad to vote, while half a million are set to cast ballots for the first time.
At 22:00 (20:00 GMT) on Tuesday, Israeli broadcasters will publish exit polls. These will give some indication of the direction of voting, but can vary significantly.
Up and down the country, Israelis will gather to watch the results trickle in, with Netanyahu's Likud meeting in Jerusalem and Eisenkot's Yashar - formed only last year - assembling in Tel Aviv.

Hundreds of thousands of Israeli soldiers and reservists will also cast ballots, but many of those votes will not begin being counted until Wednesday - meaning there may be a late boon for the right-wing parties who are thought to have strong support from that demographic.

Though often framed as a run-off between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, it is possible another leader could take power, if they were to withhold their party's support for a coalition unless given the top job.

An outcome dreaded by many is political deadlock - where no bloc is able to reach a majority, and a minority government cannot be formed. In that scenario, new elections would be called, with Netanyahu to remain as interim prime minister.
Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five separate elections as parties struggled time and again to co-operate.

articles.title: UST campus declared safe after another bomb threat
articles.summary: UST's Manila campus was declared safe Tuesday after another online threat involving explosives.

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 1:40pm
Photo showing an event at the University of Santo Tomas as photographed in September 2026.
UST via FB
MANILA, Philippines — The University of Santo Tomas (UST) has been declared safe after receiving another bomb threat on Tuesday, October 27, the second such incident this month.
In a statement Tuesday, October 27, UST said its Manila campus had been declared safe by authorities as of the morning.

"The University is actively coordinating with the Philippine National Police and related government agencies to investigate and address the safety threats circulating online. Upon recommendation from law enforcers, no evacuation order was issued," it said.
The university added that law enforcers and campus security personnel had completed their assessment and declared the campus safe for occupancy.

According to a spot report by Manila Police District Police Station 14, UST Detachment Commander Joseph Badinas and College of Rehabilitation Sciences Acting Dean Donald Manlapaz alerted law enforcement after a representative of a college-based organization received a threat through Facebook Messenger at around 6 a.m.

The sender, whose account name was "TIGER TTIGER," claimed to have overheard a conversation in a library restroom about plans to detonate explosives and carry out a shooting in three university buildings.

The report said the same account later sent messages to the UST Central Student Council at around 7 a.m. and the Central Commission on Elections at around 7:40 a.m. The account was deactivated at 7:45 a.m.
Following the 7:40 a.m. report, police personnel were dispatched at 7:45 a.m. and arrived at the buildings mentioned in the threat by 7:55 a.m.
The incident remains under investigation, according to the Manila Police District.
UST also received bomb threats on October 23 after two threatening letters were found in separate toilets inside the university's Medicine Building. Police later found no explosives on campus.

articles.title: Albanese promises ‘swift response’ on MP safety as he mulls panic buttons for politicians
articles.summary:
Senator Fatima Payman also criticises former colleagues over lack of staffing given to her office

Anthony Albanese has promised a “swift government response” to safety threats to MPs and…
articles.byline: Josh Butler and Sarah Basford Canales

blocks.text: Anthony Albanese has promised a “swift government response” to safety threats to MPs and floated the provision of duress alarms for electorate offices, saying politicians and their staff have put up with threats for too long.

The prime minister’s pledge to the Labor partyroom came hours after senator Fatima Payman again slammed her former government colleagues over the lack of staffing given to her office, controversially asking: “Is the prime minister waiting for something, like what happened to Dr Helen Haines, to occur to my office?”

MPs across the political divide have spoken forcefully of the need for more protection for their offices after the alleged attack on the Indi MP last week, raising alarm about threats and violence directed to their staff. Politicians are also revealing the scale of abuse, online and offline, directed toward them, including death and rape threats.

In the first Labor partyroom meeting since the alleged attack, Albanese gave a long address, saying this week “must be a turning point” for civil discourse and how threats are responded to. He also conceded there needed to be more investment in security and safety for politicians.
Albanese said MPs have had to “put up with the threat environment for too long”, that the government “need to do more”, and “more can and should be done”.
“You’ve all dedicated so much to the safety of others in the workplace. I’m determined to make sure we do everything for your safety and the safety of your staff as well,” he said.

Albanese did not give specifics, but promised a “swift government response” on safety, and noted numerous MPs had raised the prospect of receiving duress alarms, or panic buttons, to alert authorities of a safety incident. This was among a “series of options” under consideration.
The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, also told the meeting that the government was looking at safety at polling booths around election time.

Government sources said numerous changes were being considered, with a fulsome response and proposal likely to be revealed in coming days. MPs have raised a wide range of concerns, including greater security and hardening of their electoral offices, better communication with federal police, and resources for security at their private homes like CCTV and lighting – all options understood to be under consideration.
An ongoing review into commonwealth workplaces will also be expedited by Labor, with recommendations specifically about safety and security to be delivered soon.

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told his MPs in a Coalition partyroom meeting of ongoing conversations with the government about personal safety and the importance of getting it right, but did not raise any specific proposals.
Payman speaks out

Payman, who quit Labor in 2024 to sit on the crossbench, on Monday night lashed out at the prime minister for not responding to a request for additional staff in line with other independent political offices.
after newsletter promotion

The prime minister has discretion over the allocation of personal staff, which are typically more senior advisers. All politicians receive electoral office staff, but Payman has zero advisers while 16 other crossbench MPs and senators shared 30 advisers, according to an internal document tabled in the hearing.

In a Senate estimates hearing, Payman questioned minister Don Farrell whether the staff allocation shortfall was due to Albanese having a personal gripe with her, claiming her staff were severely overworked.

“If [Albanese] cares so much about the welfare and wellbeing of people who work in this building, then I implore you [Farrell] and the prime minister to please look into the fact that my staff are burning out,” she said.
“Is the prime minister waiting for something, like what happened to Dr Helen Haines, to occur to my office? To me? For him to take our request seriously?”
Farrell and other Labor senators in the hearing strongly rejected the insinuation, but Payman refused to withdraw the comments when asked until her staffing request was dealt with.

Payman told Guardian Australia last week there had been a massive increase in the number of death threats and hate comments since 2024 when she defected from Labor. Payman said her office manager had opened mail last year containing human faeces, resulting in a biohazard team having to respond.

“We had all these people in hazmat suits come through [the office],” she said. “The trauma that that inflicts on my staff members is horrible. No office or no worker should ever have to deal with that kind of crap.”

articles.title: Israel election live: polls open in most consequential vote in country’s history
articles.summary: Most polling shows prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition will lose its majority, with Gadi Eisenkot the leading opposition contender

blocks.text: Polls open in elections for Israeli parliament

Hello and welcome to our coverage of the Israeli elections. Polls have opened in the first election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023, Israel’s subsequent destruction of Gaza, and the launch of its war with the US against Iran.

Most polling shows prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition will lose its majority in the 120-seat Knesset, but the opposition bloc will probably also fall short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.

For Netanyahu, 76, who has led the most far-right government in Israel’s history, the stakes are both political and personal. He is on trial for corruption in three separate cases, despite interventions from Donald Trump, who called for a pre-emptive pardon in the long-running saga and even wrote to Israeli president Isaac Herzog on Netanyahu’s behalf. The cases are ongoing.

blocks.caption: Ballot boxes are set up at a school in Tel Aviv. Photograph: Nir Keidar/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: It was on Netanyahu’s watch that Hamas militants broke out from Gaza three years ago to kill nearly 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians, on the deadliest day in Israel’s history. This election is widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership since those attacks.

The IDF’s globally condemned assault on Gaza, which has killed at least 75,000 people and been deemed a genocide by a UN commission, academics, legal scholars and Israeli and international rights groups, has left Israel a pariah on the world stage.

Three years of regional conflict followed the 7 October attacks, including this year’s war on Iran, which sparked an ongoing global energy crisis and has killed thousands of people, mainly in Lebanon and Iran.

blocks.caption: A man looks at the wreckage of an Iranian missile that landed near the West Bank city of Jericho in June. Photograph: Mahmoud Illean/AP

blocks.text: What is more, under Netanyahu’s government there has been an unprecedented, aggressive surge of deadly extremist settler violence to bolster Israeli control in the occupied West Bank, as settler militants and their political backers – who have propped up Netanyahu’s government – exploited their seat at the cabinet table and expanded with impunity.

Indeed, settlement expansion has been a key feature of Netanyahu’s re-election campaign. However, it is also a driving force behind Israel’s growing international isolation, with many of its traditional allies condemning “settler terrorists” and announcing plans to impose sanctions.

In Jerusalem

Israel is holding its first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks, the deadliest day in the country’s history, which resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians.
Since then Israel has pursued a war of annihilation in Gaza, launched two inconclusive wars with Iran, and intensified a campaign of state-backed ethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bank.

Domestically the coalition formed by Benjamin Netanyahu has taken aim at democratic institutions, including the supreme court. Many Israelis have described this election as the most consequential in their country’s history.

articles.title: 4 key takeaways from Ottawa's city election
articles.summary: In many ways, the city council that's sworn in to lead Ottawa through the next four years will look very much like the last one — including the mayor's seat — but there were some important shifts.

image.caption: Mark Sutcliffe arrives as his election party after being re-elected as mayor on Monday night. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Ottawa·Ottawa Votes 2026
In many ways, the city council that's sworn in to lead Ottawa through the next four years will look very much like the last one — including the mayor's seat — but there were some important shifts.
Turnout dips, gender breakdown shifts

Voters have had their say, and in many ways the city council that's sworn in to lead Ottawa through the next four years will look very much like the last one — including Mark Sutcliffe in the mayor's seat.
That may come as a disappointment to those who wanted the city to move in new directions, but there were some important shifts in the unofficial results.
Plus ça change
With the sole exception of Allan Hubley in Kanata South, every single one of the 22 incumbent councillors who ran for re-election is heading back to city hall. Two of those were acclaimed.

With Mayor Mark Sutcliffe holding the mayor's chair, that means there will be just three new faces around the council table next term: Erin Coffin, who beat Hubley, Joanne Chianello, who took mayoral contender Jeff Leiper's vacant seat in Kitchissippi, and Chelsea Walton, winner of the seat vacated by Glen Gower in Stittsville.
Considering how frequently both candidates and voters talked about change this election, there was remarkably little of it once all the votes were counted.
‘Our message resonated with voters’: Mark Sutcliffe speaks to supporters
Gender breakdown
Ottawa’s next city council will have more women than men by a count of 13 to 12. That hasn't happened since amalgamation.
Sixteen men were chosen in 2022. One left for provincial politics, two did not run again and one was defeated.
A woman replaced all four men; one was Isabelle Skalski, who won a byelection in 2025. The other three were elected on Monday.
In municipal elections between 2006 and 2022, between four and nine women were voted to council. When Skalski won last year, she became the tenth woman.
"I think it's really awesome," said Alta Vista Coun. Marty Carr, who was re-elected Monday night.

"[The women on council] have been a little bit overworked," Carr said, because female councillors have to be on more committees than their male counterparts to ensure that committees have gender equity.
‘I’m pretty excited about this’: Ottawa’s next council to have more women than men
Turnout
Preliminary results on Monday suggest voter turnout was quite low.
36.2 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot for mayor; the lowest turnout since 2003.
It’s down from 43.8 per cent in the last election.
In terms of total vote, about 314,400 people cast ballots this time. That’s only about 2,000 fewer votes than in 2022, but there were about 145,000 more eligible voters this time.
People vote on municipal election day in Ottawa. (Francis Ferland/CBC)
Survey says...

While candidates and other media outlets released their own polling numbers during the campaign, CBC reported on an opinion survey by Quorus Consulting Group last week that showed Sutcliffe with a single-digit lead over Jeff Leiper, the three-term councillor who stepped down to challenge him.

A breakdown of the survey results from all voters, including those who expressed no preference, placed Sutcliffe at 28 per cent, Leiper at 24 per cent, Neil Saravanamuttoo at seven per cent and Alex Lawson at four per cent.
Monday's unofficial results showed those four candidates finishing in the same order.

articles.title: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll
articles.summary:
Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom

Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in…

blocks.text: Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.

The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.
The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.
AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.

The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.

The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.
The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.

“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.

The US has banned humanoid robots from China, citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.

As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.

But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.
Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.

“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.

blocks.caption: Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings. Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.

Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.

On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.

China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.

This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum, an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.
Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.
