articles.title: As Dizon exits, DPWH reinforces LGU role in projects
articles.summary: Outgoing Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon said that the DPWH has revised its project approval policies to require coordination with local government units, as Giovanni Lopez prepares to take over…

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 12:13pm
Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon on Oct. 20, 2025.
The Philippine STAR / Jesse Bustos

MANILA, Philippines — Outgoing Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon said Tuesday, October 27, that the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) has revised its project approval policies to require coordination with local government units (LGUs), as Giovanni Lopez prepares to take over as the department's chief.

During a joint press conference with Lopez on Tuesday, October 27, Dizon said the department instituted a formal mechanism earlier this year to involve LGUs in public infrastructure development, with the goal of including local governments in the planning process as early as the budgeting phase.

"At the minimum, a Certificate of No Objection is required from the LGU; either (a) Certificate of No Objection, local masterplan or regional masterplan. These were not required in the past, but they are now," Dizon said in Filipino.
"Hindi na puwede 'yong mga DE (district engineer) gagawa na lang ng project kung saan-saan na 'di alam ng mga mayor," he added.
(District engineers can no longer get away with implementing projects wherever and without the knowledge of the mayor.)

These changes echo Malacañang's directive to strengthen LGU oversight of DPWH projects, issued after Bulacan Gov. Daniel Fernando claimed that around P41 billion worth of flood-control infrastructure in the province had not been coordinated with local governments.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. previously ordered a revamp of the approval process in September 2025 to address the removal of a rule requiring local governments to officially receive projects under former president Rodrigo Duterte's administration. The revision ensured that infrastructure projects could only be tagged as completed after they had been accepted by the concerned government units.

Uncompleted structures marked as finished by the DPWH helped expose alleged ghost flood-control projects and prompted parallel investigations by the House and Senate into various projects, several of which were in Bulacan province.

State witness Henry Alcantara notably certified some of these structures as completed during his tenure as Bulacan 1st District engineer, including a P55-million flood-control project in Baliwag. Alcantara's former aide, Wirt Walter Rosales, confirmed on October 23 that he delivered billions of pesos' worth of alleged kickbacks from flood-control projects to fugitive former party-list congressman Zaldy Co from 2022 to 2024.
Included in the "acknowledgment receipts" signed by Co's aides were separate sheets of paper indicating the project and the percentage of the kickback.

Carlo Rivera, an engineer alleged to have run errands for Alcantara, testified earlier Tuesday in the bail hearing for former House Speaker Martin Romualdez's plunder case involving the alleged P7.4-billion government infrastructure kickback scheme.

articles.title: Excitement 'beyond Hope' as B.C.'s next premier promises to bring rural, northern perspective to top job
articles.summary: Though he was born in New Westminster and raised in Surrey, Lorne Doerkson moved to the B.C. Interior as an adult, working for newspapers in Salmon Arm, Prince George and 100 Mile House before…

image.caption: Lorne Doerkson announces a campaign promise for wildfire mitigation in Summerland, B.C., on Oct. 2, 2026. (The Canadian Press/Aaron Hemens.)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Though he was born in New Westminster and raised in Surrey, Lorne Doerkson moved to the B.C. Interior as an adult, working for newspapers in Salmon Arm, Prince George and 100 Mile House before settling in Williams Lake in 2001. And he isn't shy about making his love for the region known.
Lorne Doerkson moved to B.C. Interior as an adult, and isn't shy about making his love for the region known
For the first time in decades, British Columbia will have a premier from north of Metro Vancouver following a general election victory.

Though he was born in New Westminster and raised in Surrey, Lorne Doerkson moved to the B.C. Interior as an adult, working for newspapers in Salmon Arm, Prince George and 100 Mile House before settling in Williams Lake in 2001.
And he isn't shy about making his love for the region known.

"I love Cariboo-Chilcotin," he enthused in his election night victory speech, calling Williams Lake home while also giving specific mention to key northern and Interior cities, including Fort St. John and Quesnel.
WATCH IN FULL: New premier-designate answers questions after historic victory in B.C. snap election

"For a very long time, a lot of British Columbians have felt like Victoria forgot about them, like the map maybe stopped at Hope," he said, referencing the community often referred to as the unofficial border between southern B.C. and the rest of the province.
"But tonight the whole map counts."
The last party leader from north of Vancouver to win an election was Bill Bennett, who left office in 1986.
Dan Miller served as premier and interim leader of the B.C. NDP for six months while representing the North Coast, but he never led his party in a campaign.
An incoming premier from "beyond Hope" has others expressing optimism for the future of the region, too.
"Having someone from the Cariboo step into this role is a proud moment for our city and region," Williams Lake Mayor Surinderpal Rathor wrote on Facebook.
"I look forward to ensuring the priorities of Williams Lake remain part of the provincial conversation, including health care, public safety, infrastructure and a strong local economy."

"Alex Fraser is smiling tonight," said incoming Quesnel mayor Coralee Oakes, referencing the former B.C. transportation minister, who represented the Cariboo region from 1969 until 1989 and was responsible for many infrastructure projects in the region.

Former B.C. Conservative Party leader Trevor Bolin, now preparing for his first term as mayor of Fort St. John, said he "couldn't be more proud" to see a rural premier-designate getting ready to be sworn in.
Doerkson resides in Williams Lake in B.C.'s Cariboo-Chilcotin region, known for events like the Williams Lake Stampede. (Simon Charland/CBC)
Challenges ahead

Doerkson delved further into what perspective he would bring to the job during a media scrum Sunday morning, directly addressing voters in "rural and northern British Columbia, the Interior, the Peace, the Island and the coast."
"It has been a long time since you've had a premier from where you live," he said.
"I know what it means when the mill closes, when the ER shuts at night and when there's fire on the ridge. Under this government, you will never be an afterthought to the public service."

Speaking as part of the CBC Daybreak North political panel Monday, former B.C. Liberal MLA Shirley Bond, who lives in Prince George, said Doerkson's challenge would be delivering on the message of change he's promised.

items: What to expect from the new B.C. Conservative government

blocks.text: "Keeping emergency rooms open, I don't think [anyone] is going to disagree on that," she said. "The question is, how do you get there?"
Likewise, University of Northern British Columbia political scientist Jason Morris said Doerkson would still have to pay attention to the population centres in southern B.C.
LISTEN | Former northern MLAs on B.C. electing a premier from the region:
Daybreak North15:17Post-election northern B.C. political panel
"The role of a premier is to be a formal symbol of the province that is expected to effectively engage with and listen and represent citizens from all parts of the province," he said.

"The balance of the population in British Columbia is concentrated in the metropolis areas of Vancouver and the southern tip of Vancouver Island, and that is always where a significant amount of power and influence is going to be held."

items: Lorne Doerkson is B.C.'s new premier. Who is he?

blocks.text: Doerkson has made sure to connect his message to southern B.C. as well, praising businesses in Vancouver and Surrey and stating "a mine opening in the north keeps a port busy in Delta."

articles.title: Ukraine and Russia begin Oleshky ceasefire for aid mission
articles.summary: Around 2,000 people remain stranded in the city of Oleshky, facing severe shortages of food and medicine. The Russian-occupied town has been devastated by fighting and flooding since Moscow's…

image.caption: Ukrainian authorities have used drones to deliver food and medicine to residents stranded in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky [FILE: September 12, 2026]Image: 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen"/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russia and Ukraine began a localized ceasefire early Tuesday to allow humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.
Both sides confirmed that the truce took effect at 3 a.m. local time (0100 GMT), following an agreement brokered by US first lady Melania Trump.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces had stopped shelling in the Kherson sector to prepare for the humanitarian operation.
Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets also confirmed that Kyiv was observing the agreement.
"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honoring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.
However, it could not be independently verified whether fighting had decreased.
What is the humanitarian situation in Oleshky?

Around 2,000 people, including up to 50 children, remain trapped in Oleshky, according to Ukrainian and US estimates. The town had about 24,000 residents before Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The United Nations says residents face severe shortages of food and medicine. Mines and drone attacks have made it difficult for them to leave.

blocks.caption: International media have limited access to Oleshky, making it difficult to independently assess conditions in the town [FILE: September 22, 2026]Image: Ukrainian 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen"/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Former residents told news agency AFP earlier this year that people remaining in the town were starving, sometimes hunting pigeons or surviving on food grown in their gardens.
"They've forgotten what bread is. You need flour for bread, and there's not even flour left," said Olga, who was in contact with two families still in Oleshky.
Oleshky lies across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson.

blocks.caption: Floodwaters submerged large parts of Oleshky in June 2023 after the collapse of the Kakhovka dam on the Dnipro River [FILE: June 10, 2023]Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russian troops captured the town during the first days of the invasion in 2022. It suffered further destruction in June 2023 when the collapse of the Kakhovka dam caused widespread flooding.
What role did Melania Trump play in the ceasefire?
The White House said last week that Melania Trump had helped secure the agreement after holding talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine.
Her office said the first lady had also met United Nations officials who briefed her on conditions in Oleshky.
Announcing the agreement on Friday, Trump said civilian officials from both countries would visit residents to assess their needs.

blocks.caption: US first lady Melania Trump has taken on an unusually prominent diplomatic role in efforts to address the humanitarian crisis in Ukraine [FILE: October 19, 2026]Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Doctors, food, drinking water and medicine are expected to reach the town before evacuation corridors are opened.

"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," Melania Trump said.
Ukraine has accused Russia of preventing residents from leaving, an allegation Moscow denies.
Neither side has provided details about who will monitor the ceasefire. Reports have also differed over its duration, with one account saying it could last through Saturday.
What happened in Kyiv after the ceasefire began?
Russian missile attacks continued elsewhere in Ukraine as the localized ceasefire began.
Explosions shook Kyiv shortly after 3 a.m. local time Tuesday, according to witnesses, while air raid alerts sounded across several regions.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the attacks had damaged the Southern Bridge and associated subway infrastructure. City authorities said traffic on the bridge had been suspended.

blocks.caption: Buildings in Kyiv were damaged by Russian missile strikes, which also left several people dead or injuredImage: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

blocks.text: On Monday, a Russian missile attack on Kyiv killed at least one person and injured 10 others, including students at a dormitory. Further attacks caused casualties in Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.
"It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote after the attacks.
Could the Oleshky ceasefire help revive Ukraine peace talks?
The limited truce in Oleshky comes ahead of another round of US-mediated peace talks between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv, expected in November.
Negotiations have been effectively frozen since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February.

blocks.caption: The last trilateral peace talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US took place in Geneva in February 2026, ending without a breakthrough [FILE: February 17, 2026]Image: Yekaterina Chesnokova/ITAR-TASS/IMAGO

blocks.text: Previous attempts to establish ceasefires have repeatedly failed amid deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine.
More than four and a half years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians have been killed, while millions have been forced to flee their homes.

articles.title: Jay-Z to perform at Super Bowl half-time show
articles.summary: Jay-Z has been involved with the show for years but has never before performed at the NFL championship game.

blocks.text: Rapper Jay-Z will perform at the Super Bowl half-time show in February, the NFL has announced.

Jay-Z's company Roc Nation has produced the half-time show since 2019, and he plays a key role in selecting each year's performer. But the hip-hop mogul has not previously performed himself at the NFL championship game, and the announcement did not specify if he would be the sole headliner.
"Anticipation as to who Jay-Z might have guest star at halftime for the big game will now kick off," the NFL said in a statement. "Of course, his wife, Beyoncé, will be atop the list."
Next year's Super Bowl LXI will take place on 14 February near Los Angeles.
The announcement was made after Jay-Z performed two shows last weekend at the Los Angeles stadium where the Super Bowl will be played.
The LA shows were part of a tour to celebrate the 30th anniversary of his debut album Reasonable Doubt.
"From 'Reasonable Doubt' to standing on the Super Bowl halftime stage, this has been a journey," said Jay-Z, whose real name is Shawn Carter.
"Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world's biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true."
NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said he "couldn't be more excited for fans around the world to experience the artistry, creativity and cultural impact he will bring".
"When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that Jay-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him," Goodell said.

articles.title: Truce begins in wartorn Ukraine city after it was announced by Melania Trump
articles.summary: The ceasefire is meant to allow aid deliveries and the evacuation of civilians.

blocks.text: Ukraine's parliament commissioner for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, confirmed in a social media post that the ceasefire had begun.
"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.
Oleshky was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Residents were trapped with scarce food between Ukrainian positions across the Dnipro River and Russian forces to the east.
The city was home to 24,000 people before the war. Now Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.
The White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured the ceasefire in Oleshky.
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she said in a press release.

While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.
In August 2025, she penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".

articles.title: Golden State Valkyries beat the Atlanta Dream to take a 3-2 lead in WNBA Finals
articles.summary: Kiah Stokes had 13 points, eight rebounds and three blocked shots as the Golden State Valkyries moved within one win of a championship in their second season, beating the Atlanta Dream 64-55 in Game…

image.caption: Gabby Williams of the Golden State Valkyries celebrates after the victory against the Atlanta Dream in Game 5 of the 2026 WNBA Finals at Chase Center on Monday in San Francisco. (Ezra have Shaw/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Basketball

Kiah Stokes had 13 points, eight rebounds and three blocked shots as the Golden State Valkyries moved within one win of a championship in their second season, beating the Atlanta Dream 64-55 in Game 5 of the WNBA Finals on Monday night.
Valkyries score 64-55 win, could close out series on Thursday afternoon in Atlanta
· The Associated Press
· Posted: Oct 26, 2026 10:54 PM EDT | Last Updated: 2 hours ago

Angel Reese finished with seven points, 15 rebounds and five assists – a big difference from her two standout performances in the first two games of the series at Chase Center. Reese shook her head when whistled for the second of her three offensive fouls with 7:43 to play.
Fans screamed and clapped thunder sticks following the final buzzer as Stokes spoke from the floor to chants of “MVP!”
“We appreciate you,” a smiling Stokes said. “We got one more.”

On a night leading scorer Gabby Williams struggled to find her shooting touch, Golden State found that “strength in numbers” mantra coach Natalie Nakase has praised all season long and everybody made an impact. Veronica Burton had 13 points and eight rebounds.

items: Potential decisive Game 6 of WNBA Finals moved to Thursday afternoon in Atlanta before NBA contest
Valkyries beat Dream 67-62 to even the WNBA Finals at 2-2

blocks.text: On Saturday, Nakase had changed up her lineup for a 67-62 Game 4 win by inserting Tiffany Hayes and Kaila Charles into the starting five. She stayed with those two Monday night, and it worked again. Hayes, who played 10 seasons for Atlanta and came out of retirement two years ago, had 12 points – and Nakase has said she wants to win it all for the veteran guard.

Williams began 2 for 11 and missed all four of her three 3-point tries, but she converted a three-point play with 9:08 remaining put the Valkyries ahead 49-42 and finished with nine points on 3-for-14 shooting and six rebounds.

Atlanta will now try to stave off elimination at home Thursday in Game 6 and force a deciding Game 7 back here at Chase Center on Saturday. The Dream hurt themselves with 17 turnovers that led to 21 points for Golden State.

Stokes hit a key 3-pointer with 2:46 to go in the third quarter and another with 7:21 left in the game, which ignited chants of “Ki-ah! Ki-ah!” from the crazed, rally-towel waving “Ballhalla” home crowd at Chase Center.

items: Dream star forward Angel Reese voted WNBA defensive player of year
More basketball coverage

blocks.text: Stokes has recorded three or more blocks in six straight games, tying her with Lisa Leslie in 2003 for the longest such streak in a single WNBA postseason.
The Valkyries used a dominant second half after they led 25-22 at the break, the lowest scoring first half combined score in WNBA Finals history.
Rhyne Howard’s three-point play with 4:59 left in the third pulled Atlanta within 34-31, but after that it was Stokes, Burton and the Valkyries coming up with all the crucial plays on both ends.

Golden State owner Joe Lacob promised a championship within five years in a bold declaration when the expansion franchise was granted to the Bay Area three years ago, yet this season has exceeded even what he could have envisioned.
Neither team could find a flow from 3-point range in the first half as the teams combined to shoot 5 for 29 from deep – 3 of 16 by Golden State and 2 for 13 by Atlanta.
Earlier Monday, the league announced Game 6 would be played at 17,000-seat State Farm Arena in Atlanta starting at 12:30 p.m. EDT on Thursday – a time when many fans on both coasts will be working.

“I’d like to see it be a national holiday for all WNBA championship games so whatever somebody can do,” Dream coach Karl Smesko said. “I hope everybody gets to see it somehow and I know that for some people it’s not realistic, they have jobs and won’t be able to make it. So I’m disappointed for that but I’m really hopeful that as many people can see the game as possible.”

articles.title: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk
articles.summary:
US military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxis

One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles…

blocks.text: One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.

The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa, has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.

The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China, Russia or North Korea.

Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.

blocks.caption: A US military plane takes off at Kadena air force base on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa. Photograph: Issei Kato/Reuters

blocks.text: The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.

American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.

In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.

China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over ⁠cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.

It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan, where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.
With Reuters

articles.title: Philippines urges more equitable UN Security Council as global conflicts on the rise
articles.summary: The Philippines is calling for the expansion of the United Nations Security Council to between 21 and 27 members to ensure greater representation of developing countries and small nations.

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 10:36am
Philippines President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. addresses the 77th session of the United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City on September 20, 2022.
AFP / Angela Weiss

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines is calling for the expansion of the United Nations Security Council to between 21 and 27 members to ensure greater representation of developing countries and small nations.

Enrique Manalo, the Philippines' Permanent Representative to the United Nations, pressed UN member-states to consider reforming the council to reflect the "contemporary composition of the United Nations and principle of sovereign equality," according to a Department of Foreign Affairs release on Monday, October 26.

The UN General Assembly held a debate on October 22 that focused on reforming the structural makeup and veto powers of the Security Council, the body whose mandate is to take action during major geopolitical crises.

During this discussion, the Philippines "reiterated its support for expanding the Council to between 21 and 27 members, while preserving meaningful opportunities for small and medium-sized States to participate in its work."
The Philippines also recognized Africa’s concerns on their lack of representation in the council.
The Security Council's five permanent members were chosen in 1945 based on the dominant Allied powers that won World War II.
These are the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union (now Russia), the Republic of China and France.

All five countries hold permanent veto powers, which gives them an oversized say in global security decisions. This has often resulted in deadlock when their interests clash with resolutions backed by the council's other members.
On top of the five, there are ten non-permanent members elected to the council for overlapping two-year terms.
Manila in June lost its bid for the single Asia-Pacific non-permanent seat to Kyrgyzstan.
Greater transparency, inclusiveness
The Philippines also urged "greater transparency, accountability and inclusiveness in the Council’s working methods," according to the department.
This includes "enhanced participation by elected members and stronger engagement with States affected by Council decisions."
Manalo also urged more regular interaction and consultation between the Security Council and the broader General Assembly.
Global conflict has reached unprecedented levels, with interstate conflicts hitting their highest count since World War II, according to a report by the Peace Research Institute Oslo.
In 2025, there were at least eight interstate conflicts – twice as many as the previous year and the highest number recorded since 1946.
Beyond the record-high number of interstate conflicts, the report also stated a whopping 245,000 people were killed in battle-related violence in 2025, making it the third deadliest year since 1989.
The United Nations' World Social Report 2026 had previously identified the veto powers of the UN Security Council as a major stumbling block to responding to major global conflicts.

articles.title: Harry Kane, Alexia Putellas capture Ballon d'Or wins
articles.summary: Harry Kane became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the Ballon d’Or on Monday thanks to his prolific scoring last season, while Spain star Alexia Putellas won her record-equaling third women’s…

image.caption: Spain and Barcelona midfielder Alexia Putellas, right, and England and Bayern Munich forward Harry Kane pose with their trophies on stage after receiving their Ballon d'Or awards for the best female and male footballer at the Palladium Theatre in London on Monday. FRANCK FIFE / AFP via Getty Images)

blocks.text: Soccer

Harry Kane became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the Ballon d’Or on Monday thanks to his prolific scoring last season, while Spain star Alexia Putellas won her record-equaling third women’s title after leading her former club Barcelona to multiple trophies last season,
Kane is 1st English man to win in 25 years; Putellas wins for 3rd time
Harry Kane became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the Ballon d’Or on Monday thanks to his prolific scoring last season.

Kane scored 73 goals for club and country last campaign – he was Europe's top scorer – and smashed scoring records in Germany for Bayern Munich and at the World Cup, where he captained England to a third-place finish.
The 33-year-old Kane says winning the prestigious individual award was built on so much more.

“Anything is possible with hard work, when no one else is watching, to go through the ups and downs, to learn through resilience, determination and self-belief,” an emotional Kane said in a message to young players, after reflecting on his early career struggles.

“My journey wasn’t straightforward. I wasn’t the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs,” he added. “I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration as well.”
Kane was followed in the voting by Kylian Mbappé, Lamine Yamal – voted best young talent for a third straight year – 2024 winner Rodri and record eight-time winner Lionel Messi.

Kane thanked his teammates, coaches, parents, children – “It's past your bedtime” – and wife Kate, “ my best friend. We’ve been through ups and downs for sure. You’re my biggest supporter. You always want the best for me.”

items: More soccer coverage

blocks.text: Kane led Bayern to the Bundesliga and German Cup double, scoring a hat trick against Stuttgart in the cup final. Bayern also reached the Champions League semifinals.

At the World Cup, he scored six times to pass Gary Lineker as England’s all-time leading World Cup scorer and placed himself among the all-time top five in tournament history. His lineup lost to Argentina in the semifinals but beat Mbappé's France for third place, England's best World Cup placing in 60 years.
An Englishman hadn’t won the Ballon d’Or since Michael Owen in 2001.

“It's massive for England, for our country. [The ceremony] being here in London was a good omen for me,” Kane said. “It's been too long. Certainly [there have been] incredible English players... To put us back on the map, to put us here with this trophy I'm extremely proud. Playing for England is my biggest honour, the thing I love to do the most.”
Putellas hat trick of awards
Earlier, Spain star Alexia Putellas won her record-equaling third women’s Ballon d’Or after leading her former club Barcelona to multiple trophies last season including the Women’s Champions League.
Putellas, who joined London City Lionesses in the offseason, also helped Spain win the Women’s Nations League last December.
The 32-year-old midfielder ended Spain teammate Aitana Bonmati’s three-year reign.

Putellas won the prestigious award in 2021 and 2022, tore her ACL and saw Bonmati rise to stardom. Bonmati, who completed her women’s Ballon d’Or three-peat in 2025, was not on this year’s shortlist after breaking her leg in December.
There wasn’t a women’s Ballon d’Or until 2018, when Ada Hegerberg won it.
Putellas urged young players to approach the sport with “love and passion.”
“Believe in yourself, that’s the most important thing,” she said. “If you have a dream, go for it, even if at some point you have to start from zero.”
Putellas had joined Barcelona in 2012 and called her time at the Catalan club “something special.”
“I'm really grateful for having 14 seasons as a player [at Barcelona],” she said. “What I experienced last year was like a perfect story.”

articles.title: Ex-FBI chief James Comey faces federal charges for third time
articles.summary: Comey's lawyers say the case stems from alleged disclosure of classified information to the New York Times in 2016.

blocks.text: Federal prosecutors have taken steps to charge ex-Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director James Comey with leaking national defence information, according to a court filing.
It marks the third time the justice department has moved to bring criminal charges against Comey, a longtime critic of President Donald Trump.

Few details are provided about the two counts in the three-page filing, but Comey's lawyers said in separate court papers that the case stemmed from an alleged disclosure of classified information to the New York Times in October 2016, while he was head of the FBI.
Comey denied any wrongdoing in a video posted on Substack on Monday, calling the charges an "appalling abuse".
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the department of justice, one that we cannot become numb to," he said in the clip.
"Nothing's changed with me - I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people and I still believe the independent federal judiciary."

His lawyer, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement that two different teams of prosecutors had investigated the alleged disclosure to the New York Times a decade ago during the first Trump administration.
"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said.
The attorney said the court filing "purports to charge Mr Comey with crimes that he did not commit".
Comey was charged in Washington DC through a criminal information, which is a formal written charging document filed directly by a prosecutor.
This is different to a criminal indictment, which must be approved by a grand jury, a group of citizens sworn in to review if evidence is strong enough to prosecute.
Comey was fired by Trump during his first term, after the former FBI director opened an investigation into claims of Russian meddling in the US 2016 presidential election.
Since then, Trump has repeatedly called for his prosecution, and these charges are the administration's third attempt to do so.
Comey was first indicted by a federal grand jury in September 2025 on charges that he had lied to Congress during testimony and obstructed a congressional proceeding.
He pleaded not guilty the following month before the case was dismissed in November.
In April 2026, Comey surrendered to authorities to face charges alleging that an image he briefly shared on social media posed a threat to Trump's life.
The case stemmed from a 2025 Instagram post by Comey, which contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47".
"Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump, the 47th president.
Comey denies any wrongdoing, saying he did not know what the numbers meant, and accusing the prosecution of political motivation. That case is ongoing.

articles.title: Lula's comeback in Brazil dents Trump's ambitions for Latin America
articles.summary: The Trump-Lula relationship may have thawed, but several issues could reignite tensions between the two leaders.

blocks.text: "Brazil will not accept being anyone's backyard," Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva declared in his election victory speech, a message squarely aimed at Washington.

Domestic elections are rarely won on foreign policy, and this one was no different. But Lula's defiance against what he has described as US interference in Brazilian affairs evoked a patriotic spirit that proved an effective campaigning tool.
It also chimed with his wider brand of politics as a former union leader: standing up to powerful figures.

Paradoxically, it seems to have earned him President Donald Trump's respect. "I like Lula, we get along well," Trump said, responding to the result. "I didn't take sides," he added, before calling the election "terrible" and "rigged".

If that sounds muddled, it is because the relationship between the two men is not straightforward. Trump did not explicitly endorse Lula's rival Flávio Bolsonaro, who has refused to recognise the result despite the Supreme Electoral Court finding no evidence of irregularities. But Trump was a close ally of Flávio's father, the former President Jair Bolsonaro.

When I spoke to Lula at his residence about a year ago, relations had hit rock bottom. He told me he had "no relationship" with Trump, that they had never spoken, and that he had no intention of picking up the phone. Trump had recently imposed punitive tariffs on Brazil, largely as a political response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial, which the US president called a "witch-hunt".
Rather than tiptoeing around Trump, as some US allies did, Lula fought back – and it paid off.
He made fiery speeches invoking Brazilian sovereignty, attacked US interference in the judicial process, and took to wearing a blue cap reading "Brazil belongs to Brazilians".
His approval ratings jumped.
He accused the Bolsonaro family, who had lobbied for the tariffs, of being unpatriotic – a blow to a political right that so often claims patriotism as its terrain.
Even some in the agricultural lobby, typically strong Bolsonaro supporters but reliant on US trade, thought Lula had a point.
The US eventually backed down and reduced the tariffs, although they have since risen again.
Relations then improved.
The two men spoke at the United Nations and later met in the Oval Office, where Trump called the talks "very good" and Lula said he left "very satisfied".
Another indication, perhaps, that Trump likes a strongman.
So why might Trump be unhappy with the result?

Latin America has swung to the right, with Ecuador, Chile, Colombia, Argentina and Peru all electing presidents closely aligned with the Trump administration. Trump has sought to use these allies to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere, a strategy he has dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine".
Christopher Sabatini, senior fellow for Latin America at Chatham House, notes that Trump thought Brazil would be the "10th and biggest prize" after Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round.
Brazil is Latin America's largest economy, and the younger Bolsonaro was expected to join Trump's "Shield of Americas" coalition against narco-trafficking.
Brazil also holds the world's second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals after China, and the US had been eyeing preferential access.
The relationship has thawed, but with four more years ahead for Lula, several issues could reignite tensions.
Brazil accused the US earlier this year of trying to cast doubt on its electoral system and denied visas to two state department officials planning to visit.
The US called this "baseless" and revoked the Brazilian ambassador's visa in response.
If Trump keeps calling this result "rigged", further diplomatic fallout is likely.
Lula has also vehemently opposed US military action in the region, from the seizure of Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela to the bombing of alleged drug-trafficking vessels.
He lambasted Washington for designating Brazil's two major gangs as terrorist organisations after lobbying from Flávio Bolsonaro, and warned of attacks on Brazilian sovereignty.
It is a sensitive subject for a political left that remembers the region's brutal 20th Century dictatorships, many backed by the CIA in the name of stopping communism.
Then there is US tech.
Lula's campaign accused Meta of favouring Flávio Bolsonaro.
Meta denied this but admitted moderation issues and technical errors had wrongly removed some posts or limited their reach.
Lula's supporters responded by sharing his messages through a 10-million-strong WhatsApp group to bypass the algorithms.
Separately, the Trump administration is unhappy with Pix, Brazil's instant payment system, which has boosted the economy, but which the US sees as taking business from Visa and Mastercard.
The relationship has exposed political divisions.

In the campaign, Bolsonaro supporters waved US flags at their rallies and, in one case, an inflatable saying "Trump Nuke Brazil", while Lula and his supporters accused Flávio Bolsonaro of protecting US interests over Brazil's.
Still, tensions can be overstated.
The US remains Brazil's second-biggest trading partner after China, and for now the two leaders get on.
Whether that lasts will depend on how far the US tries to intervene in Brazilian affairs, and how bullish Lula is in response.

articles.title: US seeks new charges against former FBI chief James Comey
articles.summary: The Trump administration accuses the former FBI director of leaking classified information a decade ago. Comey denies wrongdoing, while his lawyers argue the case is legally invalid and comes too…

image.caption: James Comey posted a video message on Instagram responding to the latest attempt to prosecute himImage: James Comey/Instagram/REUTERS

blocks.text: The US Justice Department has launched a third attempt to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey, accusing him of illegally disclosing national defense information in 2016.
Court documents unsealed on Monday reveal allegations that Comey directed a subordinate to share classified information with a journalist.
The case marks another escalation in President Donald Trump's long-running conflict with the former FBI chief, who has denied wrongdoing.
What are the latest allegations against James Comey?
The case centers on an October 2016 New York Times article about a secret US surveillance order involving internet company Yahoo.
The order reportedly required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. It had been issued by a secret intelligence court.
Prosecutors allege that Comey instructed a staff member to contact a New York Times journalist to correct inaccurate information published by news agency Reuters the previous day.

blocks.caption: US President Donald Trump has repeatedly accused former FBI director James Comey of wrongdoing, while Comey has denied the allegationsImage: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to the Justice Department, this resulted in the illegal transfer of classified national defense information to an unauthorized person.
However, the allegations have already been investigated twice.
Federal authorities began examining the disclosure in 2017. Prosecutor John Durham recommended against bringing criminal charges in December 2018, according to Comey's lawyers.
A second investigation, launched in 2019 under the code name "Tropical Vortex," was also closed without charges in February 2020.
How are Comey's lawyers fighting the new charges?
The Justice Department filed a legal document known as a "criminal information" in early October, shortly before the 10-year deadline for prosecuting the alleged offense.
Unlike an indictment, a criminal information does not require approval from a grand jury or judge.
Prosecutors say the filing allows them to extend the statute of limitations, which determines how long authorities have to bring criminal charges.

blocks.caption: A courtroom sketch shows former FBI director James Comey alongside his lawyer Patrick Fitzgerald during his arraignment in 2025 [FILE: October 8, 2025]Image: Dana Verkouteren/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Comey's lawyers dispute that interpretation. They argue that federal law explicitly requires an indictment within 10 years and that the government's filing does not meet that requirement.
They have asked a judge to dismiss the case. A ruling is still pending.
Comey's attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, also pointed to the two earlier investigations.
"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said.
Responding to the latest allegations in a video posted on Substack, Comey condemned the prosecution.
"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice," he said.
"I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."
What other criminal cases does James Comey face?
The latest case is the third criminal proceeding brought against Comey since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
In September 2025, prosecutors charged him with making false statements to Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding.
A federal judge dismissed the case after finding that the Trump-appointed prosecutor who brought the charges had been unlawfully appointed.

blocks.caption: Former FBI director James Comey testified before the Senate Intelligence Committee in June 2017 about his dismissal by Trump and the Russia investigation [FILE: June 8, 2017]Image: Andrew Harnik/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In April 2026, Comey was indicted again, this time over an Instagram photograph showing seashells arranged to form the numbers "86 47."
The Justice Department interpreted the numbers as a threat against Trump, arguing that "86" referred to killing someone and "47" identified Trump as the 47th US president.
Comey denied threatening Trump's life and has sought to have that case dismissed.
Why has Trump targeted former FBI director Comey?
Comey was appointed FBI director in 2013 by Democratic President Barack Obama.
His relationship with Trump deteriorated shortly after the president took office in 2017.
Comey resisted Trump's request to pledge personal loyalty during a private dinner.
Trump fired him in May 2017 while the FBI was investigating Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and possible connections to Trump's campaign.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump and James Comey initially appeared to have a cordial relationship before the president fired the FBI director in May 2017 [FILE: January 22, 2017]Image: Andrew Harrer/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: The investigation was subsequently taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller. It established that Russia had interfered in the election but found insufficient evidence to prove criminal coordination between Moscow and Trump's campaign.
The two men have remained bitter political opponents. Trump has repeatedly accused Comey of treason, while Comey compared the president to a mafia boss in his 2018 memoir.

articles.title: Bato’s wife defends fugitive senator: ‘He’s not an enemy’
articles.summary: The wife of fugitive Sen. Bato Dela Rosa issued a public appeal defending her husband, urging his former political allies and powerful figures to stop using him for personal agendas and to end what…

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 9:36am
Sen. Bato Dela Rosa and his wife, Nancy, at the Senate on July 22.
The Philippine STAR / Mong Pintolo

MANILA, Philippines — The wife of fugitive Sen. Bato Dela Rosa issued a public appeal defending her husband, urging his former political allies and powerful figures to stop using him for personal agendas and to end what she described as his "persecution."
In a Facebook post, Nancy Dela Rosa, Bato’s wife, said that he is not “their enemy nor the enemy of this state.”
“Thank you for helping me realize that there are millions who still believe and support him,” Nancy said.
“Please do not use him for your personal agenda. He has helped you in countless ways and he has done you no wrong personally. He needs your help, not your persecution,” she added.
On October 23, the government put a P50 million bounty on Dela Rosa, who has been in hiding since May this year due to an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC).
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has also ordered Dela Rosa's arrest to be carried out nonviolently and lawfully.
Remulla said Dela Rosa was in Mindanao, being protected by a “powerful group” with which the government is currently negotiating for his turnover.
While Remulla maintained that the government can arrest the senator, launching a hard tactical operation is off the table due to the risk of casualties.

“We do not want a civil war to start because of our arrest of one man. We want to do it properly and we want to do it judiciously, and we want to do it cleanly,” Remulla said in an ANC interview on October 20.
The ICC unsealed an arrest warrant for Dela Rosa on May 11, ending his nearly six-month stint in hiding when he surfaced at the Senate.

Just days later, hours after a violent standoff on May 13 between Senate security and National Bureau of Investigation agents, Dela Rosa fled the premises early on May 14 aboard a van owned by Sen. Robin Padilla.

articles.title: Albay bridge stalled for over 15 years to open before Undas
articles.summary: The first two lanes of the Kilicao-Binitayan Bridge in Daraga, Albay will open on Friday, October 30, nearly five months after Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon ordered the completion of the project…

blocks.text: October 27, 2026 | 9:30am
The Kilicao-Binitayan Bridge in Daraga, Albay, which is set to open its first two lanes on Oct. 30, 2026, after being stalled for more than 15 years.
Department of Public Works and Highways via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The first two lanes of the Kilicao-Binitayan Bridge in Daraga, Albay will open on Friday, October 30, nearly five months after Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon ordered the completion of the project that had been stalled for more than 15 years.

Dizon inspected the bridge on Monday, October 26, with Albay Gov. Noel Rosal and Albay 2nd District Rep. Carlos Loria to check its readiness ahead of Undas, following President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s directive to make infrastructure projects that could ease travel accessible before the observance.

Dizon first inspected the bridge on May 3 and was surprised to learn that the project had been delayed for more than 15 years. He then ordered the acceleration of construction to ease the burden on residents who had relied on an old Bailey bridge to cross between Barangays Kilicao and Binitayan.

“Bago mag-Undas, bubuksan na natin itong first two (2) lanes ng tulay. Kaya naman palang mabilis eh, hindi na aabutin ng taon. Utos ng pangulo ‘yan, in 5 months, pwede naman palang gawin. Nagawa natin,” Dizon said in a video posted on the Department of Public Works and Highways’ (DPWH) Facebook page.

(Before Undas, we will open the first two lanes of the bridge. It turns out it can be done quickly, without taking years. That was the President’s order. It turns out it could be done in five months. We did it.)

The bridge opening came as the Marcos administration announced a Cabinet reshuffle on Monday, transferring Dizon back to the Department of Transportation (DOTr) and appointing Transportation Secretary Giovanni Lopez to lead the DPWH.

Presidential Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano said Dizon would focus on easing daily commutes, shortening queues at the Land Transportation Office, eliminating fixers and advancing mass transportation projects. Lopez, meanwhile, was tasked with institutionalizing reforms at the DPWH amid corruption allegations involving flood control projects.

The reshuffle reverses the changes made in August 2025, when Dizon moved from the DOTr to the DPWH following the resignation of then-Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan amid controversy over alleged anomalous flood control projects.

During his tenure as DPWH chief, Dizon led efforts to investigate alleged anomalies in flood control projects, including filing cases against contractors and department officials and blacklisting contractors implicated in irregularities. He also inspected questionable projects and testified in court over an allegedly substandard P289.5-million flood dike project in Oriental Mindoro. — with a report from Ian Laqui

articles.title: Opposition leader María Machado returns from exile to a Venezuela reshaped by Trump
articles.summary: Machado returns with Trump's blessing, even if Washington is happy with Venezuela's existing leader - at least for the time being.

blocks.text: Watch: Crowds welcome Venezuela's María Corina Machado after months in exile
ByWill Grant
BBC's Mexico, Central America and Cuba correspondent

Driving down roads lined with jubilant supporters from the western state of Lara to the capital Caracas, Maria Corina Machado's return to Venezuela could hardly have been more different to her exit 10 months earlier.

Colourful, loud, open and defiant, it stood in stark contrast to the way the Venezuelan opposition leader slipped out of the country in the dead of night in December last year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo.

She had been unable to make it back to her homeland until now, thwarted on several occasions by the Venezuelan government - and by the Trump administration, which insisted the "time wasn't right" for her return.
Now, it appears, it is.

"Maria Corina is the indisputable leader of Venezuela," says 20-year-old Gregory Noriega, wearing a sweatshirt emblazoned with the logo of the opposition movement Vente Venezuela. "Her return represents hope."
Gregory Noriega

"This is a step forward in the electoral process which we've been waiting for since last year," echoes 18-year-old Hilary, who turned out on to the streets of the capital hoping to catch a glimpse of the opposition leader on her victory lap.
"She's returned after the double earthquakes when Venezuela needs her," adds her friend, Manuel. "The whole country is behind her to show that now Venezuela isn't scared."
Much has changed since Machado left Venezuelan soil to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
Then-President Nicolás Maduro is no longer at the top of the Venezuelan government.
Maduro was forcibly removed from power by US troops on 3 January, and whisked to New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges – to which he's pleaded not guilty.
He was replaced by his former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has turned the page with Washington in ways few could have imagined.
The bilateral relationship is today unrecognisable from the years of mutual animosity during the reigns of President Hugo Chávez and then his handpicked successor, Maduro.
The new circumstances throw up some interesting conundrums for both sides.

When Machado left Venezuela, she had long been considered Washington's favoured alternative to Maduro. She returns to find the Trump administration perfectly happy with the one they've got – at least for the time being.

blocks.caption: Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado greets the crowd gathered around her vehicle on October 25, 2026 in Caracas, Venezuela

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
The Trump administration recently signed a major oil deal with Venezuela which gave the US a 100-year concession over a staggering 65bn barrels of Venezuelan crude oil.
The deal was reached in conjunction with a Venezuelan private company called North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) run by a businessman with a chequered past, Alejandro Betancourt.

Machado has openly criticised the deal which the Rodríguez government reached with the US, albeit careful to direct her criticism at Caracas and at Betancourt rather than President Trump, to whom she gave her peace prize and whose trust and support she craves to move forward.

President Trump has repeatedly said how satisfied he is with Delcy Rodríguez, calling her "wonderful" and "a terrific person". This was the vice-president of an administration he previously described as made up of "narco-communists".
But the outpouring of jubilation for Machado's caravan into the capital shows she can still count on significant support on the streets, says Venezuelan political analyst Beningno Alarcon.

"The return of Maria Corina Machado, in my personal view, is the most significant [political] event since 3rd January," says Alarcon. "It means the most important political leader in Venezuela is back in the country."

"The reception for her return shows that her ability to mobilise her support remains intact, which means the opposition in Venezuela now has something very solid: a leadership which is present on the ground as opposed to solely in exile," he says.

Alarcon provides some evidence that the opposition – and the public at large – feel more emboldened since 3 January, a situation he believes will become only more pronounced with Machado's reappearance.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Political analyst Beningno Alarcon

blocks.text: Political analyst Beningno Alarcon

For instance, a joint study by the political think tanks Polis and Nexo suggests that Venezuela saw three times as many street protests in the first nine months of this year as in all of 2025, with demonstrations spanning a range of issues, from politics and working conditions to water supply.
Furthermore, there's evidence that the repression of such protests has reduced by more than half.
In such an environment, the return of a figurehead like Machado can galvanise an electorate that has spent years fearful of the consequences of speaking out.
Her return also needs to be seen within the context of the wider talks brokered by Washington between the Venezuelan government and the opposition towards a negotiated political solution.
Certainly, the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, was quick to say her "safe return" to Venezuela was "the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks".

The Nobel Peace Prize winner still faces charges in Venezuela ranging from treason to conspiracy of insurrection. For years, she and her supporters have dismissed the charges as politically motivated and baseless.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Young supporters of Maria Machado

blocks.text: Young supporters of Maria Machado

Having made at least eight attempts to return to Venezuela by air and by sea before the Trump administration gave her the green light, Machado now knows she has Trump's blessing to be back on home soil – a position Delcy Rodríguez is both unwilling and unlikely to challenge.
She called Machado's return a "show" and the entire cross-country event, which was livestreamed by her supporters over the weekend, was studiously ignored by state television outlets.
But Rodríguez, too, needs a harmonious relationship with Washington if she is to avoid a fate similar to that of her predecessor and indicated she might be prepared to hold talks with Machado.
For as much as Trump has complimented Rodríguez, he has also made it clear that Washington expects nothing less than her full submission and malleability on key issues like energy.
Some reports have even suggested all major decision-making in the oil-rich nation is being largely dictated by Secretary Rubio via regular WhatsApp calls to the interim president.
The young supporters gathered in droves in Caracas to cheer Maria Corina Machado home say their fears of criticising their government or demanding change are vanishing.
Her return marked an irreversible political transition in Venezuela, they insist, one which they could barely fathom when she left for Oslo just a year ago.
Watch: December 2025 - BBC interview Nobel Peace Prize winner María Corina Machado
Additional reporting by Vanessa Silva in Caracas.

articles.title: Australian politics live: Fatima Payman linking Haines-style attack to staffing allocation is ‘outrageous’, Labor says
articles.summary:
Follow the day’s news live

  • Get our breaking news email, free app…

blocks.text: Payman asks if PM is ‘waiting for what happened to Helen Haines’ to occur again

blocks.caption: Sarah Basford Canales

blocks.text: Sarah Basford Canales

At a late-night Senate estimates hearing, independent senator Fatima Payman accused the prime minister of being “petty” by not granting her additional staff members after she defected from Labor in 2024.

Payman has long argued her office is understaffed as part of a personal gripe Anthony Albanese has with her, but she drove the point home amid escalating threats of political violence. The senator told Guardian Australia last week her staff had also had to deal with human faeces being sent to her office, prompting the intervention of a biohazard team.
Payman said she had requested an additional adviser, in line with other independent political offices, two years ago but the prime minister had yet to process the request.

Payman said the extra adviser would assist her office dealing with the “psychosocial hazards” imposed on her staff since leaving Labor. A document tabled showed she had no advisers, which can be paid more, while most other independents have one or two advisers.
Payman continued, butting heads with the trade minister, Don Farrell:

double quotation markPlease raise this with the prime minister. Because if he cares so much about the welfare and wellbeing of people who work in this building, then I implore you and the prime minister to please look into the fact that my staff are burning out. They can’t take this any longer. Is the prime minister waiting for something like what happened to Dr Helen Haines to occur to my office, to me, for him to take our request seriously?
Farrell responded: “Look, I personally think that’s an outrageous suggestion, Senator Payman.”
Payman said: “I can’t believe that I’m saying that or making that suggestion, because it’s been two years.”
Farrell asked Payman to withdraw the comments but Payman said she wouldn’t until Albanese processed or responded to her staffing request.
Key events

1h agoPayman asks if PM is ‘waiting for what happened to Helen Haines’ to occur again

blocks.text: First AUKUS nuclear sub to come to Australia revealed
Washington has revealed the first nuclear submarine that will deploy to Australia under the AUKUS agreement, five years after the $386 billion defence pact was signed.

The USS Colorado, a 10-year-old Virginia-class submarine, will make its new home at Western Australia’s HMAS Stirling from late 2027, defence minister, Richard Marles, revealed in a joint statement with his US and British counterparts on Tuesday.

It’s the first of up to four American submarines, and one from the UK, set to rotate through the base while Australian Defence Force personnel get to grips with owning and operating nuclear submarines.
But Colorado’s arrival in Australia will be controversial because of outrage sparked in June over revelations the US would deliver lesser equipment than first promised.
Original AUKUS plans had Canberra receiving two used vessels and a brand new Virginia-class submarine before building one of its own in Adelaide.

The fact Washington would now be sending second-hand vessels was described as “trash” by Tasmanian independent senator and army veteran Jacqui Lambie, but ministers and top military brass at the time insisted used subs were the best option.
- Australian Associated Press

blocks.caption: Tory Shepherd

blocks.text: Tory Shepherd
UN experts ‘disappointed’ after major parties block bill to ban shackling during childbirth
UN experts are disappointed that bills to ban shackling during childbirth and strip-searching children were blocked by the major parties.
Independent senator Lidia Thorpe introduced the bills to the Senate, where Labor and the Coalition blocked their progress.
The United Nations Human Rights Council special procedures experts said in a statement that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women and children were disproportionately affected by the measures:

double quotation markIt is disappointing that parliament was not given the opportunity to formally decide on reforms aimed at protecting the dignity, bodily integrity and rights of women and children deprived of liberty. The failure of these bills to proceed should not mark the end of efforts to address these longstanding human rights concerns. We encourage Australian authorities and parliamentarians to continue pursuing reforms.

blocks.caption: Lidia Thorpe. Photograph: Jay Kogler/EPA

blocks.text: Shoebridge calls for ‘ethical Australian AI’ after cyber threat warning
The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, has said a report from the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) about AI threats to online infrastructure highlights the need for investment in another option.
He told reporters:

double quotation markWe need investment in an Australian ethical AI, which we can have some kind of comfort in, and not just simply relying upon these same US tech bros who are producing the threats to our very system … the idea that you invite the robbers in to protect the family silver is pretty bloody extraordinary.

The ASD report warned businesses and critical infrastructure must use cutting-edge AI models to defend against digital threats, raising alarms that artificial intelligence is enabling more dangerous threats than ever.

blocks.caption: David Shoebridge. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP
Penry Buckley

blocks.text: Penry Buckley
Minns says federal government must be ‘serious’ about meeting migration targets amid One Nation surge

The NSW premier, Chris Minns, says the federal government must be “serious” about meeting net migration targets as polling in the Hunter suggests Labor and One Nation are neck-and-neck in the key region.

A poll commissioned by Advent Energy, who are responsible for an offshore gas proposal off the Hunter coast, suggests support for Labor and One Nation at the upcoming state election is at 32% each in the region ahead of the March election. The Coalition was at 14%.
Minns was asked on 2GB this morning what he had done to lobby the federal government to bring down migration. Minns, a frequent critic of net migration under the Albanese government, said:

double quotation markThe best thing I can do is say what I’ve said privately, publicly, and I’ve said it on this program, and that is, we have to be serious about the target rate for migration and meet it. There’s no use saying, well, we’re going to have on average 200,000, a little bit more than that per year, and then it comes in at 300,000, because then people lose faith in the system. Now, in fairness to [the federal government], they’ve worked hard over the last 3 months to say these are the new limits.

The Albanese government has promised to achieve net overseas migration (Nom) of 245,000 in 2026-27 and 225,000 in 2027-28, while the Coalition says if elected it would more than halve Labor’s Nom target in the first two years from 2028-29.
One Nation has said it would have net-negative migration levels for three years, followed by a Nom “ceiling” of 130,000.

blocks.caption: NSW premier Chris Minns. Photograph: Steven Markham/AAP
Caitlin Cassidy

blocks.text: Caitlin Cassidy
‘Selective editing’ of estimates videos ‘humiliate public servants unfairly’, senators told
Female public servants are subject to “vile and misogynistic” comments underneath social media videos shared by parliamentarians, Senate estimates hears.

Jim Betts, secretary of the department of infrastructure, transport, regional development, communications, sport and the arts, was asked about a submission sent by the Australian Secretaries Board to a joint committee on parliamentary standards. It expressed concern that public officials were increasingly subject to “ridicule, hostility or abuse” when excerpts of proceedings from parliamentary inquiries were uploaded on social media “without context”.
Liberal senator Sarah Henderson pressed that “being able to highlight on social media and using the vision which is made available through the parliament is a fundamental function of this committee”.
Betts replied that there was already 14 hours of footage from Senate estimates yesterday that is now in the public domain, and the submission contained “stark” examples of selectively edited videos.

double quotation markThe concern that was expressed by the secretaries board was about the very selective editing of those videos, the overlay of commentary and other captions which were entirely designed to humiliate public servants unfairly … What we also find is … that the comment section on websites hosted by senators and other parliamentarians contain often vile and misogynistic comments about female public servants.

blocks.caption: Department of infrastructure secretary, Jim Betts. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP
Benita Kolovos

blocks.text: Benita Kolovos
Victorian Labor pledges to expand workplace protection orders to hospital workers
People who are violent or abusive to health workers could effectively be banned from hospitals in Victoria if Labor is re-elected.

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, is holding a press conference to announce if Labor is re-elected next month, it will expand the workplace protection order scheme – that allows retail stores to ban aggressive customers – to hospital settings.

Under the plan, people who are violent or abusive to health workers can be hit with a workplace protection order (WPO), which effectively bans them from hospitals for up to 12 months. Anyone who breaches a WPO faces up to two years in prison or a $50,000 fine.
Labor will also create a $30m fund hospitals can apply for to improve lighting, CCTV and other safety measures.
Carroll says:

double quotation markOur nurses and midwives and health professionals go to work every day to make sure we have a healthy community … They are the heroes of our community, and I’m very pleased to say, under my leadership, we’ll do everything we can to protect them through workplace protection orders.
He says people subject to a WPO will “still be able to access healthcare” in an emergency but there will be “guardrails” in place when they receive that care.

blocks.caption: Ben Carroll. Photograph: Rob Prezioso/AAP

blocks.text: Aged care algorithm ‘fundamentally flawed’, Ruston says
Opposition aged care spokesperson, Anne Ruston, has urged the government to listen after a damning investigation by the commonwealth ombudsman.
She told ABC Radio National:
double quotation markWe’re really hopeful that now the government has this independent report, it will actually listen and say that their algorithm process is fundamentally flawed.

The ombudsman’s report followed reporting by Guardian Australia that older people were being left distressed and without adequate care after their home support needs were assessed by an “inhumane” algorithm as part of the government’s mandatory Integrated Assessment Tool.
Security reviews ramp up for MP offices over attack fears
Some politicians will receive security updates in their electorate offices after raising concerns about threats in the wake of the alleged attack on Helen Haines.
At least nine MPs will have security crackdowns accelerated for their electorate offices, the finance minister, Katy Gallagher, confirmed, after they raised concerns last week.
Security in Parliament House’s public places will also be stepped up.
Gallagher did not specify which MPs were affected.
– Australian Associated Press
Jacinda Ardern joins University of Sydney as lecturer and mentor

In news adjacent to federal politics, former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern has revealed she will lecture and mentor at the University of Sydney after moving to Australia earlier this year.
Based in the school of public health, she will host guest lectures and masterclasses and engage in mentoring.
Teal and regional independent backers were Farrer independent’s top donors
Continued from the previous post:

The top donor, Regional Voices Fund, backs independent candidates in regional seats while the second-highest donor, Keldoulis Investments, owned by Robert Keldoulis, is a major backer of Climate 200 – the funding vehicle that supports teal independents in getting elected.
Overall, Milthorpe spent $1,708,845 on her campaign, receiving $1,680,439 in donations and gifts.
Candidates endorsed by political parties, like Farley, are able to defer the campaign spending reports until February the following year when political party annual returns are published.
As a result, Farley’s electoral returns show he spent only $5,119 on his campaign and received no donations. This figure will likely be updated in February.
Farrer independent spent $1.7m on byelection campaign, electoral returns show

The independent candidate, Michelle Milthorpe, received almost $1.7m in donations from more than 5,000 donors in her campaign against One Nation in the seat of Farrer earlier this year, electoral returns show.

Milthorpe, backed by regional independents, including Helen Haines, ultimately lost the battle to One Nation’s David Farley in Sussan Ley’s former seat, 42.45% to Farley’s 57.55% on a two-party preferred basis.
The returns data, released by the Australian Electoral Commission yesterday, shows $670,653 of the total amount – or about 40% – donated was over the declaration threshold of $17,300.
The top donors for Milthorpe include:

items: Regional Voices Fund Pty Ltd: $215,000
Keldoulis Investments Pty Limited: $117,000
Keep Them Honest Pty Ltd: $75,000
Climate 200 Pty Limited: $61,653

blocks.caption: Independent candidate for Farrer Michelle Milthorpe. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP

blocks.text: More respectful discourse is ‘what Helen Haines would want’: Richard Marles
The defence minister, Richard Marles, hopes politicians continue to show respect and civility for more than a day, following the outpouring of support for independent Helen Haines:

double quotation markI really hope that all of us can do better … we need to really try and collectively engage in bringing the temperature down, and have a much more respectful and civil discourse. And I know that’s what Helen Haines would want.

articles.title: Reader Q&A: After Lula’s sensational victory in Brazil’s presidential election, post your questions for the Guardian’s Latin America correspondent
articles.summary: Having lost the first round of Brazil’s presidential election to far right rival Flávio Bolsonaro, incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spectacularly triumphed in the second. What comes next for…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips, Michael Hubbard and Guardian moderators

blocks.text: Key events

items: 24m agoWelcome to the Conversation

blocks.text: Welcome to the Conversation

blocks.caption: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Photograph: Amanda Perobelli/Reuters

blocks.text: After losing the first round of Brazil’s presidential election to far right rival Flávio Bolsonaro, incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, better known simply as Lula, pulled off the most stunning political fightback in modern Brazilian history by winning the second, in so doing securing a fourth presidential term. It will see him become the country’s longest-serving leader.

The result – 51.79% to Lula, 48.21% to Bolsonaro – was delivered after a supreme court judge had extended polling time by two hours, and after Lula’s camp accused their opponents of sabotaging public transport in an attempt to keep their voters from the polls. It was the first time in Brazilian electoral history that a first-round verdict had been overturned.

But Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year jail term for his part in an attempted coup after the last presidential election, refused to accept the result – just as his father had done, four years before. He called Lula’s victory “sacanagem”, a Portuguese word that roughly translates as “bullshit”.

Brazil remains a deeply divided country and Lula will have to navigate a hostile Congress, packed full of Bolsonaro allies, if he is to make significant legislative changes in his fourth term. His options are also constrained by a gloomy economic outlook, with Brazil experiencing soaring debt and entrenched structural problems. As he turns 81, will the re-elected president have the energy to face down the far right opposition for another four years and to lay out the ground for a credible successor?

And what does Lula’s latest victory mean for the wider region, and for the country’s relationship with Donald Trump’s administration? In the Guardian’s Opinion pages columnist Jordana Timerman wrote that “Lula’s victory shows that the rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible. But the movement retains substantial electoral support, influence over the political agenda and a powerful ally in Washington.”

The Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips will be answering your questions on the election result, what it means for Brazil and the wider region, and what the country’s future may hold, here from 15:00 GMT on Tuesday 27 October. Comment with your question below, or email conversations@theguardian.com
