articles.title: England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or
articles.summary: The England captain ends his country's 25-year wait for the prestigious award after scoring 73 goals for club and country last season, beating competition from Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe.

image.caption: Kane, who is 33 years old, hails from London and is considered one of the greatest football players in the world Image: Franck Fife/AFP

blocks.text: England captain Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or for the first time on Monday, becoming the first English player to receive the prestigious football award since 2001.
The 33-year-old Bayern Munich striker was honored at a ceremony at the London Palladium after scoring 73 goals in 65 appearances for club and country last season.
The Ballon d'Or, awarded by French magazine France Football, is one of football's most prestigious individual honors, recognizing the world's best players.
The last English player to win the award was former Liverpool striker Michael Owen, who claimed the prize 25 years ago.
Why did Harry Kane win the 2026 Ballon d'Or?
Kane's remarkable goalscoring record helped Bayern Munich secure a German league and cup double last season.
The former Tottenham Hotspur forward also led England to the World Cup semifinals, the country's best finish since winning the tournament in 1966.

blocks.caption: Harry Kane also received the Gerd Müller Trophy, awarded to the season's top goalscorer, after netting 73 goals for Bayern Munich and EnglandImage: Matthew Childs/Action Images/REUTERS

blocks.text: Kane has finished as the Bundesliga's leading scorer for three consecutive seasons. He was also Europe's top club goalscorer during the 2025-26 campaign.
At Monday's ceremony, Kane thanked his Bayern Munich teammates for their support.
"Without you guys (his Bayern Munich team-mates) and the rest of the team it wouldn't be possible, the way you guys push me, the way we compete. So thank you very much," he said.
Kane also paid tribute to his former club Tottenham Hotspur, which he joined at the age of 11, as well as his England teammates and family.
"To my wife Kate, my best friend. We've been through ups and downs. You are my biggest support and I felt like you wanted this more than me," he said.

blocks.caption: Barcelona's Lamine Yamal was among Harry Kane's strongest rivals for the Ballon d'Or, alongside Kylian MbappeImage: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Reflecting on his career, Kane encouraged young footballers to pursue their ambitions despite setbacks.

"I hope my journey, it wasn't straightforward, I didn't go straight to the top, I had to experience a lot of loan moves and fight my way to get to where I am now. I hope that can give you inspiration."
Kane faced strong competition from Barcelona's Spanish teenager Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid's French forward Kylian Mbappe.
He joins Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen among the English players to have won the award.
Who else won at the 2026 Ballon d'Or awards?
Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas claimed the women's Ballon d'Or for the third time in her career, having previously won the award in 2021 and 2022.
The 32-year-old was recognized after a successful season with Barcelona, winning the treble and scoring 21 goals across all competitions.

blocks.caption: Spain's Alexia Putellas won the women's Ballon d'Or for the third time in her careerImage: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Putellas also played a key role in Barcelona's Champions League triumph, contributing seven goals and seven assists during the campaign.
She joined English club London City Lionesses in July after spending 14 years at Barcelona.
Her victory ended a run of three consecutive Ballon d'Or wins by fellow Spaniard Aitana Bonmatí.
Barcelona's Lamine Yamal won the Kopa Trophy for the best young male player for the third consecutive year, while his teammate Vicky Lopez claimed the women's award for the second year running.
Barcelona coach Pere Romeu was named women's coach of the year, while Spain manager Luis de la Fuente won the men's coaching award.

blocks.caption: Spain coach Luis de la Fuente beat Arsenal's Mikel Arteta and Aston Villa's Unai Emery to win the men's Coach of the Year awardImage: Franck Fife/AFP

blocks.text: Spain goalkeeper Unai Simon received the men's Yashin Trophy, with Cata Coll winning the women's equivalent.
Barcelona was named women's club of the year, while Paris Saint-Germain took the men's award.

articles.title: Brazil: defeated Flávio Bolsonaro ordered to surrender passports
articles.summary:
Far-right senator banned from leaving country as supreme court judge’s ruling makes reference to money-laundering case

The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro was banned from leaving Brazil…

blocks.text: The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro was banned from leaving Brazil and ordered to surrender his passports just hours after his dramatic loss in the presidential election to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
The ruling was issued by supreme court justice Alexandre de Moraes, the same justice who oversaw the trial of the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for attempting a coup.
Bolsonaro posted a video saying the decision was based on an interview his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, gave last Friday urging his brother to leave Brazil if he lost the election.

On Monday night, Bolsonaro’s party issued a statement acknowledging the election result, saying: “We recognise the presidential result proclaimed by the electoral court, but believe that the questions raised need to be properly clarified through a balanced and democratic political debate.”
Bolsonaro, like his father four years ago, has still not conceded defeat to Lula.

The court’s brief ruling regarding his passport only refers to a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating Flávio Bolsonaro over his possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme. The ruling orders him not to have any contact with his friend Willer Tomaz, a lawyer linked to betting companies that police suspect were being used to launder about £680m.
It also cancelled all of Bolsonaro’s passports, including the diplomatic one he holds as a congressman, and ordered him to hand them over within 24 hours.
Bolsonaro was the first to speak publicly about the matter, before Brazilian media were even aware of the judge’s decision.

In a video posted on social media, he said he had just left a visit to his father, who is under house arrest in Brasília, when “Lula’s federal police were at his door and in the middle of the street, and I was served with an order to hand over my passports and I am also prohibited from leaving the country”.
He added that, although his brother – who is in self-imposed exile in the US – told a US podcast on Friday that he favoured the senator leaving Brazil if he lost the election, “I never said that”.
When his Senate term ends early next year, Bolsonaro will be out of public office for the first time in 24 years, and therefore without the special jurisdiction afforded to officeholders.

He is under investigation in another criminal case, too, over what happened to the £20m he was captured on tape asking a disgraced banker accused of corruption to provide for a biopic about his father.
The Folha de S.Paulo newspaper reported that Flávio Bolsonaro had been persuaded to drop his plan to seek to annul the election, which he had announced after the result was declared on Sunday night.

Bolsonaro had claimed that the two-hour extension of voting – intended to allow voters who had been unable to access the mandatory free public transport to cast their ballots – had harmed the election, despite the fact that his own campaign had also argued for an extension.
According to the newspaper, allies and lawyers told him his argument was legally weak.

Bolsonaro had still not publicly reversed his demand for an annulment, and in the same video he said he would file another case to have Lula’s ticket disqualified over alleged abuse of economic power, a similar case to others his legal team brought during the campaign.

articles.title: Jordan says its military struck 'militant hideouts' in Syria after deadly church attack
articles.summary: Jordanian armed forces carried out strikes on "militant hideouts" in Syria that it said were linked to a deadly church attack on the kingdom last week. Syria gave a different account.

image.caption: Earlier on Monday, Jordanian security forces arrested three suspects related to the terrorist attack on the Hammoud Church in Karak GovernorateImage: Alaa Al-Sukhni/REUTERS

blocks.text: Jordan said late Monday that its air force has struck military hideouts in southern Syria after determining that suspects linked to last week's deadly church attack were hiding there.
Jordanian forces said the deadly attack on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church was linked to "terrorist groups" hiding in Syria.
Jordan's armed forces said the strikes on southeastern Syria was carried out in coordination with Damascus.
But Syria gave a different account, saying it had launched an investigation into the Jordanian attacks.
A health official told Syria's state news agency that at least five civilians, including women and children, were killed as a result of strikes carried out by Jordan, Reuters reported.
Jordanian security forces arrest 3 men in Karak province
Jordanian security forces earlier on Monday morning arrested three men in connection with last week's deadly terrorist attack at the Hammoud Church that killed nine people and injured 40 others.

Officials said the arrests took place following a dawn shootout with the armed men who were discovered hiding in an abandoned house in the Karak governorate, located some 120 kilometers (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman.
All three suspects were wounded in the operation, but Jordanian security forces reported no casualties.

"The security services have fulfilled their duties, resulting in the capture of those who carried out this terrorist act," said Jordanian Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya in a phone interview with state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka on Monday.
"[The suspects] put up fierce resistance but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries."

He added that there were "three individuals involved" who were "identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident" and that the security services had "employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them."
Jordan's King Abdullah called for 'iron first' response
King Abdullah II of Jordan had ordered authorities to respond with an "iron fist" against anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.

"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," he added in a statement on Monday, following the arrests, which relatives of the victims had said brought some relief.

"Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief — and the grief of the Jordanian people — not just for us, the families of the martyrs," one relative, himself a survivor of the attack, told Al-Mamlaka.

blocks.caption: King Abdullah II (center) visited victims in hospital and called for Jordanian security forces to respond with an "iron fist."Image: Royal Court of Jordan/Handout/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: Who carried out the attack in Jordan?

There has been no claim of responsibility for Friday's deadly attack and Jordan's Public Security Directorate has not named the suspects or publicly ​identified possible affiliations with any Islamist militant groups.

Attacks on Christian minorities are very rare in Jordan, a relatively stable Middle Eastern state which is a close ally of the United States and which maintains diplomatic and military relations with neighboring Israel.

articles.title: Jordan attacks militants in Syria in retaliation for last week’s church attack
articles.summary:
Jordanian air force says it carried out strikes against ‘terrorist groups’ tied to killing of nine in Karak

Jordan has carried out airstrikes against armed groups in Syria in retaliation for…

blocks.text: Jordan has carried out airstrikes against armed groups in Syria in retaliation for Friday’s attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the southern Jordanian city of Karak that killed nine people, the Jordanian air force has said in a statement.

It said the operation “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”. It did not specify who the groups were or the precise location of the strikes.

Syrian state media reported that civilians had been killed in the strikes. The director of health in the southern province of Daraa, where the strikes took place, told the Syrian national news agency, Sana, that at least five civilians had been killed, including women and children and a 65-year-old man.

Jordan’s armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus, but Syria’s government gave a contradictory account, saying it had launched an investigation into the ⁠Jordanian attacks, and stressed in a statement the importance of field and security coordination in border areas.

In the aftermath of the strikes, Syria said it had closed the ⁠Nassib border crossing with Jordan, suspending ⁠traffic in both directions. Nassib is Jordan’s only passenger and commercial border crossing with Syria.

Earlier on Monday, Jordanian authorities arrested three men for last week’s attack, which also wounded more than two dozen people. The arrests followed a dawn shootout, and all three men were wounded, officials said.
The attack struck the Greek Orthodox church during a funeral in Karak, about 55 miles (90km) south of the capital, Amman, on Friday. Karak is home to a minority Christian population.
The attack shocked the nation, and Jordan declared three days of mourning for the victims. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack; the attackers’ motive remained unknown.

Later on Monday, Jordan’s Public Security Directorate identified the three arrested men as brothers Hazzah Zaidan Mohammad and Mishal Zaidan Mohammad, and their brother-in-law Ahmad Sami Hussein. All three are Jordanian; they were taken into custody in Karak, south of Amman.
The agency’s chief described the gunmen as “takfiri”, a term used for Sunni militants, but said they were not tied to any organised group.

“They only represent themselves,” Maj Gen Obaidallah Abd Rabbo Al-Maayta told a news conference. He also said a large cache of munitions was found in the abandoned house where Jordanian forces apprehended the men.
Jordan’s interior minister, Mazen al-Faraya, said the attack by the three men was the result of “a terroristic, extremist way of thinking”.
“If this way of thinking is not resolved, we will see incidents like this again,” he told reporters.
Jordan’s King Abdullah II had ordered authorities to respond with “an iron fist” against what he called the outlaws of Islam and anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.
“We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he said in a statement on Monday.
Relatives of the victims said the arrests brought them some relief.

“Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief, and the grief of the Jordanian people – not just for us, the families of the martyrs,” Khaled al-Borqan, himself a survivor of the attack and a relative of three of the people killed, told Al-Mamlaka.
“Despite the sadness and pain, the news brought us joy,” Fares Halaseh, an uncle of one of the victims and a survivor of the attack, told the TV station.
But the pain remains, he added. “We will not forget this agony for years to come.”

articles.title: The U.S. put surveillance drones in the Great Lakes, and this border town mayor isn't happy
articles.summary: When Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley first spotted an unusual, unmanned vessel in the St. Clair River, he says he thought it looked "like something from Mars." Then he found out it was one of…

image.caption: Sarnia Mayor Mike Bradley says he was not informed about plans for the U.S. Coast Guard to put drones on the Great Lakes. (CBC News)

blocks.text: As It Happens

When Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley first spotted an unusual, unmanned vessel in the St. Clair River, he says he thought it looked "like something from Mars." Then he found out it was one of several surveillance sail drones deployed to the Great Lakes this summer by the U.S. Coast Guard.
'We have thousands of boaters,' says Sarnia, Ont., mayor. 'They're going to be photographed and watched'
When Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley first spotted an unusual, unmanned vessel in the St. Clair River, he says he thought it looked "like something from Mars."

Then he found out it was one of several surveillance sail drones deployed to the Great Lakes this summer by the U.S. Coast Guard to "gather critical weather data for emergency response planning, track illicit activity and keep maritime borders safe."
The U.S. Coast Guard, which operates under the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, told CBC in June the vessels aren't there to surveil Canadians. But Bradley isn't convinced.
"We have thousands of boaters on the river St. Clair, Lake Huron, Lake Erie, and now they're going to be photographed and watched," he told As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.

"Even though they're saying right now it's benign, I don't have the trust down the road, especially with the rapidly deteriorating relationship with the U.S., that they won't use it for other purposes."
CBC has reached out to the U.S. and Canadian Coast Guards for comment. Both said they could not respond by deadline.
LISTEN | Interview with Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley :
As It Happens7:00Sarnia, Ont., mayor speaks out against U.S. surveillance drones in the Great Lakes
The vessels are called Voyager unmanned surface vehicles, and each one is affixed with 360-degree high-resolution cameras, advanced radar, and automatic identification systems.
They are owned and operated by Saildrone, a private U.S. company whose $15.5-million US contract with the Coast Guard is funded by U.S. President Donald Trump's "One Big, Beautiful Bill."

“This Voyager fleet will help the Coast Guard maintain persistent, scalable maritime domain awareness across these expansive waters, identifying threats in real time and enabling focused, high-impact interdiction," Saildrone president John Mustin said in a press release.
The U.S. Coast Guard now has two sail drones on Lake Erie as a part of a new program that launched in May. (U.S. Coast Guard)
York University researcher Petra Molnar says Canadians should be concerned that this data is being collected by a private company and sold to the U.S. government.

“This is a very troubling arrangement from a privacy and accountability standpoint," Molnar, the author of The Walls Have Eyes: Surviving Migration in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, told the Guardian newspaper.

"We have very little public information about data retention, who can access what data is collected, or how people using the region recreationally [can] be swept up in a data system built for border enforcement.”
Saildrone did not respond to requests for comment from CBC.

items: On America's northern border, the threats are not unidirectional
U.S. claims about higher drug trafficking from Canada don't match the data: fentanyl czar

blocks.text: The U.S. Coast Guard has said drones are nothing for Canadians to worry about.

"They're just out there for awareness," Lt. Junior Grade Samuel Rodriguez Garcia told CBC Windsor in June, when the vessels were deployed in Lake Erie. "Think of them as mobile cameras that kind of help us gain a better insight into what's going on live on scene."
He said the vessels' cameras are monitored 24/7 by U.S. Coast Guard staff, who can also manually move the drones when necessary. But the footage isn't recorded, officials say.
U.S. and Canadian agencies, including law enforcement, could have access to the drone technology after going through the proper channels, he said.
The Canadian Coast Guard told CBC Windsor it works closely with its U.S. counterpart, but has no involvement with the drone sail program.
Mayor says he was left in the dark
The U.S. Coast Guard first announced the Voyager project in May in a press release issued by the U.S. Department of War.
But Bradley says this is the first he's heard of it.
In fact, he says he only learned what the vessel in the St. Clair River was when he was contracted by the Detroit News, which has been reporting on the drones.
As mayor of the largest city on Lake Huron, he says being kept in the dark is unacceptable.
"If the Canadian government knew and agreed to it, that, to me, is a big issue," he said. "They should have let Canadian cities, Canadian mayors, know that this was happening."
CBC reached out to Public Safety Canada for information about the drones, and was redirected to the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA).
The CBSA did not respond to questions about Bradley's concerns, saying the RCMP is responsible for "enforcing Canadian legislation between ports of entry, including on the water."
The U.S. Coast Guard sail drones will be deployed in Lake Erie and be pulled from the water once ice forms. (U.S. Coast Guard)
Bradley says it's no coincidence the project comes during a period of heightened tension between Canada and the U.S.
With both countries locked in an impasse in the trade war, Trump and other Republicans have repeatedly framed the Canadian border as a dangerous security threat.
However, the numbers tell a different story. A U.S. Border Patrol officials told Congress in June that drug seizures and arrests of undocumented immigrants are both down along the U.S-Canada border.

items: Detroit tourism bureau halts advertising in Canada amid trade war, hopes Canadians won't 'hold grudge'
Searches of cellphones, laptops by U.S. customs up more than 32% so far this year

blocks.text: Bradley called the drones "an answer to a problem that doesn't really exist." He called on the Canadian government to "show some backbone" and push back.
"The Elbows Up movement seems to have died away, and I was a big supporter of that because I know the American psyche so well from 40 years of dealing with them," he said.
"If you don't stand up or push back they will just walk all over you."
Interview with Mike Bradley produced by Chris Trowbridge

articles.title: British politicians among international delegates barred from entering West Bank
articles.summary:
Group was on visit to meet Palestinian children, farmers and civil leaders facing escalating violence from Israeli forces

An international delegation including British politicians has been…

blocks.text: An international delegation including British politicians has been barred from entering the West Bank on a trip to meet Palestinian children, farmers and society leaders facing escalating violence from Israeli forces during olive harvest season.

The delegation of 23 people, including four elected representatives, was drawn from countries including France, Spain, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Greece, Holland, Ireland and the US. It included the Labour MP Clive Lewis, the Scottish National party MP Lara Bird, the Scottish Greens MSP Kate Nevens and the former Labour MP Sam Tarry.

Lewis told the Guardian: “We were detained, taken aside and then interrogated. I use the word interrogated because people were shouted at. We were asked why we were going in, what was happening, why our stories were one way or the other. The bottom line was it was a deeply unpleasant experience.”

The delegates were set to participate in Progressive International’s Second Ramallah Congress, a gathering to oppose Israeli occupation in Palestine. The congress was organised by Progressive International in partnership with Birzeit University and includes a programme of meetings with Palestinian academics, students and civil society organisations.

blocks.caption: Clive Lewis (left) and Sam Tarry were both denied entry to the West Bank at the border crossing checkpoint. Photograph: Global Justice Now

blocks.text: Tarry told the Guardian that he thought the delegation had a “genuine chance of going across” into the West Bank but they were detained at the Allenby/King Hussein Bridge by Israeli forces in Jordan for nine hours. “They made a political decision very clearly based on the fact they didn’t want people to witness what’s been going on in the West Bank, especially ahead of the elections,” he added.

The exclusions occurred amid attacks by Israeli forces on Palestinian olive farmers and foreign press and activists in the region. International travel to parts of the West Bank is permitted but subject to military checkpoints. Earlier this month, Israeli media reported that the defence minister, Israel Katz, had instructed officials to pursue exclusion orders against activists travelling to Palestinian olive-harvesting areas.

In the first two weeks of October, the UN aid coordination office recorded at least 160 Israeli settler attacks linked to the olive harvest, often under the protection or with the participation of Israeli forces.

Israeli forces attacked European diplomats and a French mayor accompanying Palestinian farmers, while about 80 olive-harvest volunteers, including US congressional candidate Brad Lander, were also recently detained.
Bird said in a statement: “I came to stand alongside Palestinians being attacked for harvesting olives on their own land. Instead, we were turned away at the border with no reason given.

“It is more important now than ever that we bear witness and show our solidarity. But we were prevented from doing so. If Israel has nothing to hide, why is it so determined to stop us seeing what is happening in the occupied West Bank?”

Laila Hazaineh, a political coordinator for Progressive International, said in a statement: “Despite escalating violence, our delegation remained determined to cross to Palestine to participate in the olive harvest, and actively engage with Palestinian communities and institutions. Every refusal of entry will only strengthen this determination.”
The embassy of Israel has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: 'Maxxing' selected as Dictionary.com word of the year
articles.summary: "Whatever we're doing, we want to push it further," said an expert on why Americans are embracing the term, which is short for maximising.

blocks.text: Americans have gone all in on "maxxing", making it the 2026 Word of the Year for Dictionary.com.

Short for maximising, the term "can be used on its own or added to the end of any word to convey you're doing something to the fullest or optimizing it as much as possible", Dictionary.com said in a statement.
It's a major departure from two years ago, when the site, after analysing US social media trends, news stories, and search data, chose demure as word of the year. Last year's was "67".
"Maxxing is the linguistic manifestation of a culture increasingly preoccupied with getting the most out of everything," said Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for the Dictionary Media Group.

Digital media used "maxxing" nearly 19 times more in August 2026 compared to the 2025 monthly average, Dictionary.com found. The site also considered affordability, data centre, odyssey, and the shortened form of uncle, "unc", as potential words of the year.
On social media, many people in Generation Z and younger - those under 30 - post extensively about their maxxing efforts to achieve all sorts of perfection.
Influencers focused on fitness and wellness post about "proteinmaxxing" and "fibermaxxing". Those giving their full attention to improving sleep habits say they are "sleepmaxxing".

The influencer Clavicular has gained thousands of followers as he chronicles his extreme "looksmaxxing" - working to meet a set of prescribed criteria for attractiveness, with particular importance given to jawlines, eyes and physique.

"Whatever we're doing, we want to push it further," Johnson said. "But its expanding uses also reveal how people are responding to that impulse. Some embrace it. Some exaggerate it for laughs. Others subvert it entirely to describe stepping back from the relentless pursuit of more."
People were playing with the term - and idea - for decades before Clavicular started posting videos.
In the opening song for the 1990s television show The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, for example, Will Smith raps: "Chillin' out, maxin', relaxin' all cool."
"Unfortunately, by the time the dictionary gets a hold of it, that probably means that it's reached critical mass," says teacher Lauren Cella.
Cella, a content creator known for her viral Gen Z history lessons, says she and her students have been using "maxxing" for some time as a suffix.
"They're actually, in their own way, reinventing grammar, which I think is super cool," she says.
Maxxing gives the students permission to "optimise to meet a goal" or do something others might think of as "cringe", and allows them to own it, she says.
"It's a fun, harmless way that kids are expressing themselves and sharing different goals that they have," she says.

Linguist Vanessa Croft, who teaches English, says the internet and digital media make language move at "warp speed", even faster than radio, film or television ever did. As swiftly as new terms are added to the lexicon, they can just as quickly fall out of favour.
"By the time millennials and Gen X or Gen Y start using the terms, Gen Z and Gen Alpha aren't using those terms anymore," she says.
While she and her secondary-school aged students are still "maxxing" too, they are now using it "almost ironically", she says.

articles.title: UN sounds the alarm over Israel's West Bank military operation
articles.summary: The UN has sounded the alarm on Israeli action in the West Bank city of Hebron after hundreds of families were displaced at the weekend. Israel has ordered the military to demolish homes after…

image.caption: The Israeli military demolished homes in Hebron after a deadly attack there killed two Israeli soldiers [FILE: October 23, 2026]Image: Ammar Awad/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Israeli military operation in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron was met with sharp criticism from the head of the UN as well as the UN's human rights commissioner in comments made on Monday.

The criticism comes after an Israeli military operation was launched in the occupied West Bank in response to a shootout on Friday that left two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinian gunmen dead. Three more Israeli soldiers were also injured.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the military to demolish buildings in the West Bank city of Hebron and to close off the West Bank. It came just days before Israel's general election on Tuesday.
What did the UN say about Israeli operation in the West Bank?
The United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres said on Monday that "settlements are expanding, evictions are unrelenting with Palestinians driven from their lands," in a post on X.
"We are seeing an increasingly coercive environment, with the spectre of ethnic cleaning looming ever larger," he wrote.

The UN Human Rights High Commissioner Volker Türk also issued a statement condemning Israeli actions, saying the "aggressive operation" has resulted in the forcible displacement of thousands of Palestinians, "demolished homes and commercial property, and deprived residents of the ability to move freely."
"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law. Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing," he said.
Israeli army demolishes Palestinian buildings in Hebron
A UN report, also released on Monday, that accuses Israel of committing war crimes in the West Bank, was rejected by the Israeli Foreign Ministry as "propaganda."

The ministry said that the findings were "not a human rights report but a propaganda document detached from reality, aimed at undermining Israel's right to self-defense, delegitimizing the Jewish state, and legitimizing jihadist terrorism against its citizens."
What is the Israeli operation in the West Bank?
Israeli troops entered the Deir Baha neighborhood, where the assailants lived, and ordered residents to pack up and leave.
The Hebron municipality said that more than 3,000 people, including 200 babies, were ordered to leave.

The Israeli military said at the weekend that its troops were carrying out precise, targeted and thorough searches to "locate and dismantle terrorist infrastructure and locate weapons, alongside questioning suspects" in Hebron.
The military said the operation was expected to continue "for several days" and would focus on Deir Baha.
The largescale response to the firefight in the West Bank comes in the run-up to elections in Israel on Tuesday that could bring an end to Netanyahu's premiership.
Netanyahu has frequently painted himself as the only person who can keep Israel safe but his opponents have accused him of lacking a plan.
Ehud Olmert: 'Likely Netanyahu will not be reelected'

articles.title: Protest leaders urge French pupils to keep barricading their schools
articles.summary:
Activists say struggle must go on until their ‘maximum’ demands are met over teacher shortages and building repairs

French children should continue to barricade their schools and take part…

blocks.text: French children should continue to barricade their schools and take part in street protests, a student union said on Monday after the government announced a package of education measures to try to stem the crisis.

“Today we’re at the negotiating table, we’re able to negotiate with the government,” Pierre Sourzat of Les Lycéens told France Info television. “We’re in a power struggle and we still need to call for continued mobilisation to meet a maximum of our demands.”
The government told high school student representatives it would cap some class sizes and review the university application system. But Sourzat said: “We want measures, not half measures.”

More than five weeks after the start of high school blockades in September, the government made the proposals to address the demands of what has become the biggest youth protest movement in years. It has been joined by trade unions and cost-of-living protesters in regular mass street demonstrations on Saturdays.

High school pupils had demanded an end to teacher and staff shortages and for repairs to decrepit school buildings that had collapsing ceilings, mould, broken toilets, a lack of chairs and windows that did not shut.
The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said some schools were so dilapidated they were “not fit” for teaching. He announced a government loan of €4bn to regional authorities to begin repairs.

blocks.caption: Emmanuel Macron, kneeling centre, meets police officers in Marseille. He told them the authorities had ‘to hold the line’. Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/EPA

blocks.text: Responding to complaints of overcrowded classes, Geffray said class sizes for 15-year-olds in the first year of high school would be capped at 28 in the 50% of schools in the lowest-income areas, increasing to all high schools next year. He said more teaching posts would be created and there would be a review of the French baccalaureate system.

The university application platform, Parcoursup, which has been described as opaque and unfair, will be changed in 2027 and replaced by a new system in 2028, according to the government. Parliament will hold a debate on the issue on Wednesday.
The higher education minister, Philippe Baptiste, said 15,000 extra student places would be created in higher education, focusing on vocational courses.

Louis Letoublon, who attended a meeting with the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, on behalf of Les Lycéens, said: “Bravo to the high school students who have demonstrated. We’ve got something: the government is afraid and knows it must do something and listen to us. “Not all our demands were ⁠met. We’ll go on for as long as it takes.”
Baptiste said the government’s door was “open” for more discussions.
Several children have been maimed or seriously injured in the protests, allegedly by police explosive weapons. Hundreds of children have been arrested and held in police custody.
after newsletter promotion

The authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrations after France saw its worst day of violence in years on 17 October, with looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings. Curfews have been put in place in certain cities, alongside protest bans. Protest routes were pushed to the outskirts of cities on Saturday when demonstrations passed off largely peacefully.

The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said there had been a new phenomenon in cities such as Nice and Montpellier at the weekend with ultra-right groups arriving in “organised formations” and targeting protesters. Eleven suspects are to face charges.
In a visit to Marseille on Monday, Emmanuel Macron said nationwide street protests were likely continue, and that the next day of street demonstrations on 31 October would also be a “day of risk”.

The French president said the looting and vandalism seen on 17 October should never happen again. Speaking to members of the police, he said it was “not normal” for the country to be in “such a state of turmoil” six months before a presidential election.
Macron steps down next spring and the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading the polls.

Macron said: “We will continue to hold the line. If we all do our jobs well, this movement will subside – because we will address legitimate expectations, and because order will be maintained. But nothing is a foregone conclusion.”
Authorities have admitted to security and intelligence failures that paved the way for the clashes on 17 October.

articles.title: A bad omen? Syria bans women from university courses
articles.summary: The recent announcement that Syrian tertiary institutes will not allow women into some courses has triggered debate. Critics worry it may be a sign that the new Syrian government is restricting…

image.caption: When Syria's dictator was ousted in late 2024, Syrian women celebrated — but many wondered how the new government, with conservative religious roots, would see women's rightsImage: Aaref Watad/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Recent changes to university admissions rules in Syria have put a dent in Lin Najab's plans. The 23-year-old from Damascus is one of the few women at her college studying mechatronics engineering.

"My original plan was to pursue a master's degree," Najab told DW. But earlier in October, new rules were announced by Syria's education ministry regarding two newly created colleges, the National University of Defense Sciences and the Syrian University for Security Sciences. The former now restricts certain courses exclusively to male students, and the latter almost all of them.
These new policies could derail Najab's plans. "Now I have to start thinking about other options," she explained. "For example, I might have to move to another province to study."
It is still possible for Syrian women to study the subjects offered by the two new security institutes, but only at other more generalist universities or colleges.

Moving to another province, away from family, brings other difficulties, Najab continued. Student accommodation in dormitories is uncomfortable, but a woman living alone is still frowned upon by conservative Syrians.

"Even if a girl decides she won't give up and wants to go study outside her province, her parents will be opposed to the idea, either for security reasons or because we simply don't want our daughters to go study somewhere else," said Najab.

blocks.caption: Females only make up just over 10% of Syria's members of parliament — 22 out of 210 politicians — despite the country's target of 20%Image: LOUAI BESHARA/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Controversial ban
The decision to ban women from courses at the new defense and security-related colleges has caused controversy both inside and outside the country.

"Gender doesn't define ability. It should be about high academic standards, the ones I'm trying to meet," Najab argued. "In Syria, we need better education and good graduates, so let's see where the best people are, regardless of gender."

Fatoun Kharbatli, an activist from Aleppo, is also opposed to the idea of limiting certain subjects to one gender. "A person should choose the field in which they see their abilities as lying," she told DW. "We were oppressed for 60 years, so now let's be a nation that keeps pace with global civilization, but without straying from respect and from the basics of our religion.
Qamar al-Yaser, a mother of three in rural Damascus, believes the ban is justified.

The sectors from which women have been excluded "require a strong physique, they need big efforts, travel, organization out in the field and may require staying overnight at remote work sites," said al-Yaser. "These conditions suit young men more than women."

A closer look at some of new admission rules indicate they may be less about restricting Syrian women from certain studies and more about keeping them out of the army. For example, attending the National University of Defense Sciences requires that students serve in the Syrian military. Graduates of the University for Security Sciences must also commit to serving up to 20 years with the internal security forces.

blocks.caption: Syria's military leadership has already rejected the integration of Syrian Kurdish female fighters into the Syrian national militaryImage: Sebastian Backhaus/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Bad omen?
Does this mean Syria's new government is heading in an increasingly restrictive direction when it comes to women's rights?

Human Rights Watch believes so. A few days after the admissions announcement, the organization released a statement criticizing it. "The discriminatory rules clearly violate Syria's international legal obligations and are part of a concerning pattern of actions by the transitional authorities that restrict women's role in state institutions and reinforce gender stereotypes," the organization said.

Besides the military college bans, there were also other, possibly even more disturbing aspects to the new admissions rules. Restrictions on female students were also applied at a railways institute in Aleppo, oil and gas training organizations in Rmeilan, Homs, Deir el-Zour and Baniyas, and a radio and television course in Idlib. Elsewhere men were barred from kindergarten and nursing school training and midwifery courses. These were to be women-only.

blocks.caption: The National Defense Sciences University in Damascus was only founded in mid-2026Image: Rami Alsayed/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: All these come on top of a number of other concerning restrictions and worrying comments by officials. The most recent incident in the education sector involved the government's alteration of school textbooks for the 2026-2027 academic year.

The education ministry had already announced it would be removing images and symbols associated with the previous authoritarian regime headed by dictator Bashar Assad. But this week journalists also noticed other changes: Pictures of females in the textbooks who had uncovered hair had been removed, or altered so they were now wearing headscarves. A bare-chested statue pictured in one textbook was now wearing a vest. A picture of men dancing was also gone.
Common attitudes towards female soldiers

Officials have said that some of the gender-exclusionary rules implemented at the new security institutes were actually carried over from the Assad-era colleges that were fused together to create them earlier this year.

Opposition to female soldiers and military leaders isn't an uncommon attitude in the Middle East's more conservative circles either. Although many Arab countries allow women to attend military colleges and serve, females are often restricted to non-combat or symbolic roles, a 2024 study by the Washington-based think tank, the Middle East Institute, or MEI, reported.

In Syria, while women have historically participated in the security services, it was "in a limited and largely symbolic capacity," the Syrian Center for Defense and Security Studies confirmed in a policy paper this year.
But just because an idea is widespread obviously doesn't make it right, human rights advocates have said.

blocks.caption: Even in Germany, women were not allowed to serve in the military until a 2001 landmark court case forced a change Image: Juliane Sonntag/photothek.de/picture alliance

blocks.text: Gender stereotypes

"Gender diversity in the security sector allows all citizens of a country to be perceived as equal in all aspects of their duties and obligations to the nation state, including defending it," Dina Arakji, author of the MEI study, argued. "Allowing women to join the military … can advance a society's perspective on females in nontraditional gender-based roles."

The admissions ban gives young Syrian women a message about what they can and cannot do, Syrian activist Rana al-Ash argued in a commentary about the ban for Paris-based organization, the Syrian Women's Political Movement.

"When these messages are reflected in admission requirements, confronting familial and societal expectations becomes even more difficult because the educational institution endorses them," al-Ash argued.
For Nadra Bunni, a Syrian analyst at the Middle East Institute Switzerland, it's still unclear as to whether "gender-based restrictions will become a feature of the new Syria."

But the anger over the admissions ban also raises another important question, she noted. "Will Syria's new authorities institutionalize an expectation that government decisions can be questioned and potentially reversed," she asked in a commentary for the online publication, Syria In Transition. "Or [will they] teach citizens that their voices carry little consequence?"
Women push for political power and equality in new Syria

articles.title: First Nations-first ministers' meeting brings funding announcements and mixed reviews

image.caption: Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson, Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak and Prime Minister Mark Carney are seen at the first Indigenous-focused first ministers' meeting in 21 years. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Indigenous

Chiefs had mixed reactions after Prime Minister Mark Carney announced both financial and political commitments as the first Indigenous-focused first ministers' meeting in two decades concluded in Ottawa.
'History will judge us by what we change,' Carney was told as meeting began
The premiers said they were there to listen and the prime minister said he was there to act. But one chief said history will judge them by a different measure.

"History will not remember us for gathering in a room, taking photographs, making speeches," Chief Sheldon Sunshine of Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation in northern Alberta told Canada's premiers and prime minister on Monday morning.
He paused for dramatic effect before adding: "History will judge us by what we change."
And thus began the first Indigenous-focused first ministers' meeting in 21 years — and the first such meeting in 119 years to focus solely on First Nations issues.
The group convened not on opposing sides but in a circle behind closed doors in Ottawa at the John G. Diefenbaker Building on Sussex Drive, where there was no shortage of calls for change.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew surprised reporters by holding up his Indian status card as he called to abolish the Indian Act. Prairie chiefs joined former national chief Matthew Coon Come demanding Canada revisit the 1930 Natural Resource Transfer Acts that handed control over resource development from the federal to provincial governments.
Carney seeks to 'commit to action' at historic First Nations-first ministers' meeting

"If this first ministers' meeting succeeds, it must come up with strong, concrete measures for next steps. If they don't do that, then this is another meeting of just talks," Coon Come told reporters.

Chiefs from Ontario called for constitutional amendments that would recognize First Nations as distinct orders of government. Grassroots activists protested outside, while inside Assembly of First Nations (AFN) leaders and Canada's first ministers debated the country's future.

As the meeting wrapped, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced both financial and political commitments. He said he shares Kinew's view that the time has come to reform or even abolish the Indian Act and would direct his ministers to work with First Nations on a path forward.
Carney 'very open' to abolishing Indian Act

He said he will instruct his finance minister to work with First Nations to develop new revenue-sharing mechanisms, including a potential sovereign wealth fund, which the AFN sought in one of its position papers circulated ahead of the meeting.

Carney also announced some proposed new spending, likely foreshadowing the Nov. 5 federal budget. This includes more than $2.5 billion over five years for emergency preparedness in First Nations communities across the country, and more than $630 million over four years for First Nations and Inuit policing.

In televised opening remarks earlier, Carney called it "sobering" that two decades have elapsed since the last such meeting, held when Paul Martin was prime minister in 2005. That meeting in Kelowna, B.C., yielded an agreement dubbed the Kelowna Accord.

items: First Nations want tangible results as 'historic' first ministers' meeting opens

blocks.text: "This is an important opportunity, yes, to share perspectives, to listen, to learn, but above all to commit to action," Carney said.

But the meeting unfolded under a cloud of skepticism, the absence of three premiers and concerns from some chiefs that the Carney government is using the meeting as political cover for its streamlining of major infrastructure projects.
The day included a blunt address from the Algonquin Nation on whose unsurrendered land Parliament Hill now sits.
"Our nation is still waiting for justice," Verna Polson, grand chief of the Algonquin Anishinabeg Nation Tribal Council, told the group.
In her opening remarks, AFN National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said nation-building "can't just be about ramming through major projects" as fast as possible.

"The national interests must also include the proposals, law and policy reforms that First Nations seek," she said. "We have been persistent and patient, but we cannot afford to wait many, many years for results and implementation."
'Our rights must be taken seriously': AFN national chief
Around 40 people gathered outside to protest AFN participating at all because it's a federally funded national advocacy body elected by chiefs and not rights-holding grassroots people.
Russ Diabo, spokesperson for the Truth Before Reconciliation Network, told CBC News the Carney government is on the wrong track.

"What [Carney] should be doing is changing the way he's interacting with First Nations and Canada and not using these administrative bodies that he controls like the Assembly First Nations," Diabo said.
Reviews were mixed coming out of the meeting.

Cody Diabo, grand chief of the Mohawk Council of Kahnawà:ke, left early, denouncing the meeting as all about "butterflies and rainbows" and not dealing with big-picture substantive issues. Hereditary Chief Na'Moks of the Wet'suwet'en Nation in B.C. felt the meeting was about finding "cheerleaders" for the federal agenda.

Others were more optimistic. Abram Benedict, AFN's Ontario regional chief, said he felt good about the investments and potential creation of a wealth fund, but there was no firm pledge to hold these meetings annually, as the AFN requested.
"There seems to be a willingness, but there was no commitment," Benedict said.
Carney said the right timeline for the next meeting is probably two years. Woodhouse Nepinak told reporters she was happy with the day and the tangible commitments secured.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Brett Forester is a senior reporter with CBC Indigenous in Ottawa. He is a member of the Chippewas of Kettle and Stony Point First Nation in southern Ontario who previously worked as a journalist with the Aboriginal Peoples Television Network.
With files from Radio-Canada's Dominique Degré

articles.title: This 3-year-old scored 10 goals. Then police showed up at his soccer game
articles.summary: The parents of a 3-year-old soccer player in Florida say the police were called to a game this weekend because their son was dominating the ball. Police have confirmed with CBC News they were called…

image.caption: A 2023 file photo of a soccer camp in PEI. Police were called to a child's soccer game Saturday in Winter Park, Fla., over complaints of an 'unruly parent.' (Jane Robertson/CBC)

blocks.text: World

The parents of a 3-year-old soccer player in Florida say the police were called to a game this weekend because their son was dominating the ball. Police have confirmed with CBC News they were called to the game over reports of an "unruly parent."
The child, Nevada, is 'traumatized,' says his mother
In the viral video posted by his parents, a three-year-old central Florida boy dribbles the ball up the field, dodging the other pint-sized players and kicks it into the net as his parents cheer.
Then the boy, named Nevada, does it again. And again. And again.

Later in the same video, which has been viewed more than one million times on TikTok since it was posted Sunday, Nevada stands on the sidelines as his father says, "they called the police on a three-year-old because he was too good."
"Because he had the ball for too long, and nobody else could get the ball, so they called the police."

The reaction online was swift, with people equally enraged over the allegations and admiration for the preschooler's skills. In the TikTok comments, some called on the parents to sue, others alleged that calling the police was racist, and many commented on the "heartbreak" in the little boy's face when the police show up.
"I'm LIVID," children's entertainer and vocal children's rights advocate Ms. Rachel posted on Instagram Monday morning, calling on soccer stars and other athletes to support the child and his family.
"This is racist, sick, traumatizing and disgusting," she added.
Former NFL quarterback Robert Griffin III called the incident "crazy," writing on X that "punishing a 3 year old child for being too good at a sport is RIDICULOUS."

CBC News has reached out to Nevada's parents but has not yet heard back. The family already had a sizeable social media following on TikTok and Instagram, where they've documented Nevada's soccer skills over the years.

The Winter Park Police Department confirmed to CBC News Monday that officers were called to a children's soccer game Saturday after a league official "requested response to a disturbance between league officials and the parents of a player."
A screen shot of a post on Threads by children's entertainer Ms. Rachel on Monday. (@msrachelforlittles/Threads)
So, what actually happened?
The official called 911 at 9:53 a.m., according to the police incident report viewed by CBC News.
In a recording of the call provided by police, the official can be heard saying he has "an unruly parent here, calling me names and having me on Instagram."
He says the parent is being "really disruptive, like following me around and calling me names. I want her to be gone."
He describes her as a Black woman wearing pink.

items: Eastern Shore parent handed ban for harassing young minor hockey referee
Parent charged for threatening player during youth soccer game in Vaughan, police say

blocks.text: The incident report says the official told police the parents were upset about their son's playing time, while the parents said their child "was being scorned for playing too well and was being taken out of [the] game."

The Winter Park Police Department said the league had asked the family to leave and offered to refund its fees. When police arrived, the official asked officers to communicate that to the family, the department said.
A screen grab of an Instagram post by illustrator and activist Nikkolas Smith, in support of 3-year-old soccer player Nevada, posted on Monday. (@nikkolas_smith/Instagram)
"The family stated the game was over and they were leaving," the police statement says, adding that the family was co-operative and no one was arrested, trespassed or forced to leave the park.
The video posted by Nevada's parents shows a Black woman wearing pink speaking with two police officers. One tells her the league office should be reaching out soon about a refund.

In a separate video, the parents claim the soccer officials repeatedly pulled Nevada from the 30-minute game after he scored and that, as a result, he played only about 12 minutes — but still scored 10 goals.
Boy is 'traumatized,' says mother
The soccer league, i9 Sports Maitland/Winter Park, told CBC News in a statement Monday that it was aware of concerns about "an incident at a local i9 Sports program" and takes them very seriously.
"We have reached out to the family and have begun a review that includes speaking with those involved," the league said.

In an interview with The Breakfast Club, Nevada's mother, identified as Martasia Griffin, said Nevada has been targeted all season because of his talent and that, at this particular game, some parents complained that no one else could get the ball.

items: Canadian athletes detail experiences with racism in sports
UN human rights office slams racist abuse of Coco Gauff, calls for solidarity to help fight it

blocks.text: She said the league director agreed it was unfair to other children and offered Griffin a refund.
"I cannot explain to my three year old son that he cannot play today because he's so good. I continued to let him play until the police walked in," Griffin said.
Nevada, she told HuffPost in another interview Monday, is "traumatized."
An Instagram post by former U.S. soccer player Eddie Johnson in which he supports 3-year-old Nevada. (Eddie_Johnson7/Instagram)
"He still wants to play soccer. He just doesn’t want to go back to that place. I don’t think that’s how he should be thinking, that as a 3-year-old he did something wrong."

Former U.S. professional soccer player Eddie Johnson posted about Nevada several times on social media Sunday and Monday, saying the boy would be joining his soccer program and criticizing how he was treated at the game.
"They wanna dim his light," Johnson posted to his Instagram stories.
"They thought they were taking your dreams away, but in reality (made) you the most famous three-year-old in the world right now."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Trump administration illegally fired James Comey's daughter, judge rules
articles.summary: Maurene Comey believes she was let go from her job as a federal prosecutor because her father is the former FBI director.

blocks.text: The US justice department illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) director James Comey, a federal judge has ruled.

Comey, who lost her job as a federal prosecutor in New York in July 2025, sued the government, arguing she was unlawfully fired because of her father, a critic of US President Donald Trump, and because of her perceived political affiliations.
Judge Jesse Furman ruled on Monday that the Trump administration must reinstate her and that she must be given back pay.
A spokesperson for the justice department said in a statement that it disagreed with the decision and "will appeal in due course".
In his ruling, Judge Furman said Comey's dismissal violated the US Constitution as well as her right to a fair legal process.
He said the US attorney general can fire federal prosecutors but only "in a particular manner and only for certain reasons".
Furman noted that in Comey's role, "she was assigned some of the country's highest profile cases and consistently received the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike".

Comey has worked on cases against the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, and hip-hop mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs, who was convicted on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends last year.
Furman ordered that Comey be given back pay from July until December 2025, when she accepted a new job.
In a statement, Comey's lawyers said: "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law."
Comey had previously said the only reason she was told about her firing was that it "came from Washington".

A complaint filed by her lawyers in September 2025 stated that they believed Comey had been fired "solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both".
The justice department said in court filings that the decision was made by former Attorney General Pam Bondi.

The Trump administration has twice brought charges against James Comey, including for allegedly lying to Congress, but that case was dismissed by a judge who said the prosecutor who brought the case was unlawfully appointed.
Earlier this year, the justice department charged Comey with knowingly and wilfully making a threat to take the life of, and to inflict bodily harm, on the president. He has denied any wrongdoing.
The case stems from a 2025 Instagram post shared by Comey that contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47".
"Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump.

articles.title: Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election
articles.summary:
Israeli prime minister increases alarmist rhetoric as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in polls

Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put…
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison and Julian Borger in Jerusalem

blocks.text: Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.
The Israeli prime minister posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation.

“Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in a social media post about Iran’s nuclear programme.

blocks.caption: An AI-generated image of a nuclear strike on Tel Aviv was posted on Netanyahu’s X account on Sunday.  Photograph: X/Benjamin Netanyahu

blocks.text: Israel’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration with Iran at a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran.
Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing.
Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran.
On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convince Donald Trump to launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February.
The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement on Monday that stopped well short of a denial of the press reports. It simply insisted that its decisions were based exclusively on “security, professional, objective and national considerations”.
Netanyahu’s warnings were a marked contrast with his triumphalism in the immediate wake of the wars on Iran that launched last year and this spring.

In March Netanyahu said Israeli and US strikes had destroyed Iran’s ability to enrich uranium and produce ballistic missiles, and in 2025 he claimed a “historic victory” over Iran that would stand for generations.

Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s most likely challenger for the prime minister’s job, expressed his confidence in Zamir. “We won’t allow the IDF to be turned into a pawn in Netanyahu’s survival campaign,” said Eisenkot, who is a retired general.

blocks.caption: Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, is the most likely challenger to Netanyahu as prime minister.  Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPA

blocks.text: Most polls suggest the mainly centre-right opposition bloc led by Eisenkot is poised to win more seats in Israel’s Knesset than the Netanyahu coalition, but neither would be able to muster the 61 seats necessary for a majority government.

The opposition would most likely be able to gather a majority and topple Netanyahu in coalition with parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, roughly a fifth of the population. But conservatives inside the Eisenkot bloc have ruled out such a coalition, raising the prospect of a minority government, another round of elections and a possible Netanyahu resurgence.

As the elections drew closer, Netanyahu framed the country’s choice as existential. He told Channel 14, which has acted as his lead cheerleader in the Israeli media: “There is a single fundamental issue here – our existence.”

He described the opposition bloc as the “left” in alliance with Palestinians, and enemies of the country. “We see what is happening in Europe. The alliance between the left and Islam might destroy the state of Israel,” he said.

The main opposition parties are rightwing or centre-right, sharing Netanyahu’s adamant opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, and who have largely supported the war in Gaza. Some opposition leaders have ruled out any kind of political alliance with Palestinian Israeli parties, who could emerge from the elections holding the balance of power in the Knesset. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote.

The opposition bloc is held together more by its shared antipathy to Netanyahu, who has dominated the Israeli political scene over the past three decades and veered increasingly towards authoritarianism, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary and turn the police and Shin Bet internal security service into political tools.
The prime minister is also in the midst of a trial on corruption charges, and his legal jeopardy could increase if he loses his grip on power.

blocks.caption: Benjamin Netanyahu has been emphasising in his campaign the support he has from Donald Trump. Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/AP

blocks.text: In the closing stages of the campaign, Netanyahu has also emphasised the overt support he enjoys from Donald Trump, who repeated his endorsement on Sunday in a social media post, saying “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!”

The Israeli outlet Walla News reported that this repeat endorsement was a result of relentless pressure from Netanyahu’s office. It is unclear, however, whether Trump’s support will carry any weight with the electorate. The US president’s earlier “total endorsement” on 18 October made no visible difference to the polls.

In one survey, 64% of Israelis questioned said it would not influence their vote, and 17% said it made them less likely to back Netanyahu, against 12% who said it had deepened their resolve to support Netanyahu’s Likud party.

In the closing stages of the closely fought campaign, Netanyahu has also forecast growing financial isolation, saying billions of dollars in annual military aid from the US would dry up soon, and drew a rare public rebuke from the central bank for a repeated claim that Israel could use cryptocurrencies to dodge escalating global sanctions.

“Cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means to circumvent sanctions,” the Bank of Israel said on Sunday evening. “The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.”

Netanyahu had already laid out a forecast for a bleak, isolated future a year ago, when he said Israel might need to become a militarised “super Sparta”, then rowed back again in the face of fierce criticism from a horrified Israeli public.

His return to this rhetoric and the tactics of fear, particularly after unexpected losses for far-right allies in Serbia and Brazil, raised questions about whether the ultimate political survivor may finally be on the ropes.

Few among his allies or enemies expected his government to survive long after 7 October, much less complete its term. But the majority of polls have been clear for more than two years that his current coalition looks set to lose its slim majority.

articles.title: Pope's South American trip to go ahead as planned after lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: The Pope underwent surgery in to remove a tumour on the lower part of his right lung and is gradually resuming his duties.

blocks.text: The Vatican has confirmed that Pope Leo will go on his South American tour as planned, following his surgery for lung cancer.
He was diagnosed with lung cancer and underwent successful surgery in Rome on 13 October to remove a tumour on the lower part of his right lung.
The 71-year-old is scheduled to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on 6-17 November, the Vatican said, adding that the he was looking forward to it "with great joy and enthusiasm".
The Pope will follow the same programme as planned, visiting 10 cities on the tour.
"I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I've experienced so many moments of my life," Pope Leo said.
The Pope's trip will begin in Uruguay on 8 November, where he will visit the capital Montevideo, as well as other key cities.
He will then travel to Argentina from November 11-17, visiting a number of places including the capital Buenos Aires.
After that he will spend six days in Peru, where roughly 76% of the population are Catholic, and will include stops in Lima, Chiclayo, Cuzco and Pucallpa.

Peru's Cardinal Castillo, the Archbishop of Lima, has said the trip would involve young people, women who help run community kitchens and members of the country's indigenous communities, according to Vatican News.
The archbishop highlighted the Pope's close ties with the people of Chiclayo, where he lived for several years. The Pope has Peruvian citizenship.
The Catholic Church sent him to Peru as a missionary in 1985, when he was 30 years old.
He joined the Augustinian mission in Chulucanas, in the Peruvian department of Piura, and the following year, joined the mission in the city of Trujillo.
For almost three decades, he worked between the US and Peru.
Leo announced the news of his lung operation himself to the world on 11 October during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.
He reassured pilgrims that the growth was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage" but that his doctors had advised him to have it removed.
The surgery lasted for 90 minutes, and he was discharged from Rome's Gemelli hospital on 17 October.
The Pope's surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said he was in an "absolutely satisfactory clinical condition", and said there were "no clinical reasons" why the trip should not go ahead.
Tests showed the cancer was "localised".

Since his operation, the pope has been resting and gradually resuming his work. He has been "adjusting his daily schedule in consultation with his doctors to prioritise his recovery while continuing to fulfill the responsibilities of his ministry," the Vatican said.
Leo was "deeply grateful for the prayers and affection he has received from throughout the world," the Vatican said.
The Vatican said Friday that Leo would cancel a planned trip to Assisi on October 27th, on the recommendation of his doctors.

articles.title: AI company Anthropic files its IPO in hopes of raising $100 billion
articles.summary: Anthropic has filed paperwork for an initial public offering that could be one of the biggest in history. The co-founders have outlined both the benefits and the risks of AI in their pitch to…

image.caption: Dario Amodei has addressed concerns about the development of the AI industryImage: Don Feria/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic on Monday filed paperwork to make its stock market debut in what analysts say could be one of the biggest in history.
The initial public offering (IPO) could happen as early as November, reports say, with analysts putting the company at a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.
What did the Anthropic founders say about the IPO?
The seven co-founders of the company, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, outlined their vision for the future of AI in a letter to potential investors.
"We believe AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," they said.

The AI startup behind Claude also addressed the societal risks of AI as they have done before, writing that the company's leadership might have to take unusual decisions to slow down the pace of development, even if that meant falling behind competitors.
The filing toward an IPO represents a major milestone for a company that was founded just five years ago.
Money raised at the IPO could provide the company with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion.
AI is much hyped, frequently feared, and possibly overrated
What do we know about Anthropic's IPO?
Anthropic is set to trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT."
But the company is yet to disclose how many shares it plans to sell and what price, leaving that space blank in its paperwork filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday.
Anthropic filed confidentially with the SEC in June and that gave the agency time to go over the company's financial credentials before they were made available to the public and potential investors.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters.
Anthropic debut follows SpaceX IPO
The San Francisco-based company was founded by members who defected from OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, in 2021.
OpenAI, Anthropic's main rival, is also set to debut on the stock market next year.
Both IPOs are taking place amid growing concern about AI and the race to develop AI infrastructure, including data centers that consume vast amounts of energy.
The document filed by Anthropic shows that the company has seen massive revenue growth but is yet to turn a profit, much like its AI rivals.
Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026. That compares to a loss of $13 billion in the same period a year earlier.
Despite the losses, the company said that it had $112.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents as of June 30.

And as for money raised at the IPO, the offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the current record set by Elon Musk's SpaceX that ultimately raised $86 billion in what was the biggest IPO on record to date.
